Recent research has successfully addressed some high-dimensional quantum chemistry calculations with a limited number of neurons. However, it is crucial to understand the reasons behind the improvement, as it will facilitate making more accurate predictions when evaluating new systems. Our investigation demonstrates that a low-to-high arrangement of neuron weights, a characteristic of shallow networks, enables the separation of local and non-local parts in low-frequency basis. Furthermore, the presence of small weights allows small local interactions to be significantly amplified through a process called dimension jumping. These findings indicate that future modeling reliance on dimension jumping and dimension jumping-enabled weight configurations is essential for successful high-dimensional modeling. In addition, the problem of overoptimization of small neural networks, which results in excessively precise predictions with little generalization capability, can be successfully addressed by scaling up the network while ensuring presence of dimension jumping-enabled weight configurations. Our study also showcases a particularly useful pattern for high-dimensional calculations: a linear component combined with a quadratic component, which we have dubbed the 'L-Q' pattern. Our analysis further highlights the importance of high-weighy dimension jumping in achieving substantial dimension jumping, and experiments have proven more neurons are not a more reliable solution than when consistently incorporating dimension jumping into the weight distribution. These experiments have also proven a critical threshold for the linear component must be found in order to achieve optimal results. Our analysis of the why small and large weights matter in high-dimensional value prediction studies has also broken new ground, and our model's success across 18 high-dimensional molecular systems without any biasing potential information demonstrates the practical value of our findings. Ultimately, the pattern of high-dimensional value prediction emerging from our study, 'a linear component plus a quadratic one,' or 'L-Q,' or 'L-Q all around,' suggests a critical and implementable strategy for high-dimensional calculations, which has also been successfully adapted to other chemistry challenges.

Subsequently, we demonstrate that the image of a composite functor representing a product $\mathbf{d}_1 \otimes \mathbf{d}_2$ corresponds to a tensor product $V_{\lambda_1} \otimes V_{\lambda_2}$. This work provides a new perspective on the action of the affine Weyl group and $GL(V)$ on the set of irreducible modules with fixed highest weight. The study explores various aspects of chemical and electrical transport between a tip and a sample in Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) measurements. These aspects are studied in three materials: (110) doped silicon surface, (100) doped silicon surface, and gold. All experiments were conducted with a low-conductive and high-conductive tip made of carbon. As a result, three distinct image types emerged, characterized by unique patterns, indicating the presence of surface states. These image types are also associated with unique recoils when the bias voltage is altered. These phenomena are further analyzed through the creation of simulated images, utilizing a three-dimensional simulation of the (110) doped silicon surface and the 6-parameter model for the contact between the tip and sample, as proposed by Bartel. These simulations identified the crucial factors responsible for the emergence of distinct image types and recesses during STM measurements. Moreover, using the contact model and experimental data from Gergen's study on gold surfaces, we estimated the degree of tip and sample surface irregularity, finding that it ranges between 0.048 to 0.1. This led to a comprehensive understanding that, within the context of our measurements, the type of image captured is largely dependent on the type of tip used rather than the sample itself. This implies that, for effective sample analysis, it is crucial to utilize multiple tips, each with unique properties, to generate various images of the sample. These diverse images can then be combined to create a unified understanding of the sample's structure. Finally, our study also demonstrates that, using the contact model and combining information from different tips, it may be feasible to determine the sample's conductance on an atomic level, paving the way for a more nuanced comprehension of electrical transport in the studied materials. These experiments demonstrate a significant enhancement of 2 to 5 orders of magnitude in the sample conductance, resulting from the transition from low to high conductive tips. Furthermore, our findings suggest a substantial non-thermal distribution of samples conductance at ambient temperatures, ranging from 300K to 373K. This highlights an exciting area of research, the scanning of tunneling microscopy, and holds great potential to uncover an impressive, previously unseen world of electrical transport in materials. The resulting findings and analysis provide valuable insights for a range of materials and will contribute significantly to a deeper understanding of electrical transport in the (110) doped silicon surface, and other materials studied. Online community forums are notorious for having an underactive or overactive posting population. imbalance can hinder a forum's overall health. To address this issue, a pressing research question is how to effectively stimulate inactive users into more active participation. To tackle this challenge, a novel suggestion model called DualFeature was proposed. By leveraging the unique posting habits of each user and the topical structure of the forum where they participate, this model provides personalized suggestions for boosting user engagement. Specifically, user posting habits are represented by a Gaussian mixture model, while topical structure is represented by another Gaussian mixture model. To enable efficient user-user and topic-topic comparisons, both of these models are mapped to a unified space using a dual-task autoencoder framework. The model's utility was evaluated through various experiments, which showed that it effectively identified relevant suggestions. When put into practical use, it successfully encouraged users to post more frequently in a substantial range of activity levels. Notably, user experience metrics, such as satisfaction and ease of use, showed that users preferred this model's suggestions over a competing baseline option. Ultimately, this proposal sets the stage for future research to integrate this model with additional relevant features, such as natural language, to further improve user experience. We investigate the momentum dependence of static spin susceptibility in the paramagnetic phase of Heisenberg magnets, examining a cubic anisotropy as a perturbation. By analyzing the critical behavior, we find the spin susceptibility's subleading term relative to the momentum scale $k$ to be of the form $\ln^2(k_\mu)$. Furthermore, we determine the critical exponents $\nu$ and y, yielding values of 1 for $\nu$, and a value of 4 for y, in agreement with Monte Carlo simulations, while also revealing an inequivalent critical behavior compared to an isotropic Heisenberg magnet. Finally, we find these results to be valid regardless of the presence of a parity-imposed restriction on the momentum indices. If such a restriction is applied, we would observe a significant decrease in the dimensionality, resulting in a critical behavior more akin to that seen in the 1D Heisenberg magnet, characterized by an infinite y value. Our conclusions are substantiated through an analytical demonstration in various relevant contexts. Moreover, we find the mean-field theory to be responsible for the generation of incorrect results in this context, an shortcoming that could potentially be replicated in related experiments. To overcome these shortcomings, we suggest employing an effective medium theory that incorporates a momentum-dependent relaxation rate. The process of an artificial neural network adjusting its expectations in response to observed data is comparable to a lens adjusting its optical expectations. Just as a lens shapes its expectation by comparing observed light to a previously expected representation, a delta lens achieves this by adjusting the differences between two sequences of expected and observed data, known as deltas. A collection of such lenses, referred to as delta lenses, retains the ability to compare expected and observed data. This implies that a universal set of delta lenses exists, allowing for the adaptation of any artificial neural network based solely on its input and output sequences. A proposed algorithm for creating a delta lens, referred to as Temporal Shift Update (TSU), enables the creation of a set of delta lenses with a limited number of parameters. This allows for the modification of any artificial neural network by a universal set of TSU lenses, effectively transmitting the changes from the training data to the model through the intermediate set of delta lenses. This process can be further investigated using a mathematical representation, as well as through experiments which demonstrate the ability of TSU lenses to accurately represent modifications across various tasks and models after learning through context. Several potential applications and extensions of this idea are then considered. Although initially developed using a supervised approach, the concept is just as relevant in an unsupervised setting, making the TSU algorithm accessible in both scenarios. Moreover, when the goal is to understand the meaning of the modifications made by the delta lenses, an additional step can be added to interpret the intermediate set of expectations. This additional step involves using AI-powered methods to describe the numerical changes captured by the deltas, which can provide insight into the meaning of these modifications. Finally, similar universal sets of delta lenses can be designed for other types of behavioral adjustments, effectively creating a new model distinction that can be learned and understood. Potential applications in the fields of psychology and education are explored. A new data-sharing platform, known as the Behavioral Update Repository (BUR), is established to facilitate the sharing of update strategies and related knowledge. This facilitates the exchange of knowledge between researchers and fields that focus on behavioral updates, with the long-term goal of developing a system for transferring these updates more directly. This could involve developing protocols that enable the direct transformation of psychological theories into AI models, ultimately creating a bridge between these fields. A preliminary concept for such a bridge, known as the Psycho-Social Integral Bridge (PSIB), is introduced, as well as a proposal for its initial component regarding the transfer of update strategies. This could facilitate the exchange of knowledge and potentially merge these fields.

We examine the numerical effectiveness of the uniform constant phase approximation for water wave generation in numerical models of ocean waves, considering various degrees of smoothness for the wave surface. To this end, we introduce a numerical benchmark to assess the approximation's accuracy based on numerical solutions obtained using two different methods: Eulerian finite differences and Lagrangian particles. The benchmark allows us to evaluate the impact of spatial resolution and time step size on approximation errors in two key indicators: total energy and angular momentum, considering respective acceptance thresholds. Extensive numerical simulations reveal that increasing the smoothness of the input wave spectrum significantly enhances the accuracy of the uniform constant phase approximation, with approximately double the maximum acceptable time step size possible for each additional smoothness level. Moreover, our study confirms the potential of this approximation for online real-time applications, where choosing a smoothness level of two or more can allow for a much broader range of time step sizes while maintaining acceptable accuracy. Ultimately, we investigate the advantages of combining the uniform constant phase approximation with a Lagrangian method based on Lagrangian particles, finding this combination to be suitable for both offline and online applications and particularly effective when utilizing a smoothness level of one. The use of this approximation in both Eulerian and Lagrangian methods offers benefits such as increased stability and improved convergence, particularly in the context of two-scale ocean waves, while permitting the utilization of a larger time step size than traditional methods would allow. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that increasing the smoothness level or switching to a Lagrangian approach significantly enhances the accuracy of the total energy conservation, resulting in nearly perfect conservation in these scenarios. Finally, we conduct a cost analysis to determine the optimal balance between accuracy and computational cost, revealing that increasing the smoothness level has a greater impact on accuracy than advancing from a Eulerian to a Lagrangian method, while both cost and accuracy considerations suggest the optimal choice of a smoothness level of two. Consequently, in practice, a smoothness level of two emerges as a valuable and versatile option. The concept of pathwise conditioning in random fields and measures has a rich mathematical history, closely related to the change of variables formula for Gaussian fields. This involves considering a sub-$\sigma$-algebra of a larger sigma-algebra where a Gaussian field is defined, and then determining a Gaussian conditioning relative to that sub-algebra. This is in contrast to the more traditional approach of considering Gaussian processes with independent, identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples. Notable applications of this technique include inverse problems and demodulation procedures, where the objective is to extract underlying signals from observed data, as well as statistical mechanics and the theory of linear dynamics. This article aims to introduce the necessary background and provide two illustrative examples, including a simulation illustrating the effectiveness of pathwise conditioning in linear dynamics, while also highlighting an instance where the pathwise conditioning fails, demonstrating its potential drawbacks in inverse problems where hidden Markov models are applicable. Specifically, this article defines Gaussian conditioning relative to a sub-algebra as a unique real-valued Gaussian random variable, derived from the Feldman-Hajek projection, and discusses how this conditioning can be characterized through both a pointwise and almost everywhere perspective. Furthermore, this article demonstrates that the pathwise conditioning is not well-defined in processes with i.i.d. samples, illustrating its limitations in certain scenarios. Ultimately, the pathwise conditioning's unique ability to characterize conditioning at both sample paths and almost everywhere levels distinguishes it from the more conventional i.i.d. conditioning, which only yields conditional distributions and are unable to characterize at individual sample points. In addition, this article demonstrates that the pathwise conditioning's definition relies on the properties of Gaussian distributions, resulting in potential generalizations to other types of random variables and of different dimensions. It also discusses how pathwise conditioning can be characterized through both a sub-algebra and a specific linear map, resulting in multiple equivalent definitions, as well as highlighting distinctions between these distinct types of linear and sub-algebraic perspectives. Finally, this article concludes by characterizing the pathwise conditioning's relationship to its associated dual variables and encourages future research in this direction. To accelerate the learning process in continuous reinforcement learning, experience replay is widely used. The standard approach of uniformly sampling from past experiences in a replay buffer involves storing all past actions, which can lead to poor learning performance when variations of the same action are not effectively distinguished. This insensitivity causes agents to experience less variability and explore less frequently in scenarios where state variations matter. A more targeted approach, called Temporal Difference Replay (TDR), was proposed to focus on sampling near actions with high reward history, but it was discovered that TDR may not adequately distinguish variations of an action if the reward is consistent across different states. This limitation is overcome by introducing a new sampling strategy, Variancer Decrease based Experience Replay (VDER), which prioritizes actions with significant reward variability using an epsilon-greedy method. By effectively decreasing the variance associated with each action during data storage, the reward density function is approximated more accurately, which is beneficial for minimizing the off-policy error. Moreover, VDER was further enhanced by its application in Adaptive Experience Replay, an approach that dynamically adjusts the size of the replay buffer and the sampling strategy across different action families. Experimental results demonstrate that VDER outperforms Uniform Sampling and TDR in multiple challenging scenarios and even achieves improved performance when combined with an optimal case of TDR. Moreover, the proposed method achieves accelerated learning in comparison to prior research, notably Boosting in Episodic Reinforcement Learning and Action Hashing. The code and detailed analysis are available on https://github.com/azkaszap/pypers//tree/master/vder. As confirmed by further investigation, VDR improves learning outcomes by 30% in comparison to the uniformly sampled method and achieves a speedup of 2x in sample efficiency, which is even more effective when compared to a recently introduced algorithm, Boosting in Episodic Reinforcement Learning. The accelerations in learning are respectively 1.3 and 2x when compared to Action Hashing. Moreover, the proposed method has an additional benefit of a more natural behavior when comparing the actions associated with different states, which was also observed in our Adaptive Experience Replay variant. The latter even surpasses the performance of several benchmark methods, notably Uniform Sampling, TDR, and a previously introduced algorithm, both in learning acceleration and efficiency. This research proposes a new type system based on distinct semantic interpretations, one of which is subject to various non-deterministic variables influencing its operation. This interpretation is applied to a language called Josephine, a multi-paradigm language designed with safety features from Rust and the ability to execute both statically typed code in a compiled environment and dynamically typed code in a just-in-time compiled setting. To assess the effectiveness of this idea, a comprehensive test was conducted to show that safety benefits are provided in both interpreted and compiled states, and a detailed performance analysis was also carried out to compare Josephine to other programming languages. According to our benchmark, a single function call in Josephine is handled about 1.3 times slower than in JavaScript and 1.03 times slower than in Rust. However, it's also observed that Josephine maintains 90% of JavaScript's performance in a compiled environment and up to 85.7% of C++'s performance in a compiled setting, all while featuring a flexible mix of programming styles. Consequently, a prototype implementation of Josephine, put through thorough testing against over 17,000 lines of real-world code, has demonstrated its durability and usefulness. Lastly, a discussion is initiated on potential future improvements to Josephine's design, focusing on integrating libraries commonly used in web programming to make Josephine compatible with current industry practices. Josephine's code can be found at https://github.com/kuhajcz/josephine, and a web-based demo is available at https://josephine-demo.github.io. Typically, a PSF is calculated from a flux-calibrated point source within an interferometric array's observation beam. Though such a source provides high-resolution data, it is often mixed with a less resolved, typically bright, component. For instance, in the case of Total Intensity, a Franklin-Arirington source may be overlaid on a bright Mars image. Similarly, in Polarimetry, a polarized Mars image may be overlaid on a polarized Franklin-Atkinson source. In all cases, the superimposed sources complicate the recovery of a resolved PSF. In this study, a practical approach is proposed to isolate a resolved PSF from an overlaid, brighter source. This research explores the present state of document accessibility, a necessity that can enhance equality, equity, and overall user experience. In this study, we examined a diverse set of documents, including academic, professional, and informal records, to understand their accessibility features. Our analysis revealed the prevalence of document formats, such as PDF, Word, and TXT, along with their various characteristics, including the use of tables, quotes, and hyperlinks. Building on these findings, we established specific requirements for making documents accessible to individuals with sensory disabilities. To quantify the need for document accessibility, we utilized a dataset of 1.6 billion web pages from the Chrome browser, determining the document's print quality and font size. Our data revealed that only 5% of HTML documents and 21% of PDF documents can be easily accessed by individuals with visual impairments. In response, we are developing an end-to-end platform to enhance document accessibility, featuring a document conversion pipeline, a font analysis tool, and a W3C-compliant accessibility checker. Our research aims to inform policymakers and document creators about the importance of making documents accessible to all users. It is hoped that this study can inspire research and drive practical applications to address this pressing issue, ultimately benefiting not only individuals with disabilities but also everyone, thanks to technology. A associated demo project is available at https://github.com/devedge/print-disabled-docs. A larger scope of this research has been published at https://arxiv.org/submit/15859. While BERT excels at understanding sentences, its assumption that order matters can be a limitation when dealing with certain tasks and languages. This paper presents XLNet, a fully autoregressive pre-trained language model that effectively handles sentence rearrangement. Unlike BERT-based models, XLNet avoids using contextual representations that break predictability, relying instead on a universal transformer decoder to derive token representations from a permutation-free autoregressive objective. This results in a model that outperforms BERT in numerous NLP tasks, including the tasks that benefit from sentence rearrangement. Crucially, XLNet's success is achieved with a simplified model architecture, demonstrating the potential of fully autoregressive language models in achieving better NLP performance. Code and model will be made available at https://github.com/yerayd/xlnet. 

Key findings:
  - A fully autoregressive denoising approach can significantly improve NLP performance.
  - This can be achieved by sampling sentence permutations from a learned permutation distribution rather than a fixed rearrangement scheme.
  - The combination of an autoregressive denoising and unsupervised learning of sentence permutations leads to superior performance in certain tasks and populations, outperforming the BERT-like model when used as a pre-training task in NLP applications. This is particularly true for tasks that benefit from sentence rearrangement.

Recommendations:
  - Data Augmentation: Generate various sentence permutations from a single text to improve model performance. 
  - Model Architecture: A fully autoregressive denoising approach can lead to better NLP performance even with a simplified architecture. 
  - Population Analysis: Model can be effective across different population, including humans, by sampling sentence permutations from a learned permutation distribution rather than a fixed rearrangement scheme. 
  - Advice for a 5k Word Vocabulary: Use a universal language model with a 5k vocabulary to improve model accuracy and reduce computational cost. 

Advantages:

A key aspect of understanding asteroids that pose a potential threat to Earth's coastline is accurately simulating the effects of large-scale water movements following a collision. However, modeling these events accurately is highly complex and requires significant computational resources. A critical first step in mitigating such events is to predict that the initial shockwave will transition into a tsunami, a phenomenon observed in numerous asteroid impacts throughout Earth's history. Previous studies focusing on asteroid collisions have neglected this transition, often attributing it to the simplification of complex events. This study proposes that the combination of two processes - the expansion of a crater forming the basis of a layered structure, and the subsequent erosion of this structure - accurately explains the initiation of a tsunami following an asteroid collision. By applying this framework to a specific scenario involving the asteroid that caused the Chicxulub impact, we have created a generalized model that enables the simulation of varying levels of diffusion, thus providing unparalleled insight into tsunami development. Ultimately, these findings support the theory that asteroid collisions can and do result in the transformation from a shockwave to a tsunami. A major advantage of this model lies in its flexibility, as it can be applied to a wide range of asteroid sizes and varying target planet conditions, making it a pioneering innovation in the field. Furthermore, we have identified several potential factors that could influence the progression of these events, thus offering additional avenues for research. The fourth Industrial Revolution has significantly improved supply and demand connectivity in global systems, but its incorporation into optimization algorithms remains limited. particularly in real-time applications. This study examines the extent to which uncertainties can be perceived in data collected from enterprise resources planning (ERP) systems. Furthermore, we propose a new method for incorporating perception uncertainty into scheduling algorithms. This approach, which utilizes a modified Multi-Robustness Scheduling Problem (MRSP) model, enables the incorporation of both task uncertainty and perception uncertainty. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method with computational tests conducted on actual ERP data obtained from a Portuguese furniture company. The results of our study indicate that incorporating perception uncertainty into optimization algorithms can notably improve computational efficiency and robustness in real-world applications. This study ultimately presents an innovative strategy for leveraging Industry 4.0 data collection and optimization. Its findings are expected to pave the way for further research on incorporating perception uncertainty into optimization algorithms in the context of the fourth Industrial Revolution. This approach is demonstrated through its application in developing controlled residual triggering mechanisms for failure detection, utilizing a case study involving a nonlinear plane with actuator failures. Our methodology ensures the derivation of controls that not only guarantee system safety but also effectively detect faults. This research offers a practical framework for designing CP systems resilient to uncertainties, model inaccuracies, and failures, reducing the likelihood of system failures and operational disruptions. Furthermore, we discuss strategies for reducing computational complexity and outline future research directions. A scalable implementation of our methodology, including the employed tools, is presented at https://robustcp.github.io/. We have further substantiated our results through additional case studies.

Furthermore, the article will present an innovative method consisting of two parts: Firstly, it will propose a local description consisting of a set of deterministic equations defining the evolution of a given initial condition, and secondly, it will utilize a statistical framework to derive an effective nonlocal description capable of approximating the behavior of the original deterministic model while accounting for common features present across various cosmological simulations. To address these unique scenarios, an innovative formalism is proposed, allowing a direct connection to be established between the particles' cross sections and the particles' or areas' geometric properties, thereby accurately describing their scattering patterns. As exemplified by the various applications below, this approach holds considerable promise for analyzing diverse acoustic and optical acoustics-based techniques.

2. Infrared absorption by one-dimensional gratings: A well-known problem in this area can be accurately described using our approach. Additionally, our methodology can be applied to tackle related challenges such as the absorption and reflection of electromagnetic waves by similar structures.

We have explored the phenomenon of zero-point or residual energy in a blackbody hollow cavity containing parallel plates, and compared it with the energy of the Casimir effect. Our calculations, carried out assuming classical thermodynamic principles, revealed that this energy is comprised of two components, namely the residual energy of the Casimir effect and the zero-point energy of the blackbody. Additionally, we derived an expression for the change in entropy as a function of area reduction and temperature, indicating that the system exhibits spontaneous change at a certain temperature and pressure. Furthermore, we compared the magnetic properties of the residual energy of the Casimir effect and the zero-point energy of the blackbody, finding them to be analogous to those of ferromagnetic materials. The derived expressions for the energy and magnetic properties were verified through numerical computations. The findings presented in this study demonstrate that thermodynamic phenomena have a deeper significance at the quantum level and that the principles of thermodynamics can be used to describe various quantum properties of particles and fields. It is anticipated that the approach discussed here can be employed to examine the thermodynamic properties of particles and fields in diverse quantum systems. The approach, however, incurs a limitation, namely the requirement of classical thermodynamics for the derivation of quantum properties, and may lead to a discrepancy in certain cases due to the underlying physical assumptions and range of applicability of the derived model. Furthermore, this methodology does not address any physical phase transitions that may occur between the relevant quantum systems. Investigating these phenomena, which are out of the scope of this study, is necessary for a thorough understanding of the subject matter. The approach discussed in this dissertation is flexible and can be applied to various quantum systems characterised by field properties, such as electromagnetic fields, and to describe various quantum properties of particles, such as the energy of particles and the magnetic properties of magnetic substances. The underlying models rely on classical thermodynamic principles, and the following study will explore the application of these principles to the investigation of topological phenomena. The approach may incur specific limitations and can potentially describe both elementary and topological properties of particles and fields in distinct ways. The application of thermodynamics to the study of quantum systems and the description of both ferromagnetic and topological properties using this methodology will be further investigated in future works. The approach may be extended to the study of other systems, and the investigation of various quantum systems and the properties of particles and fields will continue in the upcoming study. A significant concern with location tracking is the compromise of privacy. To measure the impact of a location query on privacy, we suggest utilizing the variation in predicted location distribution before and after the query, quantified as the Kullback-Leibler divergence. Subsequently, researchers developed a privacy metric based on the relative entropy and meaningful bounds in relation to the Cram\'er deviation. The way to limit the disruption of privacy is outlined. The proposed framework applies to a broad class of location models, including Gaussian space-time models and their mixed types. Furthermore, when subject to intense tracking, a stability theorem can be utilized to establish limits on the divergence, thereby determining the limits of tolerable tracking intensity. The findings demonstrate that standard tracking methods, such as range, range-of-view, and multi-step range, have a stable impact on privacy when location conditions are consistent. The theoretical outcomes provide an upper limit on the permissible intensity of tracking, which can be utilized to calculate the privacy bounds for various location models and determine the optimal query radius to ensure privacy. The findings are supported by numerical simulations along with a case study involving GPS data. The actual privacy metrics exhibit a much more subtle relationship with the query radius than the logarithmic bounds, thus showing the practical significance of the theoretical outcomes. Finally, utilizing the stability theorem, a sequential bound can be derived for repeated location queries, which is essential for applications involving intense tracking with a high frequency of queries. The proposed approach can be leveraged to achieve a desired level of privacy at a reasonable tracking intensity while minimizing the deviation in distribution for location queries and meeting the requirements of a service or application. The parameters involved in the optimization problem can be determined through numerical calculation or simulation. By applying the proposed framework, the location privacy of users can be protected in various applications without compromising the functionality of the location-based services. The theoretical outcomes enable a dynamic balance between the quality of location services and privacy requirements while minimizing the deviation in distribution for location queries. To assess the level of privacy provided by the proposed framework, we suggest utilizing a entropy-based metric to measure the leakage in information. The proposed approach can be implemented on devices without significant computational overhead, as evidenced by a case study involving GPS data. The findings illustrate the practical applicability of the theoretical outcomes to real-world scenarios and applications. The localization of a moving vehicle in a dynamic 3D environment is crucial for autonomous driving and mobile robotics. The problem is complex due to varying data quality, motion similarities, and sensor noise., or quasi-3D behavior. We present an innovative solution called NDT-Transformer, a fully 3D point cloud-based approach that offers a versatile general filter for creating point cloud descriptors across multiple sensors. The method employs a normalized transform representation, coupled with localization as a similarity matching issue, using a transformer encoder. As a result, NDT-Transformer achieves a significant improvement in localization accuracy compared to current methods. The approach's key benefit lies in its ability to adapt to synthetic or real data generated from various point cloud descriptors. Notably, it surpasses existing methods when employing quasi-3D descriptors from LiDAR data while remaining competitive when working with full 3D descriptors from monocular images. Furthermore, a major advantage of this method is its ability to accurately localize vehicles when based solely on the rear car body, a scenario in which quasi-3D descriptors often struggle to perform well. The proposed approach utilizes a specialized transformer encoder designed for 3D localization, an innovation in its own right, as it effectively tackles the localization of a moving vehicle in a dynamic 3D environment. The approach can be found on github.com/alireza-farahi/NDT-Transformer. The proposed method's performance has been evaluated based on two existing real-world datasets, the KITTI dataset, and a new self-sufficient dataset generated from a vehicle mounted camera. As a result, a critical need for methodic dataset generation for localization research is identified. This study examined how sampling datasets and applying across-subject regression affect the precision of resting-state fMRI connectivity models, with a particular focus on whether a priori knowledge of brain regions can be utilized. Our results indicate that a combination of dataset sampling and across-subject regression techniques can be utilized to enhance the precision of these models, with a notable improvement achieved through the use of BIScA datasets and across-subject regression. Furthermore, our findings suggest that a more precise model can be built by leveraging a priori knowledge of brain regions, which further validates its application in brain network research. By conducting an extensive evaluation of existing methods, our study aims to provide valuable insights that can guide future research in this area. This paper introduces PESTO, a first-of-its-kind language model for code-mixed text recognition and processing, specifically designed to handle code-mixed texts in languages such as N'Ko, Wolof, Hausa, and Omala, which are commonly used in Africa. These languages combine Latin and local scripts, resulting in unique sequences of characters. PESTO overcomes existing language model limitations by embracing the transition points between codeswitched segments. Initially, each sentence is represented using a fixed positional embedding scheme. A learned attention mechanism then applies a non-linear transformation to handle potential gaps or anomalies in positional embedding. This allows the model to effectively utilize pre-existing monolingual transformers, like BERT. To facilitate the development of high-quality training datasets, a novel method using text normalization with a linear transformer is proposed. Experimental results demonstrate PESTO's performance superiority in processing code-mixed texts. Additionally, a large N'Ko-Wolof dataset collection and benchmarking process were conducted to support the model. The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/andreawieczek/PESTO. Recent predictions indicate that H$_{3}$S may become the next high-temperature superconductor at extremely high pressures, possibly reaching 150 Kelvin under 300 thousand times atmospheric pressure. If this were the case, it would be the first superconductor at such a high pressure and the material would also be the first to have a special type of energy gap that doesn't follow certain rules. Researchers have created a theory model that takes into account how energy groups in the material relate to each other, however this model assumes that the material's atomic spheres are separate and do not overlap. Now, a new study suggests that this is not the case and that the overlap occurs at around 270 thousand atmospheres of pressure where the material's energy groups meet. Using computational methods the researchers examined how the material's atomic spheres in H$_{3}$S change under different pressures and at different temperatures, and found that the pressure at around 270 thousand atmospheres where the energy groups meet is important. The researchers noticed that at this pressure where the energy groups meet, the material's energy behavior changes dramatically and this change could affect its ability to become a superconductor. The role of van Hove singularity at this pressure where the energy groups meet was also investigated and the researchers discovered that it plays a significant part in determining if the material will become a superconductor or not. The researchers noticed that at this pressure where the energy groups meet and also where the material's energy groups change dramatically, the pressure necessary to create the special type of energy gap in the material is lower than initially predicted. The predicted influence of isotopes on the material's ability to become a superconductor at this pressure where the energy groups meet was also investigated and the researchers discovered that their effect is less than predicted at lower pressures too. The researchers noticed that their own theory model as it is constructed, the pressure necessary to create the special type of energy gap in the material is higher than initially predicted. The researchers discovered that it is possible that the pressure necessary to create the special type of energy gap in the material is lower than initially predicted and that the material's atomic structure plays a significant part in determining if the material will become a superconductor or not. The critical temperature of the material was also investigated and the researchers discovered that their computational method allows to create a dependence of this temperature on pressure which shows that the pressure necessary to create the special type of energy gap in the material and the temperature at which the material becomes a superconductor and the isotopes influence all change

Mobile robots require efficient motion planning capabilities to reach their destination in a timely manner. However, in dynamic environments, such as navigating through crowded areas or obstacle-ridden roads, conventional planning methods lead to poor performance. A promising approach to mitigate these limitations is to implement spatial restrictions that minimize interactions with moving obstacles. Unfortunately, generating such restrictions with precise timing for numerous moving obstacles is computationally infeasible. This work aims to overcome this challenge by dividing the planning area into smaller sectors, restricting robot motion within these boundaries, and optimizing paths accordingly. A practical algorithm is presented to automatically generate these sectors and restrict robot motion for optimal performance. In contrast to traditional methods, our approach enables a significant reduction in the planning time, with the added benefit of reducing the planning horizon by up to 65%. Furthermore, our method's efficiency is showcased through extensive real-world navigation trials, where the robot successfully navigated through various dynamic scenarios without human intervention. Evaluation results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in achieving compact trajectories and a higher speed of arrival at the destination, while with only occasional guidance from a human trainer. The empirical findings indicate that by leveraging spatial restrictions and optimizing sector dimensions, the robot's average time of arrival can be accelerated by up to 57%. The proposed planning framework effectively addresses the time complexity issue associated with motion planning in dynamic settings. In particular, our method's performance surpasses the state-of-the-art motion planning algorithms with a notable improvement of up to 40% faster planning times on average. A comprehensive evaluation of this plan has been demonstrated through various dynamic scenarios. Current visual relocalization techniques face difficulties when dealing with prolonged video sequences beyond 100 frames, often encumbered by large memory requirements. Surfel-based relocalization methods, on the other hand, store a compact 3D model of the environment and generate more accurate results, but tend to struggle with identifying corresponding pixels during the initial stages. To overcome this challenge, we develop a technique that leverages the intimacy between 3D surfaces and visual appearances to introduce a two-part feature extractor. This innovative design enables a part that focuses on extracting low-frequency visual characteristics similar to those found on 3D surfaces, while the other captures high-frequency visual details. Our proposed model uses a dual-camera geometry inference approach that takes both 3D surface and low-frequency visual feature similarities into account. This results in a substantial reduction of processing time, accurately localizing the camera's position in real-time. Our extensive tests confirm that the proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques, even when the 3D map becomes less precise. This work introduces an innovative algorithm for user selection and data encoding in MIMO collaborative networks, which combines the principles of sparse signal recovery, single-user power optimization, and group sparse user selection. By leveraging the group lasso optimization technique, our algorithm addresses the challenges of user selection and encoding within MIMO systems, ultimately leading to the reduction of the transmit power required for each user. Building on previous channel grouping methods, our algorithm formulates an optimization problem that incorporates a lasso term to achieve group selection, which is then solved using an alternating algorithm that first fixes the selection variables and then solves for the remaining encoding variables through zero-forcing. Empirical performance evaluations validate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm, demonstrating significant power savings in MIMO collaborative networks, with notable gains observed under moderate and severe channel conditions. Furthermore, our algorithm outperforms its benchmarks in terms of power savings, with its performance gap consistently emerging as a substantial improvement. Moreover, our algorithm exhibits superior performance, with reductions of up to two times those of its benchmarks in extreme channel scenarios where more robust techniques like max-min optimization would otherwise be necessary. Finally, our algorithm shows a notable performance gain over its main competitor in MIMO collaborative networks, with reductions of up to six times those of its benchmarks when evaluated under more extreme channel conditions. In continuous double auction settings, researchers have developed the Q-procedure as a conceptual tool to predict the equilibrium price and quantity levels that would yield the greatest revenue for bidders. This price, known as the Q-price, is often theoretically shown to be beneficial only under the assumption that all bidders act independently. However, studies on the Q-price have concentrated on the performance of a single strategy. Consequently, the Q-price's ability to effectively converge in scenarios where multiple bidders employ diverse tactics remains an area of inquiry. Our research aims to explore the Q-price's performance when a broad range of bidding strategies exist. We employ both simulation and analytical methods to examine the Q-price's consistency in capturing the market equilibrium, focusing on the effects of varying sample sizes, degree of private knowledge, and diversity of tactics involved. Beyond the Q-price, our study contributes to the understanding of the consistency of the Generalized Modified Mean Price (GMP) estimator, providing a clear roadmap on the choice of parameter values that guarantee optimal results. The mean price's performance in continuous double auctions is also assessed for consistency. Our comprehensive study aims to offer higher confidence levels for theoretical findings relevant to the double auction literature. A related JavaScript application allows users to interactively explore the effects of diverse bidding tactics on the Q-price, revealing intriguing graphical patterns that can aid researchers in the exploration of the Q-price's performance in different tactical scenarios. Our study's findings indicate that the Q-price's ability to effectively converge may be compromised when a wide range of bidding strategies exist. Consequently, a more advanced approach, such as the GMP, is recommended for use, especially with smaller dataset sizes. When dealing with larger datasets, the GMP's Q-price and revenue optimality properties begin to diverge. Based on our study's results, the GMP appears to capture the market equilibrium reliably across a wide range of bidding strategies, yielding consistent and accurate revenue forecasts. Our research raises important questions about the design of the Q-price data and the impact of various bidding strategies on the Q-price, which may be addressed through future research. A JavaScript application, available at https://double-auction-estimator.webappa.net/, enables interactive exploration of the effects of different bidding strategies on the Q-price. Our research offers a theoretical and practical assessment of the performance of a family of price estimators, starting with continuous double auctions and extending to broader estimation problems. The connection between nematicity and superconductivity remains a major mystery in iron-based superconductors. To investigate this relationship in a well-established superconductor, we carried out an ab initio study of LiFeAs, a compound known for its direct band inversion. This study centers on the anomaly in chiral gauge theories and its robust form. 
The robust anomaly function is inherently chiral-independent and its evaluation for two robost anomalies confirms their relation to the MIJT invariant. 
Also investigated are the stages of chiral gauge theories which arise from the anomaly and the MIJT invariance, encompassing cases of gauge theories with p-form fluxes and their associated torsion states. 
The smallest unit of a stable anomaly configuration is identified as the a 2-form, which also serves as the robust anomaly in this context. 
Furthermore, the concept of stability is shown to be equivalent to topological stability and the smallest topological charge configuration is identified as the U(1) 2-form bundle. 
Also explored is the relationship between the anomaly and the MIJT invariance in string theory and the role of the robust anomaly in stages of chiral gauge theories and torsion states. 
Theoretical evidence is presented that torsion can arise even in theories without supersymmetry and it is argued that the stable anomaly is the fundamental unit of torsion. 
Also discussed is the fact that the stable anomaly is the source of stages of gauge theories with p-form fluxes and MIJT invariance but not topological QFT invariance. 
Lastly, the stable anomaly is identified as the anomaly that arises in the T^2 gauge theory which has no MIJT invariance nor topological QFT invariance. 
The theory's gauge group is proposed to be $SU(2)\times SU(2)/\mathbb{Z}_2$. 
We provide an appendix outlining a proposed search for stable anomaly (or robust anomaly) configurations. 
The stable anomaly is the first known anomaly of topological field theories. 
Anomalies in general may or may not be topologically stable; in the context of this work, the smallest unit of stable anomalies is the robust anomaly. 
The stable anomaly (or robust anomaly) is the inherent property of chiral gauge theories; that it is also the smallest unit of torsion in p-form fluxes is the further proposal of this work. 
The theoretical possibility of detecting stable anomaly through magnetic monopole searches is the final proposal of this work. 
It remains to be seen whether these proposals will be confirmed by future research. 
Notably, the concept of stable anomaly is the first instance where anomalies are identified with properties/phenomena in physics beyond quantum field theories.

This study contributes towards addressing a long-standing question raised by Tsurumi in 2019: what critical exponent $p_c$ makes the 3D stationary Navier-Stokes equations ill-posed in critical Sobolev spaces? The current work addresses this question for Besov spaces, where it finds the optimal $p_c$ value for ill-posedness to be $p_c = 3 + \frac{1}{4}$. The approach relies on constructing a specific type of perturbation with optimal regularity and a long, thin structure, which when added to an initial condition, results in an ill-posed solution. This method is further adapted to consider other types of perturbations, leading to revised $p_c$ values. The study also extends these results to consider non-Cauchy type initial conditions. The approach is innovative as it does not rely on scaling or other typical methods for solving this type of problem. The study is however limited to Besov spaces with $p \geq 3$ and may be more easily extended to other function spaces by considering alternative methods. The study affirms the previously established $p_c = 3 + \frac{1}{4}$ value for ill-posedness in critical Sobolev spaces and similarly confirms the previously established $p_c = 3 + \frac{5}{6}$ value for ill-posedness in critical Lebesgue spaces. The study is significant as it contributes towards addressing a significant open question in the field and offers a general approach for finding the optimal $p_c$ value for a wide range of functional spaces. To improve pre-trained language models (PLMs), which are the foundational bricks 
for many downstream tasks, researchers have been exploring new ways to enhance their
performance. A crucial aspect of PLMs is their capacity to understand various words 
within a given context. However, PLMs typically struggle to interpret uncommon words 
lacking in extensive training data. To address this issue, this research introduces 
Dict-BERT, an innovative method for refining BERT through two phases of supplementary 
training. Firstly, the training data is enriched with extensive dictionary-based word
predictions guided by look-up dictionaries. Secondly, the model is further developed 
using un-supervised sentence-level word prediction based on given definitions from the 
same dictionaries. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of Dict-BERT, outperforming 
competitors on a range of downstream benchmark tests, including Benchmarks for Elliptical 
Processing, Benchmarks for Commonsense Reasoning, and The Generalizability in NLP Benchmarks. 
Our Dict-BERT code is now accessible via this GitHub repository https://github.com/Ashe1998/Dict-BERT.

The feasibility of Federated Learning (FL) in educational data contexts has been widely accepted, yet its application remains limited due to ongoing research into FL's adversarial resistance. A critical knowledge gap exists regarding how FL models behave when subjected to adversarial attacks during training. To fill this gap, this paper will provide an in-depth examination of legitimate attack techniques on FL model training, with a focus on data manipulation attacks that occur within the FL framework. A new framework for such attacks will be introduced and proven effective through testing on commonly used FL datasets. An empirical analysis will also be conducted to compare the efficacy of legitimate attack techniques on FL model training, with a specific focus on educational datasets. A novel attack technique, called the Federated Poisoning Backdoor (FPB) attack, will also be developed and shown to be capable of inserting backdoor triggers into FL models without the knowledge of participating clients. FPB can target specific objectives by manipulating a single parameter during FL model training. Experimental results will also be presented to demonstrate FPB's efficacy on both synthetic and real-world educational data, with successful instances of information leakage and gratification reported. A percentage increase in FL model accuracy was also recorded using FPB on the MOOD dataset. FPB's utility will also be illustrated through its use in inserting malicious prompts in FL models trained on educational data. FPB's existence highlights the necessity of incorporating additional security measures into FL to protect against legitimate attack techniques and ensure the trustworthiness of FL models in sensitive contexts like education. FPB's code will be made available to researchers and practitioners for productive use. A trustworthiness framework for FL models is proposed, with FPB and FL model robustness against legitimate attack techniques identified as crucial components. Imagine a situation where a nation's capital is under attack from a hostile country, both physically with military force and virtually with highly advanced cyberware. The framework is put to the test in a case study where a game-based simulation is conducted to defend a capital city against a hostile country's physical and cyber attacks. The simulation provides valuable insights into how to strategically use limited defensive resources effectively, leading to several key recommendations for socio-cyberphysical disease surge capacity planning and management. Many real-world problems involve graph data, which presents challenges to deep learning due to its unique sparse structure. Effective learning on graphs requires transducing nodes into meaningful entities, but conventional supervised methods are hindered by limited availability of node labels. We introduce Informed Pseudo-Tagging (IPT), a self-supervised method that leverages partial node labels to create informative pseudo-tags for unsupervised nodes, thereby enhancing the performance of Graph Neural Networks. Unlike previous methods, IPT focuses on assigning robust tags to high-information nodes and efficiently propagates these tags throughout the graph. IPT significantly outperforms prior studies by achieving improved results with reduced computational requirements. The code for IPT can be accessed at https://github.com/zjupc/Informed-Pseudo-Tagging. Further details are available in the paper published on ACL2022. We have also submitted a later version of this study to publish at NeurIPS 2023, titled Unsupervised Graph Transductions with Robust Pseudo Tags and Mutual Information Matching. The code for this submission can be accessed at https://github.com/zjupc/Unsupervised-Graph-Transductions.

The requirements for the precision of algorithms used in the analysis of private, distributed machine learning data pose special challenges. Specifically, when working with possibly inaccurate input data, even the best efforts to ensure data privacy will result in a precision compromise. In this research, we primarily focus on the development of private algorithms for learning decision trees that can handle datasets marked with errors. To this end, we have expanded an existing BPTree method by integrating it with a differentially private algorithm for learning, while also evaluating various data processing techniques to maximize effectiveness. We have also modified an alternative learning algorithm known as EdgeSplit, similar to BPTree, to make it more reliable. Through extensive testing, we have analyzed the efficiency of several combinations of data processing and tree learning methods, comparing their results to those obtained from non-privacy-enhanced tests conducted over artificially created datasets. We have also evaluated the impact of different scanning methods on the overall precision of the models, ultimately selecting a method that provides the best trade-off between precision and reliability for the selected data processing and tree learning methods. We have demonstrated the practicality of our approach by applying it to real-world datasets. We believe that our contribution has significant implications, given that the majority of existing research in private machine learning requires precision, while our approach provides a more robust solution. We have also introduced a novel efficiency metric, able to handle datasets with errors, for evaluating machine learning algorithms. We have further evaluated the efficiency of the private learning algorithms from multiple perspectives, including time, distortion, and the fidelity of the models. Interestingly, our results show that providing data privacy in general, and learning decision trees in particular, results in a precision loss; therefore, choosing an unencrypted approach offers better precision. To mitigate this shortcoming, we have proposed a general strategy for enhancing the precision of machine learning algorithms that rely on data privacy, as well as a general strategy for evaluating the efficiency of these algorithms. Lastly, through a cost-benefit analysis, we have determined that our approach can provide a tenfold improvement in precision over a non-precision-based metric with a minimal additional computational cost, while offering about an order of magnitude better results than a publicly available machine learning library called Jacks. To facilitate the assessment of privacy in machine learning algorithms, we have applied several established metrics to our method, demonstrating its effectiveness. Consequently, our research provides a precision guarantee for a class of machine learning algorithms used in data privacy applications. Currently, network assessment and analysis tools are readily available for experts, but more advanced tasks such as network optimization remain limited to researchers with specialized programming skills. Our work focuses on developing a Bayesian framework for selecting the optimal chain event network configuration from multiple options, using Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. This framework utility is illustrated through two real-world case applications, one involving an analysis of Russian smallpox transmission in the 18th century and another examining the differential equation modeling of HIV dynamics. From these applications, we determined that integrating mathematical models with discrete network configurations is beneficial. Next, we aim to extend this work to enable fully customizable models that allow the incorporation of various discrete network configurations and continuous parameters via maximum a posteriori estimation. This model can be used to make parameterized network models available to both experts and non-experts, facilitating their exploration and diagnosis. Future endeavors will incorporate disease dynamics models into the Bayesian framework to facilitate the one-stop modeling of chain event networks. Moreover, we will offer users the capability to fit their own networks directly from data, enabling the analysis of unrelated events and locations. Ultimately, this product will provide an accessible and user-friendly tool for examining various scenarios. One such scenario is the fitness competition between HIV and antiretroviral therapy, which could be achieved by fitting model parameters while keeping the network configuration fixed or by concurrently optimizing both the network and model parameters. Last but not least, we aim to offer an accessible and graphical user interface for our tool that is accessible to both experts and non-experts, allowing the analysis of various discrete chain event networks and their corresponding continuous models via interactive diagnostics. This interface will utilize an interactive Python console for the execution of methods using Scipy and Theano, a dynamic web interface designed with Dash, and a graphical user interface incorporating interactivity from Dash and Plotly. Although this product is still in development, we have successfully applied the Bayesian framework in two real-world case applications. Moving forward, we intend to expand this product into a user-friendly, interactive tool for various chain event network configurations and their corresponding models, distinguishing ourselves from existing tools and providing our users with network configuration and model parameter options. This product is intended for public health professionals, researchers, and practitioners who can utilize it for parameterized modeling, network configuration analysis, and diagnosis. Once completed, this tool will represent an innovative user-friendly and interactive model analysis tool that goes beyond the current state-of-the-art. Consequently, we plan to release this product as an open-source tool focused on chain event network configurations and their corresponding models

It is established that the stochastic Loewner equation's branching loop family can be characterized as a specific type of Schramm-Loewner equations' solution, and this fully captures the geometric value of the SLE curves. A simplified mathematical approach to identifying the branching loop family in the simply connected domain is developed, leading to a precise mathematical representation of the SLE curves. Furthermore, the Chen-Carlen quantum mechanics framework provides insight into the probabilistic evolution of the branching loop family, and this is grounded in a study conducted by Kapelansky. Our work is built upon the recent findings of Miller and Sheffler regarding the conformal gluing of quantum disks, and these findings are extended to address the SLE module. A comprehensive analysis is provided of the SLE curves' deep invariants, including their spatial scaling, chirality, topological properties, and their characteristic behavior under conjugation. Our work is completed by illustrating, through rigorous mathematical means, the integration of quantum mechanics and conformal gluing. In the process, new invariants of the SLE curves are discovered. It is also demonstrated that the SLE modules can be perfectly matched with the MRS modules developed by Miller, Sheffler, and Tang. Consequently, the SLE modules can be employed within the context of their modular bootstrap program. Notably, the SLE curves' self-similarity and conformal symmetry are closely tied to the quantum mechanics of the Chen-Carlen model. Our work is grounded in a study conducted by the second author, in which it was observed that the scaling limit of the Chen-Carlen model's observables yields conformally invariant values. In the present work, this fact is reinterpreted within the conformal gluing framework. In this context, the SLE curves can be viewed as a result of a quantum mechanics evolution driven by a specific potential. Consequently, the conformal symmetry of the SLE module, and thus the SLE curves themselves, arises from the properties of this potential. Ultimately, the SLE curves' conformal symmetry is viewed as a manifestation of their deep quantum mechanical nature. Our work is built upon a series of papers, and these studies are at their core a theoretical exploration of the probabilistic evolution of the Chen-Carlen model. In the model, this probabilistic evolution is controlled by a specific Hamiltonian, and it is through this list of prior works that the SLE curves' deep quantum mechanical nature, and thus their conformal symmetry, emerges. This research outlines the initial phase of a more extensive project, where we investigated the impact of image preprocessing on a morphable model using a representative dataset, MORPH-II. The problem of connected vehicle platoons forming in a network is an important issue in intelligent transportation, where a comprehensive differential game model is proposed to address the fundamental question of how the priority of vehicle entry into a platoon is determined. Each vehicle seeking to join a platoon contests against others by making a donation of a constant, and through a process involving differential equations, the relative standings of these contests are calculated. The outcome reveals that the order of contest finishes naturally forms a necessary condition for entry into a platoon, and it is shown that this condition is sufficient with the proper choice of parameters. Additionally, a technique is developed to account for cases where two or more contests finish tied. Let's consider an example where two vehicles conttend for a spot in a platoon. Numerical solutions to this scenario reveal that a change in the speed of the leading vehicle can either increase or decrease the likelihood of the trailing vehicle filling the spot, and a deeper understanding of this is gained through examining speed distributions rather through their means. Furthermore, it is determined that a change in the distribution of the leading vehicle is capable of switching the odds of the trailing vehicle's chances, and a unique aspect of their interconnectedness is found when the leading vehicle slows down but the trailing vehicle accelerates. Finally, a linked system representing the interactions of a large number of vehicles is analyzed using two techniques used to study such systems in the literature and a large number of vehicles contending for a plathom in the given model is examined. Machine learning interacts with users through text-based interfaces like command-line prompts, risking non-conformity with local data protection laws when corresponding metadata is collected. This can lead to accidental PHE disclosure, a privacy threat that logistic regression models are particularly susceptible to. To mitigate this risk, we developed a novel trait-based logistic regression concept, where metadata is isolated from user inputs in Bayesian training. Our approach ensures models are uninformative about PHE without requiring a formal proof, as demonstrated through successful application in a high-profile PHE publication challenge. Notably, our method does not compromise model efficacy, outperforming non-interaction-based baselines in terms of publication accuracy and validation accuracy. This research showcases how the integration of statistical mechanics and machine learning can address the PHE publication avoidance challenge while ensuring models operate independently of metadata to avoid PHE disclosure. The generation of AI-driven content is growing at an accelerating pace, often in the form of texts and images created with the intention of deceiving humans. As these content forms become increasingly prevalent, distinguishing real human created content is becoming more difficult. Specifically in the case of deceptive product reviews, identifying them is crucial due to their potential to manipulate consumers' purchasing decisions. A particular method called NeuralSevere has shown impressive fake detection capabilities using SEBERT, a BERT-based model pre-trained on a large dataset of severe reviews. However, such approaches typically struggle when applied to neutral reviews and tend to overfit their training data. In this study, a new approach using a BART transformer model is applied to neutral reviews, which proves more resilient to dataset drift. Additionally, employing BART model yields significantly improved results compared to the existing state-of-the-art NeuralSevere method. Our research reveals that BART's performance is largely attributed to its unique pre-training objectives of denoising and paragraph rearrangement, which help it generalize better across various review styles. Moreover, the findings suggest that a relatively small fine-tuned model called BART-SEVERE has great potential for cross-domain applications and could serve as an effective fake review classifier. Our proposed model BART-SOFT exhibits an impressive softening effect on the model's decision boundary, which reduces class confusion and helps the model cope with more severe fake review labels. Overall, the study's findings are likely to be extended to the broader realm of NLP content creation classification where a large portion of data is typically labeled as neutral. It is anticipated the model can effectively classify them. Moreover, the model's ability to handle out-of-domain applications by fine-tuning it on real-world data is likely to be extended to the broader realm of NLP content creation classification. Finally, the model's decision boundary shows a softening effect which likely reduces class confusion. The key findings of this study can effectively motivate researchers to explore alternative models that help the model to better cope with more severe fake labels and reduce label imbalance. The emergence of topological order in disordered systems is being increasingly linked to their low-temperature electronic properties. Our investigation focuses on how disorder affects the ordering process of antiferromagnetic metals, which inevitably results in topological order. We show that both amorphous and polycrystalline paths to this order lead to a chiral spin-polarized superconductor when containing rashba-like spin-orbit interactions, which may be applicable to materials like amorphous Pb$_{1-x}$MnSe$_4$ as suggested in [Phys. Rev. B 99, 125151 (2019)]. We particularly explore the polycrystalline route in detail, which provides an distinct opportunity to experimentally investigate the Majorana edge modes in a chiral superconductor by enabling a finite range of variations in magnetic field orientation with no alteration in the physical phenomena occurring. Furthermore, our research reveals a novel phenomenon in systems lacking inversion symmetry but possessing dynamic inversion symmetry due to a DC voltage applied across a sample of non-uniform thickness, which creates protected zero modes within a massive version of a p-wave superconductor. This proposal presents a realistic pathway for experimenters to access such modes through the use of a thickness gradient, which also arises in the polycrystalline route of topological order formation. Additionally, our research demonstrates that a Rashba-like spin-orbit interaction has a significantly increased effect when the sample is subjected to a strong external electric field, indicating a promising thermal phase transition in such systems. Upon cooling, a spin liquid turns into a chiral superconductor characterized by the emergence of a spin-polarized phase at a particular temperature, marked by the emergence of a thermal window during which the system exhibits coexistence of these two phases. Upon further cooling, this phase transition is reversed and the sample becomes entirely comprised of the chiral spin-polarized phase upon reaching its lowest temperature. Upon reaching this lowest temperature, a significant window of parameter space, in which the thermal phase transition occurs, is opened up for experimenters to detect chirality in materials such as PbSe, PbMnTe, and other similar materials. Furthermore, our research describes a complementary mechanism of topological order formation in systems with strong and variable chemical doping. Upon reaching this lowest temperature, a significant window of parameter space, in which the thermal phase transition occurs, is opened up for experimenters to detect chirality in materials such as PbSe, PbMnTe, and other similar materials

Future large-scale radio interferometers, such as the Square Kilometer Array, will necessitate a novel, high-density beamforming architecture to minimize costs and optimize performance. Implementing a traditional grid-based calibration approach in these systems is unfeasible due to their inherent computational complexity with a grid-based approach. In this paper, we propose a new calibration strategy to address this limitation by leveraging sparse Fourier Transform algorithms via graph theory to develop a new calibration method with a significantly more efficient scaling factor of O(N log N). The results of our simulation trials suggest that this new approach is very effective in maintaining accurate calibration with realistic signal-to-noise ratios of up to 50. The new calibration strategy is of particular importance for large-scale interferometers of the future. The implementation of this new approach is detailed in the accompanying source code on GitHub. The computational complexity of the new calibration strategy is discussed in the paper. We have investigated the polarized gluon transverse-momentum asymmetry in the Z boson production at the LHC within the O(α$_s^3$) accuracy, determining a specific matrix element, A$_g(q|N)$, necessary for the variable flavor number scheme. This work involves examining multiple polarized anomalous widths, starting with the collinear approximation. By matching these results against the fixed-order calculation, we obtain the desired matrix element, A$_g(q|N)$. Our calculation shows that this matrix element can be expressed as the sum of two color-triplet scalar functions, F$_{Lg;1}$ and F$_{Lg;2}$. We have further determined the relationships between these scalar functions and their non-polarized counterparts. Moreover, we have derived the QCD anomalous dimension of the polarized gluon transverse-momentum asymmetry, which is found to be independent of the scale. This work marks the first time a complete, dimensionless series of theoretical calculations has been obtained for the polarized Z-boson production at O(α$_s^3$) accuracy. We have further verified that the obtained theoretical predictions match the measurements of individual parton pairs' polarized cross-sections. On the other side, the obtained theoretical predictions can be tested by comparing them with the combined data of individual parton pairs' unpolarized cross-sections. The obtained theoretical predictions show that the Z-boson production can be accurately described by the theoretical predictions across the entire measured momentum range. The obtained results suggest that the theoretical predictions could be improved by incorporating the effects of higher-order QCD calculations and additional parton distribution functions that incorporate the effects of small-$x$ phenomena and saturation. By incorporating these effects, we demonstrate that the theoretical predictions can be further improved and the experimental uncertainty can be effectively reduced. The obtained results show that the effects of higher-order QCD calculations and additional parton distribution functions, which are obtained in the next-to-high-energy (NHE) framework, can naturally lead to a good agreement between the data and the theoretical predictions in the low-$Q^2$ regime, while the effects of these perturbative QCD calculations are partially compensated by the non-perturbative QCD effects in the very low-$Q^2$ regime. The obtained results also suggest that the theoretical predictions can be further improved by incorporating the effects of even higher-order QCD calculations that are scheduled to be performed in the near future.
