To determine atmospheric properties through spectroscopy, precise data on the absorption properties of various atmospheric components are necessary. Despite its importance, there is no comprehensive dataset available for giant exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres. We developed EXOPLINES, a repository of absorption cross-sections for $300$ molecules relevant to giant exoplanet and brown dwarf environments. Our database includes temperature-dependent and structure-driven opacity data for $114$ molecules, enhancing the accuracy of atmospheric modeling and model-data comparison for subjects of interest. For additional accuracy, we used a range of potential values for unconfirmed parameters in line broadening and shift adjustments. Our database is tailored towards giant exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres but can also be applied to similar atmospheres of smaller exoplanets, such as hot Jupiters. Our research aims to make EXOPLINES available and contribute it to the development of more effective observation strategies and data analysis for the mentioned subjects. The database can be accessed at: \url{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.73764}. Its application is illustrated through its integration in two atmospheric models, FASTWAVE and IMPACT. Using these models, we determined the effects of different opacities on spectral models of various test objects, revealing noticeable differences in the spectral models generated with EXOPLINES for subjects such as HD189733, V889 Her, and W4518-45. These effects not only affect the interpretation of spectral properties but also the determination of atmospheric properties, such as the pressure-temperature profile of 51 Peg b, where our research reveals a difference of $2.5$ in the surface gravity between the high and low metallicity scenarios. The differences between the high and low metallicity scenarios are shown to be significant for various atmospheric properties across different subjects of interest. For instance, in the case of HD189733, its mean molecular weight is expected to vary by a factor of $3$ for high and low metallicity, leading to considerable differences in atmospheric temperature and pressure. We examine a class of random weakly periodic quantum low-density parity-check codes with uniformly distributed non-zero Pauli operators in the parity-check matrices. Lacking a constructive method for these codes, we develop a stochastic approach by linking them to conventional non-degenerate LDPC codes used in classical communications. Notably, the probability of a single qubit being incorrect when checking a specific parity check is associated with the probability of a classical LDPC code vector containing exactly one ones. By applying the recently established convergence properties of these codes, we prove that the latter probability asymptotically converges to $1-e^{-\frac{m_c}{2\delta^2}}$ where $m_c$ represents the average number of checks per information bit and $\delta$ represents the minimum non-trivial probability of a qubit being correct when checking a parity check. Consequently, we derive an upper limit for the probability of a single qubit being incorrect when checking a specific parity check in the quantum codes. Moreover, we develop linear duration quantum LDPC codes whose complexity is similar to that of the original codes and preserve the quantum properties of the original codes. Notably, the duration codes have the same number of qubits per check as the original codes and are efficiently decoded using a bit-flip or rectangle quantum LDPC decoder. Furthermore, we establish an upper limit for the probability of a single qubit being incorrect when checking a specific parity check in the duration codes. Comparative simulations are performed to assess the performance of several quantum LDPC code types including the original codes, duration codes, draw-rescaled codes, conventional non-degenerate LDPC codes, and classical repetition codes. The simulation results reveal significant gains in error threshold, density, and code complexity for the proposed duration codes. Moreover, the proposed duration codes achieve comparable performance to optimal minimum-weight-pulse codes with the potential for substantial reductions in duration and improved reliability. Finally, the theoretical validity of the simulation results for the draw-rescaled quantum LDPC codes is established. The theoretical framework can be extended to develop variational quantum LDPC codes whose complexity is similar to that of the original quantum codes and apply the deterministic approaches of [39, 40] to obtain substantial rate gains. Moreover, the proposed draw-rescaled quantum LDPC codes can be optimized using simulation methods described in [41] to achieve superior performance in a wide variety of applications. The framework can be extended to derive other quantum LDPC code variants whose complexity is similar to that of the original codes and develop efficient classical decoding algorithms for these codes.

In the context of creating fault-tolerant distributed systems, a key problem is data replication to ensure data availability even if some nodes fail. While achieving complete replication results in optimal fault tolerance, it leads to excessive storage needs and squanders valuable network resources. As a compromise, a more efficient method called the r-dominating set (r-DS) or covering set (r-CS) has been developed. This system involves spreading data across a number of copies equal to r, ensuring full accessibility if up to r-1 failures occur. Recently, a distributed algorithm was introduced that creates a precise r-DS ensemble for any given r, but only works effectively for large-scale graphs with low 'girth.' A new distributed algorithm is presented here, using a graph analysis approach that allows for the creation of a near-optimal r-DS ensemble for sparse, high-girth graphs with a given set of parameters. It extends previous work by allowing for the selection of a desirable value for r and generating distributions adaptable to various distributed file systems. Notably, our algorithm has a computational complexity directly proportional to r, making it more efficient for smaller r values while still offering fault protection. Moreover, our experiments demonstrate that while r-DS ensembles may not always match the optimal CS size, our algorithm consistently produces r-DS ensembles whose size exceeds the optimal CS size in nearly 90% of cases considered. Our analysis also reveals the relationship between the size of the r-DS ensemble and the number of copies r for various CS sizes. Our experimental results show our algorithm performs well in the distributed setting, outperforming a greedy approach that lacks graph analysis. Finally, our experiments compare the performance of the r-DS algorithm against a replication approach based on the degree of vertices for a dataset consisting of images. The results obtained demonstrate that the surface area required by r-DS is less than that required for replication and the material storage requirements for the dataset 'Images.' Neural radiance fields (NeRF) produce high-quality images by approximating a scene's indirect illumination using continuous, volumetric functions. RFs require sparse, 2D data and numerous 3D samples for optimal results. This has been a significant limitation for applying NeRF-based techniques to dense video datasets. We address this by proposing BFF, a new method for generating images from dense video sequences. BFF uses a volume field that takes a 3D vector consisting of spatial and temporal coordinates as input, thereby reducing the need for extensive 3D sampling. This allows BFF to produce high-quality images at a significantly faster rate than existing methods. Additionally, BFF facilitates real-time image generation, which can be used for applications such as video upscaling, downsampling, and trimming. We demonstrate the superiority of BFF over baseline techniques through quantitative and qualitative comparisons on challenging datasets like DTDB and DT40. Our source code is available at https://github.com/IndigoPurple/BFF. For interactive demonstrations, please visit https://indigopurple.github.io/BFF.

Reinforcement learning strategies that utilize recurrence, such as TD$\lambda$, can be effective in environments that have partial observability, even when agents can't perceive some states. We demonstrate how a specific recurrent neural network architecture can replicate the performance of TD$\lambda$ in such scenarios, particularly when processing temporal information is crucial. In these settings, agents often rely on external cues rather than internal knowledge to make decisions, leading to a scenario where external signals dominate over internal inference. We explore this phenomenon through the analysis of a case study involving the Montezuma Revenge game. Our results show that the conventional understanding of internalized knowledge in partially observable contexts may need to be revised, given these dynamics. We also introduce a potential performance metric, dubbed 'confidence', which could help gauge an agent's ability to understand its own decision-making process. This idea is particularly relevant when considering agents that rely heavily on external environmental cues in partially observable environments. Current state-of-the-art models for identifying actions in videos heavily rely on dense annotations across temporal and spatial dimensions, which can be extremely costly to produce. As a result, there has been a lack of interest in leveraging rich video data for representing contextual information. In this paper, we propose an efficient model called spot what counts that employs guided spot-masking to prioritize challenging moments and facilitates last-buffer prediction of action labels. Additionally, we introduce an innovative graph convolutive network to capture context, incorporating standard I3D features as a base. Our framework significantly outperforms previous methods, achieving an impressive 52.0 mAP on UCF101, 43.2 mAP on HMDB51, and 32.1 mAP on Okutama at 10 FPS on the Val dataset for Action Detection ECCV'2020. Our code is available at https://github.com/foei/spot-what-counts.

In our study, we investigate the combined effects of electron-electron interactions and intense magnetic fields on ferromagnetism in nickel atom, using the linked-field approximation for localized orbital theory. By employing the local density approximation, we establish a generalized form of the effective one-body potential, applicable for any intensity of the magnetic field. We demonstrate that the application of the local correlation approach yields a viable approximation of the multi-body correlation function's stationary determinant, enabling the computation of key thermodynamic properties in nickel under varying magnetic fields. Our calculations show that the application of the local correlation approach effectively captures the ferromagnetic nature of nickel even at high magnetic fields, displaying substantial magnetic field dependence. Additionally, we investigated how the intense magnetic field influences electron spin polarization, showing that it significantly correlates with the magnetic field strength. Furthermore, we discovered a magnetic field-induced transition in nickel from a ferromagnetic to a paramagnetic state beyond a specific threshold strength. These findings are crucial for understanding matter behavior in extremely magnetic environments. It is hoped that this research may stimulate a new area of investigation for atomic physics and chemistry. One of the key outcomes of this work is the demonstration of the general framework's feasibility to compute properties in a wide range of nuclear substances under intense magnetic fields. Although our framework relies on an approximate method, its effectiveness relies heavily upon the local correlation approach. Therefore, further improvements to the approximation method are necessary to broaden the scope of substances that can be computed using this framework. One potential improvement could be developing more efficient methods to compute key properties, allowing the framework to become even more effective than it currently is. With these improvements in place, it may be possible to apply this framework to a wide range of substances with various magnetic field intensities. One promising direction for achieving this could be by modifying the effective one-body potential by incorporating the difference between the actual and the effective two-body correlation function's contributions. By optimizing the method for this purpose, it may be possible to significantly enhance the accuracy of key properties, thereby broadening the scope of substances that can be computed using this framework. One of the key potential applications of this framework would be in the computation of properties for the heavy actinide and lanthanide elements. Due to their unique physics and chemistry under various extreme conditions, it may be possible to significantly improve our understanding of their behavior if the framework can effectively describe their physics and chemistry. By successfully demonstrating the feasibility of improvements to the framework, it may be possible to significantly contribute to our understanding of the atomic and chemical physics and chemistry. Educational institutions, possessing a wealth of personal student data due to resource constraints, hesitate to decentralized educational recruitment because of potential privacy breaches and communication expense concerns. We propose a pioneering approach, DP-REC (De-centralized recruitment with Differential Privacy for student RECRUITMENT), to tackle these challenges. A secure training method for the recruitment model's classifier is developed in conjunction with a statistical analysis framework for the educational industry to determine the optimal balance between accuracy and confidentiality of student data. Results demonstrate that, using the same model, decentralized training methods can achieve 65% of local pre-training accuracy at a communication cost equivalent to approximately 0.00012% of local data, rendering them substantially more efficient than purely local training. Moreover, incorporating a privacy mechanism into the training process reduces accuracy loss by 53% compared to local training. A security assessment reveals that, using the DP-REC approach, the calculated risk-based cost associated with data breaches on the recruited students' personal data is substantially lower ($5.86N)$ compared to local training ($.086N). Utilizing DP-REC, the educational institutions' recruitment process is enhanced in terms of both confidentiality and efficiency. Further research is required to enhance model accuracy while maintaining confidentiality and efficiency goals. A pilot study demonstrating DP-REC's efficiency in a real-world educational setting can be found at https://dp-rc.org. The research was published in December 2022 in the Journal of Cloud Computing. A comprehensive study of the Taurus-Perseus-Auriga star forming region employed Hubble Space Telescope images across various ultraviolet wavelength bands. These images helped distinguish three distinct sub-regions: Perseus, which is primarily classified as a filament-supported star forming region with compact cores; Taurus, a filament-supported region with dispersed star formations; and the Cloud, featuring scattered and isolated star formations. By analyzing these patterns, researchers were able to identify a phenomenon where filaments with higher star density, such as in Perseus, appear to have narrower and more defined filament structures, whereas those with lower star density like Taurus, appear to have wider and more dispersed filament structures. These observations suggest that filament compression plays a pivotal role in generating sub-megaelectronvolt magnetic fields, which in turn influence star formation patterns. Moreover, these findings reinforce the notion that star formations within filaments tend to be aligned in parallel with said filaments. Lastly, these images revealed a total of 677 ultraviolet-bright sources across the Taurus-Perseus-Auriga star forming region, which includes 463 previously undiscovered sources. By analyzing these patterns, researchers were able to detect (i) filament parallel alignments for 92% of sources, (ii) a concentration of sources near X-ray sources, (iii) a disparity in ultraviolet source density near filaments in the foreground and those in the background, and (iv) an apparent correlation between ultraviolet source density and star formation patterns. These disparities are tentatively attributed to filament compression, high-energy cosmic rays, and protostellar winds, respectively. Finally, these observations serve as a groundwork for discussing the broader role of filament structure in regulating, influencing, and reflecting various aspects of star formation. As such as these systems are crucial training data for developing computer simulations of star formation. Such as these systems are also crucial tools for deepening our understanding of star formation in general. Moreover, these various factors likely have a lasting effect on a star system long after the star formation process has concluded. A potential area for exploration, these factors could potentially account for a discrepancy, which is tentatively attributed to the paradoxical scenario, where dense star formations within filaments fail to ever become visible to telescopes, as their matter is instead drawn towards higher energy states. If this is the outcome, these star formations may play a pivotal role in regulating, influencing, and reflecting various aspects of star formation. Tables play a significant role in determining the effectiveness of document search. Nonetheless, extracting and matching table data from PDF documents poses a complex challenge. To address this problem, this work presents an innovative approach that incorporates Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to enhance table retrieval. Tables in a given query and a corpus are first localized using region proposal networks, then carefully cropped and aligned through tailored image processing procedures. Subsequently, the extracted table regions are segmented into cells, which are represented as graph structures and fed into a stacked GNN. This GNN architecture leverages graph Fourier transform-based convolutional operations to capture relational patterns in tables. To optimize table recognition and retrieval, this method also proposes a novel attention-based mechanism, which allows users to input queries of varying lengths and achieves improved results. Our proposed approach has been extensively tested on the TREC Tables dataset, which comprises table-based documents, and our findings reveal significant performance enhancements of up to 25.71% mAP rating compared to strong baseline methods. Our code is available on GitHub for further reference at https://github.com/amberwang88/Graph-Table-Retrieval. Experimental outcomes also highlight the effectiveness of incorporating GNNs for table recognition and the importance of tailored image processing procedures in table PDF retrieval. To facilitate easier code reproduction, the required datasets, including the TREC Tables and TableQA, can be downloaded from https://github.com/amberwang88/dataset_download. Furthermore, our findings show that incorporating GNNs results in notable outcomes in low-confidence sample identification and demonstrates their resilience to domain shift in homograph attack scenarios. Ultimately, this research showcases the capabilities of GNNs in deep learning systems designed to locate and analyze visual tables and highlights their potential applications in low-shot learning and domain adaptation. Our proposed approach has been successfully applied to the development of TableQA, a benchmark dataset and challenge initiative that aims to drive innovation in this area. More information on this initiative can be found at https://tableqa.org. Our research has also received funding from the following sources: Samsung AI Global and Mobility Genome Editing. A comprehensive overview of our research and the related resources can be found at https://amberwang88.github.io/Graph-Table-Retrieval.

We examine multi-phase gametrees where players may possess limited knowledge, leading to a situation of incomplete information. Our focus lies on understanding the thought processes behind these incomplete information games. To achieve this, we create a computational model consisting of three stages that represent different phases of the game. The first stage involves predicting the next phase based on the current stage, the second stage involves deciding on optimal actions to reach decision-making phases, and the third stage involves determining optimal actions at decision-making phases. The feasibility of our three-stage model is then investigated by checking its consistency across each phase. Additionally, we demonstrate that any instance of the first phase can be resolved using polynomial time computation, while deciding the second and third phases are problems that fall under NP. Next, we show that any instance of the first phase with a specific property has a guaranteed optimal strategy for the second phase. Our study provides theoretical insights that aid in developing effective two-phase games of incomplete information. To illustrate the relevance of our model, a relevant example is also discussed. Finally, an alternative model consisting of four phases is also proposed and compared with the original model. Comparative analysis between the two models reveals that the four-phase model retains all the properties of the three-phase model, while demonstrating improved guidance for players in different phases. The four-phase model also facilitates easier understanding and simpler computation of the game by dividing it into more distinct phases. Our study concludes by highlighting potential future research directions on these incomplete information games models. The experimental results also reveal that the proposed models can effectively aid in player guidance on real-world games. Ultimately, a summary of the game's properties and potential applications based on the three and four-phase games of incomplete information are provided. The results are represented using a decision tree diagram and are highlighted in the conclusion section. The decision tree diagram is available at https://drive.google.com/file/d/1pYHhR_7s4_RU4H5L9QsS2Y2u9q0w0if/edit?usd=0&usp=sharing. The conclusion ends with the future research outlook. To make the content more understandable, several key terms including imperfect and incomplete information games, multi-phase games, gametrees, thought processes, cognitive models, decision-making, and NP problems are explained in an simplified way in an appendix section for readers who are non-experts in this topic. In theoretical research, we investigate the process of three-body recombination for specific systems involving three bosons or three fermions, interacting through a single channel, which results in the formation of different molecular states. It is discovered that, under specific conditions initiated by a very short laser pulse, three-body recombination in systems with an odd number of spin particles leads to the transformation of spin particles into molecular states with unique spin alignments, which in turn implies the creation of spin-polarized molecules. Moreover, it is found that, through optical coherent control, it is possible to realize nearly 100% efficiency in three-body recombination that leads to the production of spin-polarized molecules, which further suggests a novel method to generate highly spin-polarized molecular beams. On the other hand, it is also found that, through a very short laser pulse, three-body recombination in systems with an even number of spin particles leads to the production of spin-entangled states of the molecular beam, which has potential applications in quantum information processing. These findings may offer new avenues for the experimental generation of spin-polarized and spin-entangled molecular beams, which have significant implications in the fields of atomic and molecular physics, particularly in the creation of highly polarized molecular materials. Moreover, it is also discovered that, when two spin-polarized atoms combine with a non-spin particle, it is possible to produce molecules that are not only spin-polarized but also highly aligned through a process initiated by a very short laser pulse, which has far-reaching applications in the creation of spin-polarized molecular beams and spin-entangled molecular states. Finally, it is found that, when a spin-polarized atom combines with two fermions, one of which is spin-polarized and the other is not, the resulting molecule is not only spin-polarized but also in a mixed fermion-boson state, which has significant physical implications. Moreover, it is also found that, when a bosonic atom combines with two spin-polarized fermions, the resulting molecule is not only spin-polarized but also in a mixed fermion-fermion-fermion boson state. The stability of such molecular states that arise from a process initiated by a very short laser pulse not only provides a mechanism for experimental generation of such molecular states, but also the possibility to create various types of spin-polarized molecular states as well as the possibility to create links between internal degrees of freedom and external electric/magnetic fields through optical coherent control

A distinct form of machine learning, unmonitored learning, uses unsupervised, non-targeted approaches to process data, often requiring more efficient methods to cope with larger datasets. An example of unmonitored learning is associative memory, which can operate without altering its dynamics when fully or partially connected. Researchers have proposed quantum-based associative memories, initially assuming the need for costly Grover-like oracle operations to optimize performance. However, without or with a monitor (self-monitoring or externally-checked), an alternative efficient approach using a simpler binary perceptron exists. We examine the efficiency gains from the use of these monitors, comparing them to classical systems. We also explore the optimization of performance in non-targeted quantum-based memories via pre-processing and connectivity adjustments to reduce the need for oracles. An experimental simulation using superconducting processors demonstrates the validity of our findings. Results show non-oracle, monitored systems can achieve equivalent performance to their monitored oracle-based counterparts, yielding a substantial 57 times speedup. An additional speedup factor of 1.8 can be attained by implementing the MaxMin Protocol to boost performance further. Fidelity metrics such as F1-score and Mean-Average-Fitiness-score (MAF-score) evaluate the accuracy of the retrievals. An additional degree of freedom, the use of a self-monitor (internally-checked), may offer a further efficiency boost. Quantum-based memories can serve as the foundation for a range of quantum-based intelligence architectures. Future research could also pave the way for incorporating additional building blocks of intelligence, foreshadowing the development of a comprehensive quantum-intelligence system. The challenge lies in the fact that languages with distinct intonation patterns cannot be mapped directly from the trained model, requiring a two-step process: first, modifying the sentence structure to make the pitch patterns more manageable, and second, adjusting the models' internal pitch representations. A proposed method for enhancing the flexibility of the FastPitch model involves generating timbre-preserved pitch variations to expand its representational capacity for more manageable pitch distributions. The incorporation of pitch augmentation results in a notable improvement of up to 5.22 cm/s (23.9%) in the mean average error for the TITREX-A audio quality metric across 9 languages, covering N Ari, N Kanada, N Khasi, N Sinhala, Pashto, Polish, Romanian, Serbian, Slovak, and Swedish. The improved models are accessible through the Git repository https://github.com/MatthewHintenbach/fastpitch-augmentation. For tasks such as weather prediction and video analysis, deep learning models 
can offer enhanced performance by using the spatiotemporal context. To demonstrate 
this, we introduce Hopper, a new multi-hop transformer model designed to extract
context from space and time for predictive tasks. By comparing existing methods, 
we observe that earlier methods fail to capture context from neighboring spaces 
and previous time steps. By contrast, Hopper addresses this gap by considering 
context from adjacent samples, units, and values across both horizontal and vertical 
dimensions. To efficiently process this context, we implement a novel strategy 
of aggregating information from neighboring samples, known as PLA. Furthermore, 
to accommodate large kernels and neighboring samples efficiently, we propose 
to split and reorder the features using the convergent structure within the LA. 
By incorporating our proposed aggregator and attention mechanism, Hopper's LA 
module becomes the first to generalize the attention mechanism to capture context 
across both space and time. Experimental evaluations of its performance exceed 
traditional convolutional networks and transformer models on the weather prediction 
task, delivering better performance. Hopper achieves better results on video 
classification tasks when benchmarked against state-of-the-art models, surpassing 
the performance of traditional models such as 3D convolutional networks and 
transformer models. Our code for Hopper is available at https://github.com/ziplab/Hopper.

Using a telepresence robot to interact in virtual spaces has become more common, and evaluating the user experience has become a critical factor for these interactions. This research introduces a user experience assessment method for remote robot control with a pre-requisite of real-time video feed. It combines a method for users to rate their experience while also simulating various quality levels by manipulating the remote robot's movement through random interruptions. This study proved that users are able to effectively gauge the impact of these interruptions and, based on that insight, proposed a quality metric. This metric's reliability and correlation with actual experience were evaluated through both laboratory and field tests, and it was shown to be a strong indicator of user experience, providing a practical solution for interacting with telepresence robots. Ultimately, this research provides a foundation for enabling the detection of user experience in controlled interactions, and it opens up possibilities for applications such as quality-of-experience-based feedback, user emulation, and user-experience-related optimization techniques. It could also lead to new avenues of research for managing user experience in virtual interactions. The data from this research, including the experiment results and user interfaces, can be found at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7373112.  Indices that measure the dispersion of user ratings, specifically the Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) and the Coefficient of Variation (CV), were found to be reliable indicators of quality-of-experience ratings.  In contrast to expectations, the nominal scale of users' rating choices did not appear to affect the accuracy or reliability of the quality-of-experience ratings.  While time variability did impact the accuracy of the quality-of-experience ratings, making ratings that span a long time period less reliable, the correlation between disturbance intensity and QoE was found to be consistent. Various forms of analysis, including Bayesian Learning, multivariate regression, and classification, were tested to determine the source of this correlation, and results indicated that users utilized a nonlinear decision-making process to gauge quality, and this decision-making process was influenced by the frequency and duration of disruptions. Frequency and duration were found to provide valuable information for gauging quality, and combining these metrics through a novel metric called Cognitive Bias was found to bypass the limitations of the nonlinear decision-making process, leading to accurate inferences even with minimal data. For instance, when testing the impact of a sudden change in a video feed, results showed that users could effectively gauge the impact of this change even with as little as two seconds of preceding context. This paper introduces a pairwise model that represents players' strategic decisions in the social game of Mafia. The likelihood of a player being loyal or treasonous is influenced by two factors: the number of other players who have taken specific actions, and the player's own evaluation of those actions. These evaluations depend on the payoffs players receive from various possible actions and the probabilities of those actions occurring. To determine the most likely distribution of players' internal states, we apply a machine learning technique called mean-field theory. This method enables us to account for the influence of individual decisions on their likelihood by averaging out the effects of all possible configurations. The accuracy of our model is supported by numerical simulations that show how different parameters, such as the proportion of traitors and moderator intervention, affect the outcome of the game. Furthermore, we investigated the most effective configurations of moderator intervention that can lead to a favorable outcome for both loyal and traitous players. Finally, we highlighted the significance of considering the complexities of the Mafia game and the potential applications of our model to other social games. The results also show that some configurations of the game can result in multiple stable states due to a balance of loyal and traitous actions. Additionally, traitors have a higher chance of surviving and advancing to the next phase of the game. The presence of multiple stable states may contribute to the prevalence of various social game variants in reality. The study also explored an alternative variant of the game where moderators can punish players. Mean-field analysis suggests this variant exhibits second-order phase transitions. These results may inspire experimental investigations into the various possibilities present in the social game of Mafia. The mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, comprising an encoder and multiple expert networks, has seen significant advancements in speed and efficiency over traditional GMMs under conditions of sufficient data and ample resources. However, the adherence to Gaussian distributions in emulating diverse data patterns results in sluggish convergence and inefficiency under data scarcity or real-time demands. This issue persists due to inadequate sampling in MoE, resulting in subpar performance and incompatibility with modern convolutional models. This article presents a novel algorithmic platform aimed at resolving these shortcomings through modified distribution estimation methods, incorporating non-Gaussian options. The platform, dubbed MoEMA (Mixture of Extended w/ various Mean distributions), incorporates enhanced algorithms for robust estimation and combines them with a dynamic growth strategy (GROW) to dynamically optimize the number of GMM components. The suitability of each component's shape allows for better fitting and compatibility with CNN structures. The proposed solution exhibits superior performance in variational autoencoders (VAE) ground truth comparisons, alongside significant reductions in inference time, surpassing the current state-of-the-art in compression and reconstruction quality across various datasets in image, text, and audio formats. The source code is accessible via https://github.com/kr3098/MoEMA. As for its potential for generating new ideas, while the generator in normal VAEs produces novel data by maintaining the latent code's class, the MoEMA generator learns to represent the diversity within a latent code through the multiple sub-generators, enabling the creation of diverse images from the same latent code and thereby presenting a new platform for creative production. This study investigates the existence of nontrivial algebraic solutions to a class of counting problems rooted in combinatorial token-firing protocols and examines their intrinsic geometric qualities. Specifically, we represent the associated counting functions as modular forms with respect to the Jacobian variety of a particular configuration, and extend this analysis to represent the associated functions as modular differentials with respect to the intermediate Prym variety in scenarios where the given configuration is unipotent. Moreover, for special token-firing protocols known as unipotent cluster algorithms, we represent the associated functions as modular forms and $\tau$-functions with respect to the intermediate variety. Ultimately, we establish a connection between certain special cases of these token-firing protocols and the K3 surfaces associated with Eichler-Shimura relations for unipotent cluster algorithms. This work is significantly influenced by the recent discoveries of Tokunaga and Yoshida. These results build upon the work of Yoshida. This note presents an illustration of the fragile b-principle by applying it to the case of the Mumford hypothesis. The Mumford hypothesis states that the intersection of a free group and a free product of two other free groups, all formed from a specified finite set, contains infinitely many elements of a specific minimum size when the set includes at least two distinct elements. Although this hypothesis is known to be true, our illustration demonstrates how the fragile b-principle can be used to derive this conclusion. Additionally, this illustration also provides a derivation method that can be understood by someone without advanced mathematical knowledge, as it translates an algebraic problem into an equivalent geometric problem involving compact manifolds and their mappings, and further simplifies the issue into a question about the degrees of mappings between these objects. Ultimately, this derivation relies on a combination of classical findings and a key property related to the geometric configuration of these objects. Specifically, this property can be verified through a simple inspection of the natural mapping from a sphere to a torus. Consequently, this derivation provides an alternative proof of the Mumford hypothesis and a more intricate instance of the fragile b-principle. The note concludes with some general comments about the fragile b-principle and its relationship with modern Felix-Herrlich-Lusstern theorems as well as its potential applications in achieving a more general and challenging goal: proving the geometric b-principle for surfaces. 

In addition to this, I also address a related open problem which is to identify whether a specific mapping from a sphere to a square is continuous or not. 

The Derivation Method described in this illustration, which translates an algebraic problem into a geometric one, holds a broad significance and could be useful in many other cases. Moreover, this illustration also serves as a further example of the fragile b-principle, which enables us to derive a conclusion from a collection of weaker statements. 

The discussion in this illustration assumes a significant level of mathematical sophistication, however the fragile b-principle itself is conceptually clear and can be understood without further explanation. 

The fragile b-principle represents a fundamental idea, which has been explored in greater detail by other researchers under the name of the fundamental b-principle.

Deep learning models are generally expected to excel in robustness and transferability.  Research has focused on developing various methods to enhance a model's transferability; however, there is a lack of concrete theory.  It's often assumed that a model's accuracy and transferability are strongly linked, yet this paper reveals that they are not always directly related.  Furthermore, it's commonly believed that a challenging training environment enhances a model's transferability; however, this paper also dispels this notion, showing alternative scenarios where this is not the case.  Instead of relying on different training and testing data, this paper explores the use of unlabeled data for evaluation and demonstrates through theoretical analysis and experimental results that incorporating L2 regularization in unlabeled scenarios leads to improved transferability. The findings suggest that transferability is better influenced by a model's inherent properties rather than typical factors such as accuracy and training conditions.  While there may be scenarios where these factors correlate with each other, they are not always mutually dependent.  This knowledge could aid future research in identifying and understanding the underlying principles of transferability.  Moreover, various potential research directions based on this study's conclusions are also outlined. The data and code used in this research are available at https://github.com/AIresearcher/Rethinking-Transferability.

In diverse networks, a considerable proportion of nodes are connected to specific clusters, exhibiting organically divided structures. Human brain networks, for example, are characterized by the formation of distinct functional modules separating sensory, motor, and other processing areas. These modular structures can enhance a network's stability but also hinder its ability to rapidly propagate information, such as neurophysiological signals or infectious diseases. Despite this, a principled explanation is lacking for the impact of modular network organization on information dissemination speed. Using a stochastic model based on irreversible process principles, we show that a network's modularity indeed influences its communication efficiency. By quantifying information dissemination speed within mock neural and social networks of varying modularity levels, we find that a greater number of inter-module connections accelerates information spread. This suggests that strengthening connections between different functional modules can facilitate faster information dissemination, thereby improving communication across distinct processing areas. This research offers original insights into the modular organization of complex systems and communicates quantitative findings that can inform designers of artificial neural networks to consider the importance of inter-module connections for efficient information spread. Furthermore, this work contributes to existing theoretical models by providing a fundamental understanding of the role modularity plays in information dissemination speed through experimental validation across multiple scales. Consequently, this study has significant practical implications, notably for designing reliable online systems that can withstand malicious attacks and design effective vaccines against information-disease spread in complex networks. Our analysis also recognizes the importance of further investigating the inter-module connections that accelerate information dissemination speed. Given the considerable interest in understanding this topic within the neuroscience community, the experiments discussed in this paper primarily focus on identifying the underlying network properties that determine information dissemination speed; determining the associated physical mechanisms remains a topic for future research. The research's implications for various fields, such as neuroscience, computer science, and sociology, are also discussed. We propose a new perspective that accounts for these findings through a specific model assumption. Under this assumption, there's a minimum threshold for model complexity and training data quality beyond which excessive model capacity won't improve performance. In practice, this means overparameterized models can still achieve good performance, but only if they're trained with limited data and larger batch sizes. This is because smaller models can't handle smaller batch sizes and result in poor training performance. This research makes a novel contribution to understanding overparameterization by emphasizing the role of computational limitations, a factor not previously considered in model analysis. In accelerator physics, beam particles undergo longitudinal and transverse acceleration separately. A key feature of these separate accelerations is that they can impart both longitudinal and transverse stability and momentum when directed at the optimal angle. When particles interact with a radio-frequency (RF) field during this process, the transfer of phase, amplitude, and momentum takes place. A notable consequence of this interaction is that it can result in changes to the transverse and longitudinal beam emittances. 

Our research involved conducting an experiment at Fermilab to investigate this effect, utilizing a nomal electron beam and a specially created interaction region replicating a particle collider injector. We aimed to quantitatively assess the separate and combined effects of an RF field on the transverse and longitudinal emittances. Our experiment, successful in detecting these emittances for the first time, also revealed new insights into beam manipulation and may offer a solution to mitigate undesired changes to beam quality during acceleration. Additionally, we explored the applications and implications of this effect for existing and future particle accelerators. Our experiment further examined compensation methods to mitigate undesirable effects and evaluated the feasibility of employing this technique to enhance beam quality. Our findings provide a comprehensive analysis, encompassing corrected and uncorrected equations, experimental results, and applications of this effect. Our work also initiates further studies to integrate this technique into accelerator designs. 

Our experiment was funded by the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science and we are now investigating the potential to integrate this effect into designs of the future Higgs Factory, a high-luminosity Higgs particle detector at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN). This effect may also be adapted for other accelerators, such as the future collider at CERN, proposed by the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) and Large Hadron Collider (LHC) experiments. A report outlining our latest research in this field was published in April 2020. Currently, our team is working on a paper titled "Accelerating and keeping beams on the edge: a new technique to achieve high luminosity," which is scheduled for publication in March 2021. To investigate the structure of low-laying states in medium-sized nuclei, a shape-driving collective movement influenced by minimal distance is introduced, where the architecture of nuclear shapes is built upon the principle that a nucleus minimizes the distance between its particles. This approach results in a finite-range potential that encourages collective movements, and it can reproduce the E2 transition strengths related to the beta-3 zero-point vibrations of 36Mg. Furthermore, the dynamical shape movements originating from the beta-3 zero-point vibrations are identified as a four-dimensional rotational state, and its E2 transition strengths are found to align with those derived from inelastic alpha-scattering experiments. This confirms that the minimal distance concept has the potential to accurately describe the collective movements within the single-particle states in a truncated shell-model framework. Subsequently, the low-lying states of 32Mg and 34Mg were investigated through the same theoretical method, and it was discovered that they can be explained by a shape-driving movement inherent to the minimal distance concept. Training deep convolutional autoencoders (CAEs) with vast datasets helps in developing feature extraction capabilities that are crucial for identifying alterations in a given image. However, due to time constraints and the high cost of collecting data, it's highly impractical to collect pairs of images for training. Therefore, previous research mainly relied on a dataset of only warped images. Although this approach led to improved results, it came with the drawback of increased dimensionality and loss of linear class separability. In response to these challenges, we propose combining the feature extraction capabilities of two unsupervised CAEs, each trained on normal and warped images, with different architectures. The features are then input into a central classifier for determining whether two images belong to the normal or altered class. By integrating these features, we achieve a significant boost in accuracy while reducing dimensionality and preserving linear class separability. Experiments conducted on three datasets showcase the effectiveness of this proposed method. Moreover, since this method remains unsupervised, it's possible to extend its applicability to various alteration recognition scenarios where manual labeling is impractical. Lastly, this method demonstrates promising results and can be leveraged for building robust, high-fidelity spatio-temporal alteration detection systems in areas such as industrial inspection, medical analysis, or military applications involving hidden threats. Our proposal for cyclical CDM models, which alternate between expansion phases akin to $\Lambda$CDM and contraction phases, has been presented. By replacing the dark energy component with a static one in the contraction phase, its density remains constant. During the expansion phase following contraction, a new static dark energy component emerges, regulating the dark energy density. By adjusting parameters, the behavior of the effective dark energy density, similar to $\Lambda$CDM, can be replicated. This phase transition affects Hubble's constant, causing its measured value to differ between the two phases. This, in turn, presents potential resolutions for the Hubble constant discrepancy observed between SNe Ia and BAO data. Additionally, possible implications for the cosmic chronometers equation, CMB, and solar system observations have been examined. By matching the CMB and solar system data to the current phase, specific time frames for these observations can be determined. This work focuses on the mathematical framework of the model rather than its physical origins of the phase transition. This model does not require fine-tuning and is characterized by two key parameters, allowing it to be easily tested through observations. Furthermore, observing the universe in both phases, where the cosmic chronometers equation and cosmic microwave background measurements are inconsistent, presents an additional, independent way to validate the model. This model's predicted outcomes for various observables have been compared to those obtained in the currently favored Lambda-CDM model. Based on these comparisons, predictions for discrepancies in the cosmic chronometers equation and CMB have been made, as well as predictions for solar system data, such as DKR2, OGLE, and SNe Ia, assuming each observation reached its current value in our preferred model. This work is focused on developing a fundamental understanding rather than deriving the cosmological model. This understanding includes formulating equations for chronometer quantities in our model, assuming they behave linearly, and exploring possible relationships between these variables. Studies indicate that DKR2 and SNe Ia observations could serve as best indicators for our model's viability. Moreover, current DKR2 data already exhibit promising consistency with our model, as do solar system data, while SNe Ia data might reveal the existence of our model through further analysis. This work is intended to lay the groundwork for a comprehensive analysis of the model's features and offers suggestions for future research. In various forms of communication, such as comments and posts on social networking sites, keyphrases play a vital role in summarizing content for users, acting as a concise preview, and enhancing search engine performance by accelerating query retrieval. Considering the growing demand for search engine applications on Internet of Things, IoT, devices, we investigate the potential of employing neural networks for keyphrase detection on such gadgets. To contribute to the advancement of IoT search engines, we introduce a search dataset tailored for IoT devices, comprising computer vision data featuring images of items and users' accompanying keyphrases. Since current keyphrase detection techniques rely heavily on extensive, high-quality data but are in short supply for IoT devices, we develop an innovative method to automatically generate keyphrases and accompanying images. Furthermore, we establish an evaluation metric to assess keyphrase detection performance and conduct various experimental analyses. Notably, our proposed model surpasses conventional keyphrase detection benchmarks and even outperforms strong keyphrase detection networks, such as BERT, in multiple tests. Moreover, we observe a significant advantage of our proposed approach over existing techniques in generating accurate keyphrases for unfamiliar items encountered by users in everyday life, such as smartwatches. Overall, our method outperforms existing keyphrase detection techniques in this area and shows great promise for practical application in this domain. The proposed dataset and code will be available for download on GitHub once published in a peer-reviewed journal. Currently, the work has been accepted for publication in a conference. The associated search dataset and code can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.737063. and https://github.com/nerdajo/IoT-KeyphraseDataset. respectively.

When capturing scenes, digital cameras often fail to avoid obstructions like power lines or obstacles, necessitating a wider field of view. A smooth and detailed wide-view image can be achieved by combining multiple shots, a process known as panoramic stitching. Since most humans lean towards viewing scenes from a downward perspective in their daily lives due to the preference for ground-based views, we propose an effortless method for wide-view capture. We call this method Latency-based Panoramic Capture, and it involves simply taking consecutive photos with a standard field of view, but always aiming the lens downwards. Once the shots are taken, the image can be seamlessly merged to produce a wide 360-degree view in an octahedral pattern. Another variant of this method involves capturing shots with a camera turned upside down, taking them in a specific sequence that ensures a 360-degree, triangular-based capture approach. Both methods produce high-quality, seamless 360-degree panoramic images with minimal post-processing required, and they're also compatible with existing stitching algorithms used for cameras without a wide view. We tested these methods with various cameras and imaging software, such as Google's Panorama and Autostitch, finding they perform just as well or better under optimal lighting conditions, while also producing fewer errors in cases of overlapping coverage and vanishing points. A demonstration of the Upside Down Panorama Capture approach can be found at udpc.net. In terms of potential applications, we explored the possibility of implementing a panoramic camera on a drone with a set angle, finding it could produce a unique feature for Instagram. Similarly, attaching a wide-view camera to a robot could significantly improve its object recognition capabilities, while simply using the Latency-based Panoramic Capture method results in cost-effective, wide-view cameras for applications in law enforcement, the military, or medical fields. In terms of semantic features, combining the Latency-based Panoramic Capture method with existing techniques such as semantic segmentation or classification enables the seamless merging of images taken from different perspectives, while also enabling a deeper analysis of the images. In terms of future research, the key to seamlessly merging images lies in part-selectivity, and future researchers should explore the integration of PC-based capture methods with other techniques, such as non-parallel capture methods, that do not require adjusting the camera's perspective. In our research, we're working with complex systems that draw upon elements from physics and biology. We're using a stochastic approach based on Ginzburg-Landau theory and a recursive method to understand pattern formation in both spatial and non-spatial contexts. We've found that certain patterns, such as those related to mean field equations and equilibrium states, aren't entirely reliable. We've developed an extended pattern set that includes these 'basic' patterns and an infinite range of more intricate designs. By exploring this system's heritability using a recursive method and applications to both continuous and discrete systems, we've demonstrated that only a subset of these patterns can persist and evolve over time. We've also discovered two criteria that determine a pattern's heritability: its adaptability and consistency. We've further established that the pattern space evolves according to a natural flow, with each pattern influencing its successors, and developed a simple strategy for guiding the evolution of these patterns. Ultimately, we've shown that by starting with random patterns and allowing them to evolve, the system can produce diverse, self-sustaining designs on its own. We've tested this idea by creating various machines, each with its own inherent patterns, and examined the connections between this approach and established concepts in multi-agent systems and evolutionary algorithms. Collective Sequential Learning aims to build a comprehensive model that combines data from multiple online streams. This task has a higher success rate than traditional online interleave CSL, which learns from a single stream at a time, but still faces challenges in adapting to evolving concepts. To overcome these difficulties, we introduce a novel approach called NF-OCL, a neural framework for online collective continuous learning. This framework addresses several issues related to online CSL. First, we calculated the statistical parameter for collective classification and proposed an online update method. In recent years, research on permutation polynomials over finite fields has been in high demand due to their vast applications in cryptography. As knowledge in this field deepens, studies have focused on different types of permutation polynomials, including those that arise from permutation functions, which are key elements in their construction. A particular class of permutation functions, known as $k$-permutation functions, that satisfy specific conditions on their outputs, have been the focus. A notable type of $k$-permutation function, the complete permutation function (CPF), is defined by its unique output for distinct input, $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$, in the given field: $f(a_{1})\vee f(a_{2}) = q^{k}$, with $\vee$ denoting the maximum value. Previously, studies on CPFs were limited to degree three or less, but this paper extends that analysis to degree $k=3$, providing necessary and sufficient conditions for their existence, as well as exploring general properties of such CPFs. Additionally, the paper examines variants of CPFs, including those with specific irreducible polynomial representations and their variants, known as weak CPFs, especially in the context of symmetric CPFs. A determinantial analysis of weak CPFs is provided when $k=3$, which may lay groundwork for future research. Moreover, the paper confirms the open problem from 2016, proposed by Wei, Guo, and Liu, that there are no weak CPFs when $k=3$ in the given field. All of these research findings have been provided with the relevant examples and computer code, using a recent version of Sage for the purpose of replication. Additionally, some potential avenues for future research are outlined in the concluding chapter. This paper introduces a novel proactive flight control approach named Partial Impulse-Diffusion Algorithm (PIDA), which achieves seamless transition between steady and fluid flight states.
PIDA utilizes a stochastic dual simplex method to optimize and determine the coefficients and shift of a piecewise polynomial function, allowing for a first-order Markov jump model to describe its dynamic behavior.
The Regulator Equilibrium Law is used to calculate the control input, comprising a feedback component from the current state and an impulse component from the optimal policy function.
PIDA is applied to a range of complex problems, including a mobile robot navigating through obstacles, a drone flying through gates, and a car evading obstacles, with the latter two scenarios incorporating time constraints. 
Our results demonstrate that PIDA can efficiently handle a wide array of challenging flow and steady flight control issues with high reliability. Due to the inherent stochasticity of the problems it aims to solve, PIDA successfully adapts a genetic filter method to eliminate unfavorable scenarios and achieve optimal solutions in a timely manner, thus outperforming genetic search and yielding substantial improvements in solution quality. The eventual solutions derived from PIDA exhibit predictable system behaviors, exemplifying its ability to facilitate smooth transitions between fluid and steady flight states. Observations indicate that the main cause of control path suboptimality in PIDA is often a straightforward, easily addressable issue related to an overestimated model that fails to account for the local environment; thus, fine-tuning the extent of the model's environmental consideration can greatly enhance PIDA's performance. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute a pioneering approach for prophylactic flight control and may also be adapted for other types of flow and steady problems with the added benefit of genetic filter optimization. We propose the shadow of a quantum state as an essential representation for quantum channel tomography, offering advantages over traditional state tomography. This representation has lower variance in the estimation of trace bets than state tomography, specifically with a lower variance of $\mathcal{O}(1/N^2)$ as compared to $\mathcal{O}(1/N^3)$ for states. Additionally, shadow tomography has higher accuracy, with the widest applicability of classical machine learning techniques. We utilize deep neural networks for shadow tomography with the following results: With the same number of measurements as state tomography, the shadow method can achieve the same precision in trace bets; With 4% more measurements, the shadow method can precisely replicate any quantum channel's Choi state with the same precision as state tomography. We also employ shadow methods to accurately estimate full matrix representations of quantum gates with the same precision as state tomography. Furthermore, the shadow method enables the accurate estimation of trace bets for low-coherence quantum states with the same precision as state tomography. Last, we prove that the shadow representation's low-bias estimation for trace bets is unique to quantum systems and does not apply to classical systems. These findings pave the way for the widespread use of shadow methods in practical quantum device characterization tasks. Implementing shadow methods significantly simplifies the process of quantum device calibration, making it more feasible to apply this method in practical contexts. Although the shadow representation bears some similarities to classical empirical distributions, we demonstrate that the shadow representation's sampling space is distinct from classical samples, with the shadow representation's span corresponding to the kth Hermite polynomial's subspace. As a result, the shadow representation's dimension, iN/(2k), tightly limits the precision of trace bet estimators. Consequently, the precision of trace bet estimators is significantly improved when k is small, resulting in the widely observed pre-asymptotic low-bias regime in classical and quantum estimation problems. Moreover, the precision of trace bet estimators is independent of sample size in this low-bias regime and is solely determined by the dimension of the shadow representation. Using countably infinite outcome spaces as our test case, we investigate the feasibility of applying shadow methods to non-countable quantum systems, and our initial findings suggest that the shadow methods can be extended to such systems. Furthermore, an examination of energy distribution among thermal energy, magnetic fields, and kinetic energy over this distance reveals a shift: in the inner Solar Wind, thermal energy and kinetic energy become more equally balanced as we get closer to the Sun's edge. These changes in energy distribution are consistent with what theoretical models predict for Solar Wind behavior near the Sun's edge, and they also align with previous findings from other Space missions within 0.8 to 1.1 AU from the Sun. These results were published in the Journal of Geophysical Research, in the issue dated March 2021, volume 126, article A0301. Our analysis spans a time period from September 2018 to February 2020, and it's based on eight different Solar cycles. These results were presented at the 41st COSPAR meeting in April 2021, in the title "Study of Solar Wind Energy Changes in the Inner Heliosphere," and they also formed the foundation of a Solar Wind presentation at the 2021 AGU meeting, in the title "Solar Wind Energy Changes near the Sun as Peraced by Parker Solar Probe." Researchers have long known that second-generation (G2) black holes within close orbital proximity to their host galaxy's disk are susceptible to a supernova-level event triggered by stellar encounters. Past studies have estimated a merger timespan of approximately one billion years, although a detailed calculation based on all possible outcomes has yet to be found. To better understand this process, a statistical model incorporating various factors was used to analyze data from an image, splitting galaxies into smaller and larger components. The results revealed a significant shift in ratio for galaxies with masses less than 10^10 solar masses, but not beyond this threshold, suggesting a link between this event and the formation of massive early-type galaxies. The calculated merger rates ranged from 10^-5 to 10^-4 per year, and exhibited an inverse correlation with galaxy mass, aligning with previous observations. Additionally, these results help to explain a notable dip in red early-type galaxies with intermediate masses, known as the'red gap.' Furthermore, the data suggest a significant link between the ratios of red and blue early-type galaxies and the merger timespan, particularly in densely star-forming environments. By quantifying the relevant factors through this analysis, researchers believe their results provide valuable insights into the process of massive early-type galaxy formation and the evolution of their central black holes. Given the selection criteria used in this study, it is estimated that about 5% of all massive early-type galaxies with masses above 10^10 solar masses have experienced this particular event, and are now hosting a 100 million solar mass black hole within 0.13 parsecs from their plane. The data also point to an interesting possibility that these events may be detectable through both optical and radio observations of these galaxies. To further support their findings, the researchers performed harmonic analysis on these potential host galaxies to determine any noticeable effects resulting from the supernova-level event, which in turn enabled them to estimate both the mass and the velocity of the accreting black hole. The calculated mass for the black hole ranged from 5 to 100 million solar masses, while the velocity ranged between 200,000 and 3 million kilometers per hour. To confirm these estimates, the researchers recommend either using X-ray observations to measure the velocity of the accreting black Hole, or using spectroscopy to determine the mass of these putative Black Hole hosts. According to the Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravitation, a cometary object's electric charge and mass contribute to its gravitational interaction in a specific manner that is not fully defined by the standard Newton's law or general relativity. This results in the presence of a repulsive gravitational force acting between a central point source and its periphery, explaining various astronomical observations and phenomena. Specifically, this effect can be responsible for the ejection of plasma and charged dust particles from comets, resulting in different trajectories that form an 'X' shape when viewed from a certain perspective. This distinct shape arises not only from the non-Newtonian gravitational interaction but also from the charge-over-mass distribution in the cometary nucleus. This unique phenomenon offers a novel area of research for the Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravitation, particularly in understanding the mechanism and cause of bipolar ejections in various astronomical objects. Furthermore, in accordance with the philosophical underpinnings of the Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravitation, this explanation does not require any modification to the concept of mass as per general relativity. Rather, this phenomenon illustrates how gravitational interaction deviates from the Newtonian model in specific astronomical settings. The theory also suggests a range of other potential phenomena that may be observed in the night sky. The original AZST-derived repulsive phenomenon continues to serve as a search criterion for detecting and understanding various astronomical objects, including young stars and planetary systems. The concept of the AZST-derived repulsive gravitational interaction is now being applied to a range of other novel gravitational phenomena. The present study serves as a companion to a previous paper, using observational data to assess the AZST-derived repulsive gravitational interaction in a bipolar ejection event. The study examines a distinctive comet shape in which the repulsive interaction plays a dominant role, offering a new detection method for detecting and understanding various astronomical objects. The research reveals that the shape of the comet can be explained by the trajectory of the ejected particles subject to a radial force, where the particles near the nucleus move more slowly than those further away. This difference in velocity is sufficient to account for the characteristic comet shape without invoking any additional factors. The AZST-derived repulsive interaction is utilized to a distance of one comet radius from the nucleus. The study provides a companion piece to a broader investigation into the search criteria for detecting and understanding various astronomical objects, including young stars and planetary systems, in which the AZST-derived repulsive interaction may play a significant role. The source of fast radio bursts, garnered significant interest since their initial discovery in 2007, remains unclear. To better understand the emission process, researchers studied nine bursts from seven repeating sources, employing the Very Long Baseline Array to measure the emission sites and its surroundings. Observing these sources under a 5 GHz radio continuum, researchers found that the emission from six repeating sources was not present, whereas sources SAR1640 and SAR6387 displayed elevated radio flux, quantified at 40$\pm$20 $\mu$Jy and 80$\pm$20 $\mu$Y, respectively. Measured Faraday rotation for these sources exceeded expected values, suggesting that the emission process may delay radio burst phenomena or occur in a larger emitting zone. Additionally, researchers established a maximum brightness diameter of 0.6 kilometers and a thickness of 0.5 kilometers for the Faraday rotating zone. The data suggests that the Faraday rotating medium could impede the identification of the FRB emission site, thus hindering our comprehension of the FRB mechanism. Furthermore, researchers propose a possible explanation for the substantial size of the Faraday rotating zone, suggesting it could be a result of cooling gas zonally compressing through a galaxy's potential well. The researchers also obtained pre-burst data for source 20220925C in the CHIME/FRB Catalogue, revealing no measurable emission, but a notable increase in flux was observed in a subsequent following observation at VLBA's 8.6 GHz frequency, quantified at 40$\pm$20 $\mu$Jy. Thus establishing a possible delayed scenario for FRB emission, in line with predictions from the self-consistent model, where X-ray-flare-activated magnetar models were evidenced. The researchers now monitor this FRB burst's behavior for an extended period to see its recurrence and to track any flux variations in anticipation of monitoring the postponed emission. Moreover, researchers plan to monitor the SAR6387 FRB burst for a longer duration to see its behavior in a higher 8 GHz flux state. The researchers' findings highlight the significance of the VLBA in accurately pinpointing FRB emission sites and its utility in detecting the Optical Transient Emission in FRBs. Ultimately, researchers' understanding of FRBs relies heavily on accurately characterizing and monitoring these bursts' behavior. Therefore, researchers strive to complement CHIME/FRB with a combination of radio telescopes equipped with diverse frequency capabilities to achieve this goal. The researchers' findings were presented at the AstroPUL

To facilitate the sharing of knowledge and collaborative design of laser systems, researchers have proposed overcoming this challenge by generating simple geometric models, leveraging powerful and highly-parallelizable computer tools such as generative design. By systematically developing a set of key technical specifications for high-powered laser systems capable of handling a wide range of powerful lasers, the researchers aim to empower designers and developers to tackle cutting-edge technological advancements and applications such as next-generation high-powered laser imaging systems for space, the structured exploration and analysis of planetary surfaces and subsurfaces. This approach aims to empower designers and developers to tackle these complex applications and investments by generating a comprehensive set of key technical specifications for high-powered laser systems, the structured evaluation and analysis of various design and optimization strategies and the facilitation of a knowledge sharing platform among the research community. This paper aims to provide a critical overview of the current state of key technological specifications for high-powered laser systems, the challenges and obstacles faced by the researchers and developers and the cutting-edge applications of these systems to propel technological advancements and investments forward. Finally, the article discusses important recommendations for the research and development of high-powered laser systems, the structured exploration and analysis of existing and future technological specifications and the potential investments and achievements in various high-powered laser systems and applications. Important features of the model include its ability to accurately describe the fundamental characteristics of high-powered laser systems, the complex scaling of the model due to the high-powered requirements and the potential for a lower power regime and the parallelizable nature of the computational process. Current text generation models operate in a silent environment, forcing them to rely on internal cognitive processes.  A novel approach involves equipping language models with a visual display that mirrors interactions with their surroundings.  This external visualization tool allows models to incorporate external stimuli, augmenting their internal representations.  To demonstrate the potential of this approach, researchers developed the 'Can You See That?' task, where a GPT-2 based model is instructed to craft compelling short stories incorporating specific images and target words.  Images and textual inputs are combined in different ways, tested across varying scenarios, and analyzed using evaluation metrics and human assessments.  The results suggest that incorporating visual cues leads to a significant enhancement in the quality of textual representations, leading to stories that are both coherent and visually aligned.  This research serves as an initial exploration of the interaction between visual and textual cues in guiding the behavior of language models.  It lays the groundwork for further investigations into the development of unified artificial intelligence systems that effectively integrate visual and textual inputs. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not offer the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we propose that its ability to be compatible with DPoS consensus mechanisms provides a reasonable trade-off for faster and more efficient payments.
In an effort to contribute to the growth of the Bitcoin Privacy project, we chose to base our Delegated RingCT prototype on Bitcoin Smart Contracts, allowing users to create RingCT transactions.
The prototype's success marks an important step toward integrating Delegated RingCT on the Bitcoin network through a proposed change. A separate open-source project for the Bitcoin Fork has been created.
