The 2020-2030 period has been deemed the decade when smart transportation and the widespread use of the Internet of Things (IoT) will have a profound impact on our lives, particularly in the areas of education and transportation. As the world progresses through this decade, the concept of the smart city will continue to evolve as a sophisticated integrated system combining technological advancements like 5G networks, AI, machine learning, blockchain, and deeply interconnected systems. Educating future generations on these cutting-edge technologies is essential for adapting to the rapidly changing digital environment, but has been plagued by several challenges including data security, safety concerns, and maintaining a balance between privacy and data usage. To address these issues, various frameworks have been proposed for utilizing IoT in educational settings, but most of them have been ineffective in providing comprehensive solutions. To avoid repeating these mistakes for other digital platforms and keep pace with progressing technologies, there is a growing need for a decentralized, trust-based framework that empowers individuals to take charge of their own data and offers a secure, transparent, and verifiable environment for education and skill-development. Therefore, this paper aims to introduce a decentralized, blockchain-based framework that enables users to take charge of their information and provides a secure, transparent environment for skill development and education within the context of the Internet of Vehicles (IoV). This paper starts with an in-depth examination of IoT-based educational frameworks for IoV and identifies existing gaps and challenges in these systems. It then proposes a novel framework that addresses these issues through decentralization and incorporates the unique aspects of IoT, 5G networks, and blockchain technologies for IoV. Next, we outline the comprehensive framework consisting of several layers including the resource pool, the service platform, the skill verification mechanism, the diversified payment methods, and the skill marketplace. Subsequently, we provide a comprehensive framework implementation plan, discussing essential technological components, their development, and the prototype development requirements. Finally, we highlight potential challenges and future research opportunities inspired by this decentralized, blockchain-based educational framework for IoV. The presented framework can serve as a foundation for future educational programs in this field and spark innovative research ideas for future IoT-based educational systems. This survey study covers various blockchain enabled federated educational frameworks for IoV but excludes other related topics such as blockchain enabled IoV and federated learning in IoV as they pertain to a different aspect of the technology.

Achieving ground-breaking advancements in quantum computing will necessitate the convergence of breakthroughs in two main areas: 1) the development of highly advanced superconducting qubits capable of withstanding a superconducting magnetic field, and 2) the creation of a laboratory environment with an exceptionally low-temperature platform that can sustain a weak electric field necessary for these qubits. Historically, the processing of semiconductors has required grounding setups to manage stray voltages but have not been sufficient in providing the necessary temperature conditions. Our solution lies in a new experimental setup developed at Fermilab's one-ton scale quantum facility, where a 1.3K platform with millikelvin stability and a 10V range of adjusted grounding has been successfully established using a helium-3-cooled surface mixer and a helium-3 heat exchanger. This setup allows us to demonstrate its effectiveness with a superconducting qubit. Our novel superconducting cooling system offers an affordable and highly reliable solution, providing a feasible pathway for laboratory development and experimentation. This innovation is set to revolutionize the development of quantum computing and associated applications. Our setup's exceptional performance even at elevated temperatures lends itself seamlessly to quantum error mitigation strategies. Moreover, the versatility of this system will make it an ideal candidate for research across various fields such as string theory-based post-5G communications, experimental simulations of quantum field theories, and computer simulations, all driven by the increasing demand for superconducting quantum information systems. Our work marks the first successful integration of a millikelvin platform at large high-energy facilities, paving the way for future collaborations between high-energy and quantum computing communities, ultimately paving the way for practical applications of quantum computing at the renowned research facilities of Fermilab and CERN. Our groundbreaking work opens new avenues for integrating experimental advancements in quantum computing and corresponding computational simulations and data analyses. The presentation of our work at IEEE conferences in 2021 and 2022 has garnered significant interest and attention from the quantum community. Following an introductory presentation at Fermilab's user facility in April 2021, we initiated a comprehensive study and demonstration of this system at the one-ton scale quantum facilities and small labs across the USA. Our work has significant potential for successful integration with other research facilities and laboratories, paving the way for innovative applications at the renowned research centers of Fermilab and CERN. Our study and demonstration of this system at the one-ton scale quantum facilities and small labs across the USA resulted in successful integration and demonstration of a substantial millikelvin platform.

Previous research indicates a lack of fundamental computational skills among some users, yet focuses primarily on human errors. We aim to explore non-error based issues, examining instead misuse of existing algorithms. A diverse group of five assessors evaluated a dataset consisting of 248 Python algorithms relevant to distributed ledgers, undergoing a diffusion-based review to identify implementable solutions. Out of 248 assessments, 220 were found to receive a score of at least 4, indicating an implementable solution is likely. A total of 135 out of 248 implementations scored a 5, suggesting a well-designed solution is in place. Additionally, 76 of 248 implementations failed to hash a user-provided text, causing potential security breaches, while 62 of 248 implementations failed to properly verify a public key, thus compromising security. Our findings reveal a range of non-error based issues affecting the security of cryptocurrency-related Python implementations, emphasizing a need for a systematic approach to assess algorithmic misuses. A corresponding repository is available at https://github.com/ucibsse/labs/blob/main/distributed-ledgers-misuses-in-the-wild.Insensitive, 2022.

WORTH, a real-world urban setting project, is designed to investigate the practical potential of Wireless Sensor Networks for solving complex problems in intelligent urban infrastructures. Daily life activities in cities can be analyzed by integrating sensor data with high-resolution geographic mapping. This paper presents a method for automatically categorizing data from Chicago into six distinct categories, which classify various urban sounds. By comparing sampling methods, we evaluated their impact on classification accuracy, and the resulting code is freely available online to facilitate replication. Our experiment demonstrated a 0.87 accuracy level on a large dataset of 14K samples with a modest 10-second time frame and eight-bit audio quality. Notably, this accuracy level could be achieved with only a short window of 21-second samples, which is equivalent to a 3-second audio fragment. Additionally, we observed that increasing the size of the classification dataset would further improve the accuracy level. Finally, the incorporation of city maps into the tagging process revealed significant synergies between geographic mapping and sound classification. Existing methods, such as L1-based techniques, are based on the uniform distribution model. As a result, they often yield poor outcomes. In this research, we introduce a novel model, Non-Uniform Sparse Addition Model (NUSPAN), which better captures the true nature of seismic data sparseness. A novel neural network, Proximal Mean Network (PMNet), is also designed for PMSPAN, its NUSPAN counterpart. In a graded optimization process, PMNet's first layer learns a non-linear transformation of the data, with subsequent layers learning the proximal and mean functions specific to the data's underlying distribution. When tested on synthetic data, PMNet significantly outperformed comparison methods in terms of the total absolute unweighted mean squared error metric. Even with a 1000:1 ratio of fake noise to signal, PMNet was able to successfully recover the seismic reflectivity with high accuracy. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that PMNet's performance is superior to that of comparison methods in a real-world seismic inversion setting. Deep learning has a wide range of applications in seismic analysis, but it often operates under the assumption that data is uniformly sparse. In reality, seismic reflectivity typically exhibits the characteristics of a negative power-law distribution rather than uniform sparsity, a fact that has historical implications for recovery methods. Initially, research attempted to apply L1-based techniques in a l2-norm setting but these yielded disappointing results. More recently, research has shifted its focus to the Laplace distribution and its underlying sparsity model as a means of improving seismic data recovery. However, this research overlooks another critical aspect of seismic data, namely its non-uniform sparsity. In this research, we explore the possibility of applying a non-uniform sparse addition model and proximal mean function, one that better captures the true nature of seismic data's underlying distribution and trend. This approach is grounded in the analysis of wavefunction overlaps and demonstrates universality in certain systems characterized by a zero or ground-state overlap. To support and validate this method, the researchers first apply it to a non-universal case involving the Haagerup model, and then leverage existing research on the overlap spectrum to facilitate comparisons, thereby assessing the algorithm's precision. The task of part-of-speech (POS) annotation in linguistic analysis is a crucial component that is currently facing a shortage of suitable tools for historical texts, dating as far back as the 16th century. From a machine learning perspective, POS tasks for contemporary languages are successfully performed through sequences trained on large datasets, yet the approach is not effective to classify segments from older languages without contemporary analogs. A innovative statistical model referred to as the set-valued statistical model is proposed in this research to address the issue of labeling POS in historical collections. The model was successfully tested using two collections of French texts from the Renaissance period, showing an improvement of about 6% compared to the sequence-based approach. Moreover, the model was particularly beneficial in the context of word categories that are relatively underrepresented in the training data. The model's source code, as well as the pre-trained models, are available for download on the GitHub platform. This work offers a deeper examination of smooth integrability theories and their potential non-smooth counterparts. The well-known mathematical principles of moment methods, integrability thems of Laplace and Fourier, and Wigner distributions are key tools used in this work. The moment methods and Wigner distributions play a crucial role in addressing two critical challenges faced by moment methods: the inverse spectral problem and the speed of convergence of moments. A non-smooth integrability theory is proposed for the Fourier transform by using almost orthogonal sequences and polynomial approximations to resolve these issues. Moments that are almost orthogonal with respect to a measure can be used to reconstruct a function, F, by constructing a polynomial series, P, such that the difference between F and P tends to zero at a specified rate. The approximation error in this case is independent of the sequence's index, thus generalizing the Laplace transform's integrability theorem. The Fourier transform's approximability theorem is also derived from this generalized result. Furthermore, this work proposes a new criterion for almost orthogonal sequences that improves the rate of approximation and does not rely on smoothness conditions, thus facilitating the creation of a new class of non-smooth integrability theories. The main concepts and results in this work can be applied to a wide range of fields including random matrix and quantum chaos theories. The approximations and estimates employed in this work rely on basic mathematical techniques such as linear algebra, ergodic theory, and the principles of polynomial operator inequalities. The theoretical contributions made in this work can be extended to other areas of functional analysis. The proposed framework is flexible and can be used to derive new error bounds for approximative a posteriori analysis in various contexts. The practical utility of the new error bounds for the approximation of solutions of differential equations has also been demonstrated. The original findings in this area were published in a separate paper and will be presented at the International Workshop on Two Modern Correlations in Pisa, Italy in 2021. Urban planning professionals face a problem in meeting city residents' high hopes for urban development, as officially documenting these high expectations poses a significant challenge, requiring innovative solutions to streamline the process. The system consists of a user-friendly interface for surveying city residents, collecting and visualizing their development expectations, and generating formal specifications to outline how these expectations can be met. The system also offers a functional demonstration, showcasing its practical application in Paris, the 11th arrondissement. The system's design focuses on making expectations documentation efficient, manageable, and adaptable within existing city governance structures. The documentation process involves expectation categorization, using an ontology to ensure consistent expectation topics, and formalization, utilizing knowledge representation via Description Logics for non-negotiable expectation details. Currently, the best vision-language models are too focused on what they've been taught, relying heavily on a small set of annotated images and text pairs that have been manually labeled. As a result, they struggle to understand real-world challenges like reading signs from a car window or taking photos for search purposes. To overcome this limitation, we've developed a technique that enhances CLIP models by incorporating a guidance layer. This new VT-CLIP model uses a separate network to quickly extract key visual cues from images and then uses those cues to guide the model's attention to important parts of text, such as object names in a photo of a cat on a cup. This pre-trained VT-CLIP model is then fine-tuned on challenging image and text pairs that aren't easily annotated, significantly improving its performance in tasks like zero-shot learning and real-world challenges. To make these complex image and text pairs more manageable, we've created a new dataset with over 100,000 challenging image and text pairs and demonstrated the effectiveness of this new VT-CLIP model in solving real-world challenges. You can find the code and dataset at https://github.com/whli7k12/VinVL-CLIP. For example, when shown a photo of a car from the top of a bus, VT-CLIP was able to accurately identify 'green' as its color, whereas other models struggled to do so. At the same time, when shown a photo of a car, VT-CLIP and other models were able to accurately identify 'Toyota' as its make. To measure the efficacy of our proposed technique, we've created a new RealChallenge dataset with over 100,000 challenging image and text pairs and conducted a thorough evaluation of different vision-language models, evaluating their performance in real-world challenges. RealChallenge allows us to evaluate a CLIP model's performance in a variety of tasks, such as identifying whether a photo of a car is of a Toyota. To train and test the efficacy of our proposed technique, we've used a combination of computer vision and natural language processing tools, starting with a pre-trained CLIP model and refining it on challenging image and text pairs. This combination of tools allows us to achieve the state-of-the-art in real-world challenges, improving a model's performance in tasks like identifying whether a photo of a cat is on a cup. To achieve this level of performance, we've trained and tested the efficacy of our proposed technique on challenging image and text pairs in a manual annotation process, starting with a set of challenging challenges

The performance of linear systems in the presence of disturbance is a critical
property that is typically evaluated using the sensitivity of the system. A
notable criterion known as input-to-state stability (I/S) offers a detailed
assessment, input-to-state finite time stability being a more stringent
measure. Both I/S and input-to-state finite time stability have established
connections with universal robust noninteracting multiple coPrime channels,
a specific matrix system that is resistant to row rank changes. However, the
relationship between I/S, input-to-state finite time stability, and such matrix
systems has yet to be fully characterized. In this study, we establish these
connections and also demonstrate that, in addition to being disturbance immune,
these matrix systems can seamlessly integrate any linear control method with
minimal disruption to their robust characteristics. A practical method for
verifying the noninteracting property of these matrix systems is also provided. 
This research is a combination of several previously published studies, now
revised with enhanced clarity and validity. A new interpretation of I/S is also
proposed in the context of noisy matrix systems. A notable finding is that,
despite the global instability of some of these matrix systems, they can still
exhibit local finite time stability and employ feedback controllers with the
capacity to overcome disturbances. A particular example illustrates how these
matrix systems can adapt to changes in their environment, remaining stable
despite such transformations. 
Finally, we establish a link between I/S and input-to-state finite time
stability in the context of, respectively, universal noisy single-input, n-
input, and multiple-input matrix systems. 
A accompanying document with additional examples is available online. 
The study's findings have been presented at conferences in 2019 and 2020.

We classify the module segments of the Coherent Functors spectrum, which are based on a quaternionic linear algebra system, using the principles of inversion and reparametrization in the style of Elliptic Cohomology. This forms the foundation of a modular interpretation of quaternionic Elliptic Cohomology. Furthermore, this method can be extended to the study of module segments in the spectrum of Coherent Functors based on a real linear algebra system. Notably, such a Coherent Functors bears a close relationship with K theory but the current study focuses exclusively on this phenomenon in the context of quaternionic linear algebra systems. As part of our analysis, some specific module segments have been identified and demonstrated to conform to the principles of relative local systems. Our research, which involves a detailed analysis of quaternionic linear algebra Coherent Functors, reveals that the module segments based on groups such as 2-fold coverings of SO_3, certain twisted ramified complexifications, and the spinor layer of the 4-dimensional real nondegenerate quaternionic Jordan algebra consist of rings. This represents an essential step in the development of a possible quasichain duality in Coherent Functors, which would require the development of a mod 2 dual version of cohomology-discohomology theory. Moreover, our study offers new insights into the relationships between Elliptic Cohomology, K theory, and modular interpretation of quaternionic Elliptic Cohomology. This work is based on previously published findings. A detailed analysis of the degree of freedom in the reparametrization theory, which is crucial for the identification of the Coherent Functors spectrum, is presented in the preprint arXiv:2109.14963. This degree of freedom plays a key role in the calculation of Segments of the CMQK theory, which is presented in the preprint arXiv:2109.14964. The relationship between the reparametrization theory, quaternionic Elliptic Cohomology, K theory, and topological string theories is explored in the preprint arXiv:2109.14965. A mod 2 version of the theory, which is connected to the study of reflexive sheaves on toric varities, is presented in the preprint arXiv:2109.14966. This is followed by an examination of the global version of the theory, which is related to the Fukaya-Morihy theory in the preprint arXiv:2109.

In the fields of pathology and radiology, image analysis is a crucial component that has seen rapid advancements in automated detection and diagnosis through machine learning. Research into image analysis has been accelerating, but real-world applications face significant challenges due to data interoperability, compatibility, and management issues. We've developed highdicom to address these problems, providing a set of Python tools that support the transfer of data in the DICOM format and employ standard pathology and radiology encoding. With highdicom, image files can be created from machine learning models that are compatible with digital image files, allowing for seamless compliance with relevant standards. This enables decentralized and reliable data archiving, as well as enhanced transparency in image analysis. In this paper, we introduce highdicom, discuss its underlying concepts and strategies, and showcase its utility through two practical applications. Highdicom is now available under the permissive BSD-3 license, allowing researchers to utilize its open-source library to improve the efficiency of image analysis studies. By promoting the standardization of image labels and model results, we aim to contribute to the increased efficiency of image-based research and diagnosis by bridging the gap between machine learning and medical imaging. Ultimately, we outline our proposal for a new DICOM module called pqm, representing Percentage, Qualifier, Measured, and Range, and discuss its potential integration into existing DICOM pathologies and radiology standardization frameworks. The integration of highdicom and our proposed PQM module has the potential to significantly contribute to the expanded use of machine learning in diagnostic pathology and radiology. Furthermore, we suggest establishing an open-source community to develop highdicom and, more importantly, extend the DICOM standard to enhance image analysis across the healthcare sector. We anticipate that our work may serve as a starting point for the development of more research and clinical applications. This study demonstrates that by enhancing model transparency, we can raise awareness and accelerate research in computational pathology and radiology. The utility of highdicom becomes particularly apparent when used in conjunction with other DICOM-based tools, highlighting its potential to increase its utility in image-based research and clinical applications. Ultimately, the integration of highdicom into existing clinical workflows has the potential to increase transparency and promote a collaborative research setting at the intersection of machine learning, diagnostics, and image analysis. The final strategy put forth in this study recommends developing and disseminating easy-to-use, open-source tools like highdicom and promoting a standardized approach to research in image analysis, ultimately facilitating more effective clinical applications. We've established a connection between the brane entropy and the central charge in the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence, where the brane entropy arises from the variation of the surface-distributed Einstein-Hilbert action and the Noether current associated with this action corresponds to a surface-level conformal symmetry. This led us to the discovery that brane entropy and central charge are equivalent, a finding that holds true for any state within the brane. We subsequently generalized our result to higher dimensions, showing that the configuration space of the brane's world-volume film corresponds to the symplectic leaf of a semi-simple Lie algebra and that its entropy is driven by the variation of the surface-distributed CFT action, which is governed by the Gubser-Klebanov-Polyakov correlation function and possesses a Noether current associated with a two-dimensional Virasoro algebra. Our work reveals the 2D and D-dimensional brane entropies to be equivalent to the central charge and the $\mathcal{F}_3$ coefficient respectively. Furthermore, in the context of the non-Abelian T-dual of the Witten-Sakai-Witten brane system, we've demonstrated that the brane entropy is equivalent to the Hassanein-Klebanov entropy, thereby validating the Holographic Entropy Conjecture. In the molecular world, similar objects are expected to be close together in a high-dimensional representation. Therefore, it makes sense to apply embedding techniques, popular in unsupervised learning, to molecular data to discover underlying patterns, especially when labeled data is expensive to obtain. Nevertheless, many traditional distance measures are incongruous with the diversity of molecular data. To address this issue, we propose an unsupervised method for DNA sequence representation, which effectively copes with various types of molecular properties. Our method is inspired by the idea of treating sequences as paths in a high-dimensional space, where similar sequences are represented as nearest neighbors. To measure distance between sequences, we employ a graph-based method that highlights local structure, demonstrating the applicability of our approach to real-world DNA sequence datasets. Our results show that the proposed method leads to meaningful, interpretable results. Firstly, it reduces a complex high-dimensional space to a manageable low-dimensional space while preserving key properties. Secondly, it reveals subtle distinctions in DNA sequences that are obscured within the original high-dimensional space. Finally, it significantly improves the accuracy of unsupervised learning tasks using various measures of similarity. To our knowledge, there is no direct comparison between different unsupervised embedding techniques for molecular data. Therefore, we introduce a range of benchmarking tools for evaluating such methods in the context of DNA sequences. Our research shows that the proposed method is effective in extracting meaningful features from genetic data. This paper explores the concept of image orientation in the context of visual identification tasks. We argue that the orientation of an image is an inherent property rather than a attribute. As such, it should be part of the image representation. To this end, we propose a novel neural network architecture that utilizes orientation information. This orientation-aware architecture can be applied to various tasks, including multi-oriented image classification. To accommodate images of any orientation, we propose introducing a novel $360^\circ$ rotation augmentation technique and a new convolutional layer design. The proposed convolutional layer is inspired by the hemispherical image mapping concept. Furthermore, we utilize spherical convolution for enhanced orientation-specific representation. The combination of a spherical representation and orientation-specific information enables higher accuracy in orientation-invariant image classification tasks. To validate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we developed a $360^\circ$ rotation-dataset, dubbed Rotating Birds. We also tested our method on a well-known dataset, CUB-200-2011. The performance of our method was evaluated against state-of-the-art architectures, demonstrating superior results in orientation-invariant image classification tasks. A new educational method, the "See-Think Hear-Read" approach (also known as the TaoTella and MindTella techniques), has been developed with remarkable effectiveness for teaching and improving English as a second language primarily for Chinese speakers. A key component of this innovative method is the utilization of a customised online dictionary, the MindTella lexicon, which is exclusively focused on providing definitions for entries in the form of 'word-meaning'. Inspired by the efficacy of this innovative technique, a web-based English dictionary called LitMind Lexicon (www.litmindlex.com) was created), featuring over 230,000 dictionary entries, 160,000 synonyms, and 40,000 definitions for 'word-meaning' pairs. Additionally, the website offers an extensive collection of more than 8,000 popular novels and features the 'Search-Read-Recite' system (a component of the See-Think Hear-Read method). Users can generate customised word lists, monitor their progress, and receive data analysis on word usage, meaning, and related categories. A built-in system enables word detection, definition, and categorisation via automated and human oversight. This study provides an in-depth description of the LitMind Lexicon's features and showcases its dictionary search functionality through an example video. Moreover, the research presents numerical data on its word-related metrics and provides comparison benchmarks against other renowned English dictionaries. Ultimately, the LitMind Lexicon serves as a valuable resource for second-language learners, English language educators, and word/meaning data researchers. It is available for public access at www.litmindlex.com. Young stars surrounded by gas and small particles called debris disks emit light in the far-ultraviolet spectrum through photoelectric and thermal effects. FUV emissions enable the study of highly energetic photochemical reactions on the star's surface. Observations of the active T Tauri star AU Mic have revealed sudden changes in its FUV brightness, suggesting rapid variations between calm periods and intense outbursts. Typically, these changes occur over a few hours, but the exact duration is dependent on the star's activity level. Moreover, our simulations indicate that AU Mic's FUV spectrum undergoes significant changes during this process, resulting in varying degrees of ionization across the star's surface, ranging from 10^-4 to 10^-1. Notably, this phenomenon influences the formation mechanisms of organic molecules and water, and we propose that AU Mic's eruptive phase is insufficient to explain the high levels of water vapor observed in its atmosphere. Instead, we suggest that water vapor rises from the deep atmospheric layers, whereas high levels of CO and CH are the direct result of FUV-driven reactions. CO and CH are naturally depleted during calm periods and rapidly regenerated during intense outbursts. Similarly, AU Mic's Planetary Mass Object (PMO) is subject to intense thermal degradation during star eruptions, with potential consequences for its atmospheric composition, as observed for other FUV-exposed PMOs in our database. Specifically, a high ratio of CO to CH is diagnostic of an exposed and hot PMO, as seen for AU Mic b and c. However, these ratios are largely insensitive to variations in mass, temperature, and distance from the star. Moreover, similar FUV-driven chemical reactions are likely to occur on other PMOs located throughout the galaxy, as demonstrated by our cross-correlation analysis of the FUV spectra of nearby Exoplanetary Mass Objects. As a result, it is likely that the primary source of atmospheric CO in these objects is an interaction with their star's radiation, as observed for AU Mic and other nearby objects. However, the L1 analysis lacks standardization for the concept of entropic discontinuities and the construction of entropic shocks. In an attempt to fill this gap, a study has been initiated to establish the existence of entropic shocks through the use of a specific type of vanishing viscosity approximation for scalar conservation laws. Furthermore, the study aims to comprehensively review and clarify the standards of entropic discontinuities for systems of one-dimensional conservation laws. It specifically focuses on the classical example of the Burgers equation, as well as general systems of conservation laws formulated within the framework of the vector-bundle theory of conservation law physics. A key result of the study concerns the innovation of entropic shock existence theorems for a broad category of conservation law physics models, which includes scalar conservation laws, systems of one-dimensional conservation laws, and mult-dimensional conservation laws that have been previously investigated. In this context, the study of entropic shock existence theorems for scalar conservation laws was initiated by the demonstration of the innovation of entropic shock existence theorems for the explicitly time-dependent Burgers equation via the use of the Laplace transform of the inductive limit of the entropic weak solution theory for scalar conservation laws. Subsequently, the study of entropic shock existence theorems for scalar conservation laws was extended to include the time-independent case via the use of the induction theorem for scalar conservation laws, as well as the invariance of the entropic weak solution theory under time reparameterizations. We propose an early warning system that leverages data-driven methods for predicting and analyzing dynamic processes, specifically epidemic models. Our novel approach combines a linear residual-based technique with a weighted graph network filter and an inverse model-based filter, all operating in the frequency domain. These methods are developed without reliance on process models, utilizing solely graph-theoretic and data-driven principles. Our results showcase the method's effectiveness in detecting irregular behavior in real-time within large datasets, as well as its ability to forecast future behavior under various scenario simulations. Moreover, we demonstrate that this approach can enhance noisy process forecasts by leveraging additional external signals. Finally, we show that this method can be modified to accommodate regulation tasks by incorporating weighted adjacency matrix components, allowing for the influence of selected nodes to be prioritized, and even accommodate node and graph scaling operations to accommodate intricate epidemic scenarios. Our method's practicality is validated through application to realistic cases, specifically the study of norovirus outbreaks in a hospital and that of COVID-19 infections across European nations. The dynamics of a liquid layer along a fiber are influenced by the attachment of a droplet via a narrow connection. The liquid flow is governed by the hydrostatic pressure's edge effect and the viscoelastic properties of the liquid. Consequently, the steady-state equilibrium of the system is threatened when the liquid's viscosity and surface tension are compromised, which ultimately leads to the drift of the droplet along the fiber. The added mass effect, coupled with the presence of a local flow acceleration, determines the drift speed of the droplet in two scenarios. Firstly, when the droplet remains partially attached, its motion is influenced by the flow of the surrounding fiber layer and is characterized by a critical Reynolds number below which inertial forces are negligible. Secondly, when the droplet is completely detached, its motion is influenced by the flow of a small layer near the fiber and is characterized by a critical Reynolds number that depends on the thickness of this local flow layer, rather than the entire fiber coating, for its drift speed calculation. The slip at the liquid-fiber interface enhances drapet motion by reducing the fictional drag it experiences. The established model, based on a simplified theory, is confirmed by comparative simulations with direct numerical simulations of the flow, and is also extended to consider various real-world scenarios, such as the presence of the Capillary Instability. The findings of this study may have significant implications for the understanding and explanation of certain liquid droplet behaviors observed in applications such as liquid medication delivery and spray absorption in plants. The established model, based on a simplified theory, is also capable of predicting liquid droplet dynamics in certain real-world scenarios, such as the effects of gravity and fluid flow on a floating droplet, and is shown to be in good agreement with numerical simulation results. Furthermore, the study reveals the underlying mechanics of liquid droplet dynamics and provides valuable insights for the understanding and explanation of certain liquid droplet behaviors observed in various applications. The study also reveals the added mass effect to be a crucial factor in determining liquid droplet dynamics and predicts that the instability of partially attached droplets will be influenced by the size of the droplet and its speed of motion. The Hunter-Saxton equation, closely related to Eulers-minimal-grape equation, has a particular solution known as the HS-minimal-grape, which is the integrable solution to the same ODE as the Euler-minimal-grape. This article investigates the properties of HS-minimal-grape and demonstrates its Lipschitz robustness. Furthermore, by extending a past result, it is proven that HS-minimal-grape is the only solution to the equation for Lipschitz continuous functions, which reinforces a prior discovery by Euler. Additionally, the article demonstrates that within the context of BV functions, it is proven that nearly robustness holds. Similar to the scenario with the Euler-minimal-grape, the integration of a variation of the Steiner symmetrization, which is in fact independent, reveals the robustness for $W^{1,p}$ functions for 1 < p ≤ ∞. Moreover, using a distinct and independent method from past approaches with similar characteristics, such as the Euler-Poisson equation, the article is able to extend the p variation all the way to p = ∞. Lastly, through a newly discovered independence from the robustness of the integration, a more general scenario of function sets is established and the concept of n robustness for n positive integers is introduced and proven. Consequently, the n robustness holds for n = 2, 3 with these methods and the first method is applied for n = 4. The second method is applied for n = 5. For n = 1, it is proven through a previously discovered result. The new approach to the problem is also able to prove the concept of n robustness for linear functions and the first method is applied for n = 6 and n = 7. The article concludes by comparing the results of these methods and the results of the property of robustness for function sets. The results obtained previously on robustness for function sets, such as Lipschitz, BV, W^{1,p}, and more generally for n = 2, 3, 5, 6, and 7 are all independent from the integration, which indicates that they are likely to be inherent properties. The property for n = 1 is likely to be inherent as well, and more importantly, it is proven through a previously discovered result. The property for n = 8 and above will be investigated further. Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging can be more challenging than examining muscle-related conditions due to increased curvature. While both digital ultrasound equipment and human operators have limitations that affect reliability, robotic ultrasound technology offers potential improvements by maintaining a consistent probe pressure and avoiding soft tissue compression. A previous study indicated that manual scanning is prone to errors, primarily due to operator bias. To investigate the consistency of robotic ultrasound scanning in evaluating scoliosis, we compared it with manual scoliosis assessment. Our research involved measuring saggital index (SI) degree values obtained from 30 healthy subjects using both robotic and manual scanning methods. To minimize measurement errors, we employed multi-variable regression, repeated functional data analysis, and Bayesian inference techniques. Our results showed that the robotic scanning method was more consistent than the manual scanning method in evaluating scoliosis. Furthermore, the presence of a sonographer did not significantly affect the degree values of the robotic scanning method. These findings suggest that the robotic ultrasound technology has the potential to improve scoliosis assessment by providing more accurate and reliable results compared to the manual scanning approach. In addition, the robust performance of the robotic scanning method across different probe speeds, gentle pressures, and varying curvature degrees makes it a valuable option for evaluating scoliosis. Overall, the robustness of the robotic scanning method in scoliosis assessment can be utilized in developing novel dependability metrics that take into account probe movement, curvature degree, and ultrasound frequency. These findings have the potential to contribute to the development of robotic ultrasound technology in the field of medical imaging. Ultimately, the present research contributes to the growth of reliable medical robotics applications by establishing quality attributes of a specific medical ultrasound device. To achieve this, the research employs a diverse range of reliability metrics, including system dependability metrics, frequency projection, and automatic fault detection. Our research demonstrates that the random finite automaton model can effectively capture the diverse nature of ultrasound probe's curved surface. A similar approach may be beneficial in evaluating the reliability of other complex medical devices. This research proposes a new, length-targetted synthetic speech generation approach using a non-statistical algorithm, distinct from the widely used hidden Markov model-based techniques. Driving speech synthesis through medians instead of means allows for the creation of speech lengths that are more natural and easier to understand. A substantial inter-individual variability of human speech production makes the mean underestimating the actual length of a word, rendering it less suitable for speech synthesis. In contrast, the median offers a more reliable representation of the word length, making it an optimal choice for speech synthesis. Our method first obtains a set of reference medians from a large dataset comprising references with varying lengths and then creates a set of optimized median vectors for each target word. Using a Gaussian mixture model, we break down the reference medians into Gaussian components, allowing for the smooth distribution of lengths. Optimization is then performed through a framework inspired by vector quantization to produce a close distance between the optimized vectors and their respective reference medians. Due to the size of the reference dataset, we developed an efficient algorithm that processes at least one order of magnitude better than existing approaches. In addition to length optimization, we improved the width of the Gaussian mixture model distribution by distributing narrower widths and establishing a binary code for the top-most vector of each distribution, resulting in substantial gains in optimization accuracy. A listening test was conducted on the American English vocabulary, demonstrating our approach to be more natural and of higher quality than existing algorithms. Notably, our results match or surpass the performance of the CMU Arctic dataset, a state-of-the-art dataset, in terms of speaker individuality. Moreover, our approach performs better than a control dataset with within-speaker variability. Audio files demonstrating the effectiveness of this proposed method can be found at mohaned/medianspeech. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of this research is presented in a related study, titled Non-locality in Human Speech: A Study based on Audio-Video Saliency. A broader investigation of speech production is investigated in a research article, titled Individuality in Speaker Voice. In addition, a related work on the research topic can be found at Variability in Speech for Robustness, by Mohanad Adaimy and Fadel M. Albreed. The inclusion of hate speech in social media is a significant concern, leading to mental health problems, the breakdown of relationships, and even violent behaviors. Our research focuses on detecting hate speech against the Lyngai people, an ethnic group in Cameroon who have experienced severe violence from English-speaking separatists. Our approach employs characteristic extraction, using a combination of long and short term features, and classification. During our study, we analyzed a 1.1GB dataset consisting of 51,000 sentences from social media platforms, accurately identifying 57% of the annotations. Our model outperformed four baseline models, and we found that features such as depersonalization, associated with a high level of anonymity, significantly correlated with the dataset's classes. Our findings also highlighted the connection between social media platform characteristics and the detection of hate speech. In addition to our research, we released an open-source HATE10K dataset, weighted towards English and NLP applications, to facilitate the detection of hate speech against the Lyngai people. Our results may have implications for peacekeeping efforts, particularly in areas where linguistic barriers prevail. Our main contribution is the development of a method to automatically classify texts that may contain hate speech, and our findings can be a starting point for further research in this field. Our model is suitable for use in Cameroon, an English-speaking country where Lyngai people reside. Our study has also identified areas for improvement, such as developing models that can recognize hate against Lyngai people using local languages like English, and extending our research beyond social media platforms. Our research draws inspiration from previous studies, including a formal definition of hate speech, and a study by a peacekeeping force that employed social network monitoring to detect hate speech in a specific country. Our study also highlights the significance of hate speech detection in the context of a peacekeeping operation in a particular country afflicted by a conflict. Deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) serve as an effective tool for extracting rich information in various image processing tasks. However, relying solely on DCNNs might limit their potential in multiple-input-multiple-output (MIMO) tasks. Alternative neural network architectures like recurrent networks (RNNs) or transformer encoders hold the key to enhancing MIMO performance by reintroducing circular information exchange mechanisms. We explore extending DCNNs with RNNs and transformer encoders to create enhanced MIMO architectures and investigate the impact of information circulation in these new designs. A recurrent MIMO framework was developed to validate the importance of feature exchange, and a transformer MIMO framework was proposed to demonstrate the potential of using global features from the global image. Our experiments highlight the significance of information exchange in MIMO and show that a well-designed feature-exchanging strategy can greatly improve MIMO performance. Furthermore, the source code for our proposed models will be made available.

The exploration of historical documents presents both captivating and daunting challenges. Despite being centuries old, these records contain timely information such as names, locations, and occurrences that researchers desperately need to access. However, the deteriorated condition of many documents, along with their diverse formats and scripts, creates a significant barrier to their analysis. Fortuitously, archaeological text recovery techniques, which combine computational methods and scholarly expertise, offer a solution to decipher these documents. A pivotal aspect of employing ATRE (Historical Document Image) involves curating comprehensive datasets to develop, train, and refine models that enhance document understanding. This survey aims to outline current collections used for training models in the field of historical document images, discussing their characteristics and presenting a unified classification structure to organize these datasets by their established labels. Furthermore, we examine the dominant methods utilized in the field and discuss future research directions, highlighting promising research avenues and financing opportunities associated with these tasks. Ultimately, we hope this review assists scholars in identifying available collections and initiating research on specific datasets, while also sparking discussions that can advance the community's shared interests. A new technique has been developed to tackle the challenging issue of flatness in non-repetitive motion of robotic arms, and this has been successfully tested on an IRB 6600 robotic arm under the control of a Sixx Sixxdeg six-axis system. Flatness refers to the ability of a system to move without changing direction. To facilitate this, the position and velocity of each robotic joint have been optimized in real-time using an algorithm based on a pre-defined, open-loop trajectory. A novel method employing plausibility checks has been utilized to minimize the frequency of calculations when measuring positions and velocities. This approach relies on data from both direct measurements and estimates from filters. Various tests have been conducted to assess the performance of this technique. Notably, a flat motion was demonstrated when the position data was manipulated intentionally to deviate from the actual path. Moreover, the algorithm successfully reproduced complex, hand-drawn paths when fed a continuous input from a tablet device. To measure the accuracy of the technique, the distance between the actual trajectory and the one optimized for flatness was calculated. An comparison of the results showed that the method could reduce position errors by as much as 60% and velocity errors by as much as 75% when compared to a traditional position-based control system. Furthermore, the research found that the frequency of calculations could be lowered by as much as 90% while still enabling an efficient control system. These results suggest the possibility of utilizing this technique in various applications where the cost of complex position sensors is a concern. In particular, the method could be adapted for use in industrial robots by utilizing plausibility checks to reduce the frequency of calculations when running on older models, thus enabling an efficient control system. To facilitate this, the research recommends increasing the size of an onboard memory to at least 64 KB to take full advantage of the Sixxdeg six-axis system software. In terms of potential drawbacks, the research found that the motion optimized for flatness may not always accurately replicate the intended path, and this discrepancy could be exacerbated by factors such as wear and tear on the robotic arm. An investigation into the dynamic modeling of the IRB 6600 robotic arm revealed that its second link may be subject to significant wear and could cause discrepancies in the position and velocity data. Consequently, the method could be refined further in systems where an accurate reproduction of the intended path is essential. A novel approach to analyzing numerous time-to-event data is established, centered on modeling diverse pathways of health progression. To this end, a declared hidden Markov model is proposed, which utilizes multiple hidden states to represent both visible health states and the underlying, hidden dynamics of disease progression. The model parameters are trained simultaneously, drawing on information from multiple observations, as a way to accurately capture the complex interplay between risk factors and outcomes. The strategy is demonstrated through an application to data on individuals who experienced a myocardial infarction, focusing on how various pre-existing conditions affect recovery trajectories. The model's ability to characterize individual and collective disease progression pathways is highlighted through an in-depth examination of posterior distributions, which take into account the uncertainty associated with all model parameters. The model provides a versatile framework for exploratory analysis, allowing researchers to investigate specific subsets of individuals and to pinpoint the key factors driving distinct recovery patterns. To facilitate the adoption of this strategy, an R package is developed, providing pre-built functions to support the analysis, as well as a detailed, step-by-step guide for implementing the model. The model's utility is illustrated through an application to data from the NIS-Q research study, which investigated the link between multiple comorbidities and long-term health outcomes. By adopting a multiple state evaluation strategy, researchers are able to gain a more nuanced understanding of how specific conditions intersect and influence one another, as well as how they impact the likelihood and timing of a myocardial infarction. To optimize the model for use with large datasets, two strategies are considered: dividing the sample into subsets to reduce computational load, as demonstrated through an application to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) dataset; and modeling the distribution of latent states, as a way to refine the likelihood of observing specific states at different points in time. Several options are considered for implementing these strategies, including a method that utilizes multiple parallel processing threads to improve computational efficiency. To facilitate the adoption of these strategies, a series of simulated datasets are created, representing a variety of different scenarios, as well as data from individuals who experienced a myocardial infusion, serving as a model example of numerous time-to-event data. The model's parameter estimates are analyzed in detail, including an assessment of variability, as well as a comparison of how different strategies impact model fit and inference. Despite the successful mapping of quantum mechanics into the Schrödinger equation, solving this equation for complex systems remains difficult due to its non-linear partial differential nature. One approach to overcome this challenge is to use a linear mapping with a finite basis, such as the Hartree-Fock equation. Even with this linearization, complex systems remain computationally demanding, often requiring specialized algorithms and handling of approximation issues. Another challenge arises from the dimensionality of the problem, particularly in simulations involving three-dimensional molecules interacting with electrons through one-dimensional electrons. While reduced-dimensional models can mitigate this issue, they inevitably introduce approximations. Our proposed method addresses these challenges by employing a multi-site quadrature method of dimensions equal to those of the electrons, allowing us to study one-dimensional electrons interacting with three-dimensional molecules without significant dimensional reduction. We have tested the method's accuracy in building a basis set, such as a basis set of atomic orbitals, without significant approximation errors. Our results show that the approximate solution differs from the exact solution by a small amount comparable to round-off errors, providing a high degree of confidence in the method. We have also shown that the presence of resonances in the non-hermitian problem does not affect the completeness of the basis set. One potential application of the method involves solving models of chemical reactions, using a simplified example of a quantum dot picture. Our research demonstrates that the method effectively generates well-localized, complex wave functions for complex systems without needing substantial dimensional reductions. We believe that the method could become a valuable tool for solving more complex systems such as those involved in photosynthesis. Overall, the independent nature of the quadrature method variables allows us to tackle a range of complex quantum mechanics problems, such as those related to energy calculations in molecular dynamics simulations. Our research provides a potential solution to the longstanding issue of scaling in the density functional theory. We have tested the method on small systems, such as a carbon nanotube electronically coupled to a floppy molecule, modeling the behavior of photosynthetic complexes, and efficiently solved the non-hermitian eigenvalue problem with thousands of variables. We believe that the method effectively addresses many of the complexity challenges in quantum mechanics and related areas. Our research provides a potential new tool for solving quantum mechanics problems that have been intractable for over 90 years. The goal of the Metric Dimension problem is to find the smallest size of a partitioning set S that can accurately label a graph G, by associating each vertex with a unique combination of its distances to the fewest influencing vertices in S. This problem has been extensively researched, but recent studies have struggled to take advantage of a graph's attributes to enhance the performance unless these attributes significantly affect the graph's structure, such as in the case of chordal graphs. We now introduce a novel concept called feedback vertex group, which is also influenced by another graph attribute - (s,t)-distance visibility. We show that the Metric Dimension problem can be efficiently solved for certain graph categories when considering a specific type of feedback vertex group or (s,t)-distance visibility. More precisely, the problem can be solved in O(|S| + 1^(n- k + 1)) time where n represents the number of vertices and k the number of vertices in the feedback vertex group (or (s,t)-distance visibility). This (s,t)-distance visibility attribute also allows us to analyze the impact of another graph attribute - (s,t)-visibility, which can be used as a substitute for feedback vertex number in the (s,t)-distance visibility scenario, to determine the minimum number of vertices needed to uniquely position a vertex within a graph G. If a solution set S exists, it consists of either vertices from any covering set of G or a specific subset of G's vertices. Further analysis into this (s,t)-distance visibility attribute reveals that any covering set S of G consists of either a certain type of (s,t)-distance visibility subset or a specific subset of G's vertices. These (s,t)-distance visibility substitutable sets allow us to systematically categorize them and determine the smallest possible size for such sets in certain graph categories, which can also be efficiently solved for in certain graph categories such as planar graphs, for the subproblem of finding a smallest covering set S of a given graph G where every vertex in S has at most three influencing vertices. This work introduces a novel mathematical framework for directed spaces, expanding on existing work by Guzmán-De La Mora and Peréz-González. Our approach is based on a more general definition of derivation, which is applied to a Banach module over a commutative Banach algebra. Building on this, we explore the concept of power series, differential equations, and integral transforms within these directed spaces, where the effect of the direction is encapsulated in the parameter. Additionally, we define a class of invertible operators known as power frameworks, recover previous results, and provide novel interpretations within this context. Our study is centered on the R-algebra $C_\omega(X)$, which represents continuous functions with compact supports on directed spaces $X$. Our work is an extension of the recent findings presented in a preprint by the first author, which was later published in a revised form in Journal of Banach Algebras and Nonlinear Analysis in 2020. Furthermore, this research is an extract from the author's doctoral dissertation, which was defended at the Higher School of Economics in Moscow in 2018. Lastly, the second editor's notes contain additional insights on power series in association with Picard-Fuchs equations as discussed in his dissertation, which is accessible on his website at https://people.few.e-uni.it/francos/doctoral-thesis.pdf. Our study is an adaptation of these ideas to the $C_\omega(X)$-context. From a different perspective, a similar concept of power series was explored in a preprint by Guzmán-De La Mora and Peréz-González, which was later published in a revised form in a journal in 2021. Our current research is an expansion of the findings presented in that preprint. Past climate models have suggested the existence of a "hot-house" state, characterized by extremely high surface temperatures and a lack of precipitation. Recent high-resolution models, however, indicate that this "hot-house" state might actually be marked by periodic rainfall. This phenomenon can be understood through a simplified model representing multiple layers of the atmosphere, where a stable system is found when parameters are above a certain threshold and feature periodic rainfall when slightly modified. Analysis of these models reveals that the onset of rainfall occurs in areas of convective activity outside the lowermost atmosphere layer and results in a transient instability, where the upper layer becomes partially filled with a convective region that gradually spreads downwards. As a result, the system exhibits a periodic regime of rapid cooling, increased convective activity, and increased precipitation. This cycle is in turn driven by a decrease in entropy in the convective region as it grows, where the increased entropy outside this area acts as a barrier that regulates its growth. Quantitative and qualitative studies of these models reveal a critical value beyond which the system enters a state of periodic rainfall and ultimately shows signs of instability. Ultimately, further analysis reveals that this critical value corresponds to a threshold in the system's stability, where a small modification in parameters causes a transition from a stable to an unstable system, where unstable states are marked by periodic rainfall and ultimately where conditions become unstable and precipitation occurs consistently. This transition marks a significant break in the system's behavior and has significant implications for understanding climate patterns and the system's characteristics in high-resolution models. One implication is that the "hot-house" state, as previously understood, does not actually exist, where instead a low-mass version and a high-mass version of the "hot-house" state take its place. This replacement stems from the fact that for low-mass "hot-house" states, further modification in parameters increases precipitation, whereas for high-mass states, further modification increases evaporation, where in both scenarios the system enters a state of periodic rainfall and ultimately where the increased instability in the system leads to consistent precipitation. Consequently, the "hot-house" state, as previously understood, does not actually exist, where instead a low-mass version and a high-mass version of the "hot-house" state take its place. This replacement has significant implications in understanding climate patterns and the system's characteristics in high-resolution models. We've developed a set of twistor equations that extend beyond self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its elevated spin equivalents. These new twistor equations incorporate a more complex tau-function, which differs from the standard one in twistor theory. In the process, we've also obtained new spinor equations that expand upon those in twistor theory. Notably, we've found that the elevated Yang-Mills theory at level k=2 produces a specific set of self-dual and anti-self-dual Yang-Mills profiles, which may be more widespread than just at k=2. Moreover, we've shown that a specific constraint on the tau-function, reminiscent of a concept known as multi-component, gives rise to a set of consistent twistor and spinor equations. In the context of pure gauge theory, we've identified a novel spin 3/2 fermion as a potential particle candidate. Additionally, we've discovered that the tau-function in twistor theory is susceptible to deformations along the t'Hooft lines, which takes a specific form in the context of Yang-Mills theory and results in a tau-function with logarithmic singularities. These deformations are likely to play a significant role in the Kontsevich Whittaker model and the quantum foam construction based on twistor theory. In the process, we've also shown that the theory at level k=2 gives rise to a Balitsky chain in the context of the two-loop framework. Our findings provide a potential link between the elevated spin theory and the traditional Yang-Mills profiles. These findings are expected to extend beyond the Yang-Mills theory to other areas of mathematics and physics. An inherent problem in supervised categorical image analysis involves overcoming label noise, which is inherently present in datasets. Standard deep learning techniques frequently struggle with learning a reliable model from such a dataset. This research introduces a novel method called the Bayesian Label Restoration Mechanism (BLRM) to mitigate label noise in a supervised medical image categorization context. Labeled data with high confidence and a Bayesian mechanism are used to guide the model learning process. The high confidence data points serve as supervision, while the low confidence data points are utilized in a Bayesian framework to derive the true label distribution. The model learning process is guided by both the high confidence supervised data and the derived true label distribution for low confidence data points. Experimental evaluations using two different medical image datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to standard transfer learning. In particular, it achieves an average improvement of 8.2% and 6.7% in terms of accuracy, and 10.1% and 7.9% in terms of ROC, respectively. The proposed method was shown to outperform several state-of-the-art noise regularization techniques. Overall, the proposed mechanism can effectively learn a reliable model from noisy datasets. It provides a potential solution to mitigate label noise in supervised image analysis. We introduce a new approach to defining real numbers within the HOL theorem prover, relying on real numbers being represented as pairs of times, signifying their approximations. A key aspect of this approach lies in the explicit definition of each real number, regardless of its level of precision. We provide a step-by-step description of the foundation, methods, and effectiveness of this approach, highlighting its advantages over traditional methods, especially in terms of accuracy up to a thousand times more than the default HOL representation. Additionally, we provide a proof that real number definitions in HOL can be equivalently represented as partitions of sets within a Zermelo-Fraenkel model. Furthermore, we offer a comparison with the CaMoHOL method, also used for representing real numbers in HOL, focusing on their differences in convergence speed. Besides facilitating a deeper understanding of the concept of real numbers, this approach's other major benefit lies in its reduced complexity, making it particularly suitable for defining more complex mathematical objects within domains with restricted computational resources, such as automated theorem proving and program verification. Moreover, we provide an explanation of why this definition is particularly useful and why it should be considered as the real numbers definition within the HOL community. Finally, we provide a set of open challenges that remain unsolved after using this definition and offer insights into the future developments that could be explored with this approach. 

For those interested in trying this definition in HOL, we recommend accessing the definition on the HOL Definition Repository at https://tinyurl.com/timed-defs. 

This work is a revised version of the author's master's thesis, which can be found at its original location.

breadth. This research examines the digital reach and audience of regional newspapers
in relation to COVID-19 cases and fatalities across 98 U.S. cities between July

incidence rates. By exploring these relationships, this study provides unique
insights into the complex interplay between regional newspapers, COVID-19, and
society. Our work contributes to the ongoing discussion about the role of the media
in public awareness and disease management. Ultimately, these findings shed light on
the dynamic social and cultural dynamics underlying regional newspapers, COVID-19,
and society.

By converting the total angular momentum into a Casimir invariant, we've developed a way to maintain its invariance during the simulation, thereby ensuring that initial values of higher-order angular moments remain zero throughout. This has resulted in a modified version of the RMMethod algorithm, paired with an analytical solution of the VFPM equation that serves as a test case. Simulation results showcasing the preservation of angular momentum are presented using both 3D and 6D simulations involving a system with variable momentum relaxation rates. These results highlight the significance of considering conservation principles in developing numerical algorithms. Furthermore, we've maintained consistency between the Vlasov part of the VFPM equation, which differs from the Vlasov equation, as the former incorporates relaxation processes. As an added benefit, we've developed a way to extend the RMMethod to simulate VFPM equations containing symmetrical potential dependencies. However, this extension comes with a linear increase in computational complexity for each additional dependence due to the necessity of adapting the gradient vector calculation. This algorithm is now applicable to a broader range of fundamental plasma models, including two-dimensional, 3D, and 6D simulations involving species-dependent, variable, and symmetric potential dependencies. Moreover, we've successfully demonstrated the feasibility of employing the RMMethod to simulate a Gabor solution, which highlights its utility in understanding non-intuitive dynamics. Although the paper primarily focuses on the 3D formulation of the VFPM equation with a fixed time step, we've extended the algorithm to accommodate variable time steps while maintaining total angular momentum conservation. This modification is based on a conservative numerical approach that's compatible with the RMMethod. In addition, we've developed a way to evaluate the efficiency of VFPM simulations with a broad range of collision frequencies, which indicates that the model reduces to a Vlasov equation in the zero-alpha limit. This has significant practical implications, as collision frequencies in plasma are often assumed to be extremely low. This work marks the first instance of numerically solving 3D and 6D VFPM equations with a broad range of collision frequencies, which has further demonstrated the reliability of the RMMethod in simulating these equations. Deep learning models are commonly used in computer vision tasks but often rely on comprehensive datasets that are representative of the problem they're trying to solve. Since creating such datasets is nearly impossible, experts, which are highly specialized models, can be utilized to generate supplementary data through various techniques like data mixing and parameter optimization. By leveraging these techniques, novice models can achieve top performance on challenging tasks without needing extensive training. Additionally, we present an innovative method for automatically identifying effective data mixing operations that increase the effectiveness of these techniques. By applying this method to multiple domains and using various comparison benchmarks, we discovered that data mixing operations provided several benefits including improved robustness, increased accuracy, and faster convergence of models. Abstract:

Deep learning models typically require diverse, comprehensive datasets to deliver high-quality results. Since creating such datasets is nearly impossible, experts, which are highly specialized models, can be utilized to generate supplementary data through various techniques like data mixing and parameter optimization. By leveraging these techniques, novice models can achieve top performance on challenging tasks without needing extensive training. When training a base model, it's beneficial to draw upon the knowledge embedded in multiple specialized models without needing to independently train each of them. In this study, a novel approach was developed to automate the creation of data augmentation operators for improving performance in challenging natural language tasks. By integrating our operators into traditional training methods, we observed improved outcomes. The evaluation of our approach on six prominent datasets revealed enhanced F1 scores, particularly in tasks involving relationship extraction, question answering, and named entity recognition. The spin maser is an extremely sensitive device that uses spin resonance and feedback to amplify radio frequency signals, particularly in frequencies below 10 kHz. By utilizing alkaline metals like potassium and sodium, the spin maser operates at the Rabi cycle, generating a highly sensitive receiver that approaches the theoretical limit of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. This sensitivity is equivalent to detecting movement of particles the size of electrons. By amplifying signals at very low frequencies, the spin maser is capable of enhancing the sensitivity of sensitive instruments such as seismometers used in seismology and geophysics, allowing for deeper geological analysis. A newly developed digital technology has replaced traditional analog methods to create a more reliable and robust spin maser, achieving improved performance compared to its predecessors. This improved design has increased the gain threshold at 1 kHz to 30 million times the strength of the Earth's magnetic field, allowed for wider bandwidths, and reduced machine errors. Furthermore, the modernized maser has increased the range of its split fine structure frequency to 20 times that of the previous models, enabling various applications in metrology, physics, and geophysics. This breakthrough technology has also increased the sensitivity of seismic instruments to the subtle movements of rolling glaciers, providing new insights to glaciologists. By merging digital technology with the principles of quantum mechanics, the modern spin maser has opened new avenues in quantum technology and its diverse applications across physics and geology. All the data presented in this study is available to the public, inspiring new research and collaborative efforts to develop digital quantum technologies that benefit both fundamental and applied physics, particularly in geophysics and the life sciences. A digital alkaline spin maser offers a new perspective on the intersection of quantum mechanics and practical applications, providing a valuable example of 'use-inspired' basic research that targets real-world problems in geophysics and the environment. Importantly, the described experimental setup with its small investment and quick development is within reach of individual researchers and students, embodying the principles of do-it-yourly basic research that empowers individuals to drive their own scientific inquiries. To approach this challenge, we initially revise the Lefschetz-type theorems applicable to algebraic varieties to remove restrictive assumptions, such as the requirement for a given variety to be non-degenerate in its tangent space. Next, a comprehensive proof is provided for the hyperbolicity of Néron-Severi groups of K3 varieties by generalizing the concepts of positive definite lattices and the results of Matschke and Tabachnikov. Ultimately, the focus shifts to the study of the solitude of Néron-Severi groups of K3 varieties with a focus on the dimensions less than 5, and the results are expressed in terms of the Picard numbers and the associated Gaussians of these groups. A separate section examines the associated results in the context of the moduli spaces of K3 varieties using the language of Siegel domains and the moduli spaces of their Néron-Severi groups. A separate discussion is devoted to exploring ways to generalize the results applicable to the sets derived from K3 varieties, and the resulting results are expressed in terms of the concepts of hyperbolicity, the values of the Riemann zeta function, and the properties of the moduli space of the Néron-Severi groups of the given variety.
