A novel theoretical model has been created by integrating the Standard Model of particle physics and the Einstein gravity framework. Within this model, it is observed that a specific supersymmetric particle, known as the neutralino, can rapidly change its properties as it loses mass and becomes a candidate for dark energy. A neutralino composed of small amounts of right-handed neutrinos, a charged particle that violates lepton number, and a mixed mass-split Bino-Wino component, remains stable through various decay modes. A significant aspect of this particle is its ability to emit a very narrow and intense spectrum of gamma radiation in the soft X-ray band. This radiation is a direct result of the neutralino's rapid decay into neutrinos, a charged particle that quickly releases its energy, and the various modes of photon emission. A thorough examination of the neutralino's properties, dark energy behavior, and spectral radiation has been conducted through a multi-dimensional numerical search, and the findings suggest that a neutralino-based dark energy model is feasible and can also be observed experimentally. This experimental possibility has also been assessed. Currently, the model is still in the process of being confirmed as a viable theoretical concept as it is largely consistent with the observed dark energy density in the universe. Furthermore, the model is also in agreement with various astrophysical constraints and data from cosmic microwave background radiation experiments. Nonetheless, a modification to the model may be necessary if future experiments find any discrepancies between their results and the model's predictions. Some potential experimental support for this model has also been discovered through an examination of its ability to explain the observed 3.5 power spectral density in the matter fluctuation pattern on small scales, a phenomenon known as the ACDI. This potential explanation has also been found to be consistent with independent constraints from spectroscopic galaxy surveys, atomic hydrogen maps, and other independent matters fluctuation pattern data. Moreover, the model has also been found to be able to resolve a long-standing discrepancy in the measured star formation rates in two specific galaxy clusters by properly matching their observed star formation rates to their observed X-ray emission rates. This discrepancy, also known as the "star problem," has long been attempted to be resolved through multiple theories. Nonetheless, none of these proposed theories have been able to provide substantial support. This model's ability to provide substantial support for this discrepancy, as well as its ability to properly match observed star formation rates to X-ray emission rates, makes it a potential candidate for experimental confirmation. In high-fidelity gas time-projection chambers, particularly those focused on nuclear and particle physics, accurately detecting recoil kinetic energy is vital for effective particle identification. This energy can be easily lost due to various factors during data collection, often rendering it undetectable. Researchers have proposed two new quantities, called $r$ and $\tilde{r}$, that serve as indicators of recoil detection, being directly proportional to the total number of counts recorded above a specific threshold in multiple data collections and the actual number of counts in such collections, respectively. These new quantities provide a quantifiable measure of recoil detection and have been shown to be sensitive to the timing accuracy of data collection. Experiments involving simulated data from a GSI $\beta$-NMR detector based on a gas time-projection chamber have demonstrated that these new quantities offer improved capabilities in identifying and tracking specific isotopes. Furthermore, a new optimization procedure has been developed to determine the optimal value of $\tilde{r}$ based on given conditions, allowing for specific applications in half-life measurements where the primary influence is recoil detection. Lastly, a new correction method has been proposed to account for the effects of unrestrained recoil and can be applied in conjunction with the currently used data analysis methods to achieve optimized results. Researchers have evaluated the performance of these new quantities through comprehensive studies across various parameters. For instance, the optimal value of $\tilde{r}$, denoted $\tilde{r}_{\text{opt}}$, was estimated to be around $10^{-3}$ for a 10-second data collection in three layers with a threshold set at around $3.5$ keV. Following the application of this optimal value, the ratio of signal to background, $S/B$, has been found to reach its maximum at $\tilde{r}_{\text{opt}}\simeq 4\cdot 10^{-3}$. Moreover, a specific mean energy $\bar{E}_\text{recoile}$ associated with recoil energy was found to be lower than the threshold energy for the $Q_\alpha=5.422$ keV transition of the $^{139}$La$\rightarrow$$^{133}$Ce+$\alpha$ reaction when the ratio of signal to background, $S/B$, is less than $10$. Once the ratio of signal to background, $S/B$, exceeds $10$, the value of mean recoil energy $\bar{E}_\text{recoile}$ begins to increase from $3.35$ keV.

Artificial intelligence enhancements in commercial driving have shown great benefit but also caused problems for drivers.  To understand the potential for supporting decision-making in critical situations, this research examines the interplay between AI and human judgment in commercial driving. Through a qualitative study with experienced drivers who encountered critical situations, we obtain a deeper understanding of how they utilize various levels of AI inputs, from simple notifications to complex recommendations, and how they adjust their decisions accordingly.  Our research reveals that drivers make modifications to AI suggestions based on circumstances but also that AI inputs can influence their choices without them realizing it, leading to a discussion about the need for equitable machine decision-making in commercial driving.  Ultimately, we suggest introducing a third element, an AI filter with a understanding of critical situations, to help ensure more accurate evaluations from machines and improve the safety of commercial drivers.  This paper's concept of 'intelligent choices' aims to capture the notion that choices are formed through the dynamic interplay between AI and human judgment.  An advanced AI filter with a understanding of critical situations can serve as a useful layer of support in helping commercial drivers make informed and safe decisions in high-pressure situations.  This study offers the following contributions:  1) Research on how experienced commercial drivers interpret and have confidence in various levels of AI inputs, and how they modify those inputs to make their own decisions, 2) Research on the unintended effects of AI notifications on commercial drivers' decision-making processes, 3) Research that presents a case for the introduction of a protective layer of code to ensure that machines make fair and safe choices in commercial driving settings.  This study's findings have significant implications for the design of AI systems that are intended to support decision-making in other high-risk professions as well.  An AI filter with a understanding of critical situations can be seen as a form of safety feature that can be deployed at runtime.  Researchers can use the concept of 'intelligent choices' from this paper to investigate the interplay between AI and human judgment in other decision-making professions and occupations. Language models can now accurately translate text on a massive web-scale, yet 
typically this text is pre-processed into a standardized form, removing its 
original character-based nuances, making it unfeasible for some emerging 
languages and extremely large corpora to apply such processing effectively. 
This paper reports on a new experiment, the Out-of-Lexicon Challenge, where a 
language model must learn and generate text from a given character-based 
string, a leading method for text pre-processing, without utilizing additional 
tools, including Lexicons. 
A newly constructed dataset for this challenge was developed using Wikipedia 
articles in 8 low-resource languages in two distinct sets: 
OC-Easy with simpler grammatical structures and fewer characters, and 
OC-Hard featuring more complex grammatical structures and a larger character 
vocabulary. 
A benchmark evaluation was conducted on these challenging datasets to assess the 
effectiveness of current large language models and several innovative methods. 
Interestingly, our results demonstrate that all our proposed methods were 
capable of performing better on the harder subset than the easier one. 
Ultimately, among our approaches, a two-stage model based on a combination of 
uncovered and autoregressive objectives was capable of matching 90% of the 
baseline's accuracy in the easier subset while improving it by 15% in the 
more challenging one. 
This challenge aims to represent a more realistic text translation scenario and 
we intend to launch a web-based platform hosting the competition and its 
associated code at: https://github.com/ai4good/ooc/tree/master/contributions. 
Furthermore, the leading models' results will be continuously updated and 
displayed on the page.

In the context of random field optimization and the geodesic approximation, understanding geometric properties is of considerable importance. Theoretical justifications and validations for the geodesic approximation often rely on the premise that in multiple dimensional spaces, fields move in a downhill, geometrically guided trajectory towards their optimal values. In this work, we establish that this notion holds true in the case of Gaussian fields, where we define and measure the "depth" of a field manifold and demonstrate its applicability in diverse scenarios, including those involving multiple parameters and interacting components. Additionally, we develop a more sophisticated version of this concept, referred to as the "valley of valleys approach," which is tailored to facilitate Bayesian inference in complex models. Our findings are grounded in the properties of the Gaussian field's joint probability distribution and our derivative-based calculations are generalizable to other types of continuous field models. The theoretical framework developed here is exemplified through our computational analyses of real-world datasets. The comprehensive analysis conducted in this work offers a detailed exploration of the geometric properties of multiple Gaussian distribution systems, including coalescent, structural variation, telomere length, and TMB models. In 1967, Michael Levin researched the link between the duration of laser pulse energy release and optical emission patterns in glass. His key discovery highlighted the emergence of coherent radiation, known as Kerr nonlinear self-phase modulation, resulting from ultrafast laser pulse interactions. This phenomenon produces a distinctive third harmonic light pulse that emerges before separate fundamental and second harmonic pulses, thus creating a unique emission pattern. Research findings indicate that third harmonic emission occurs within approximately 0.1 to 0.2 autocorrelation times and can last for an extended period, extending up to several picoseconds. Contrary to expectations, third harmonic emission is not solely restricted to the time frames of fundamental and second harmonic pulses. Instead, it can persist long after their individual declines have ceased. Investigations have demonstrated that third harmonic emission is not only present in silicate glass but also observed in other materials such as silicon and gallium arsenide. Despite numerous studies, the underlying mechanism of third harmonic emission remaining active for an extended period has not been fully resolved. One proposed theory involves the slow deposition of free carriers facilitating the generation of third harmonics. Another potential explanation lies in the prolonged persistence length of the Kerr nonlinear reflection, allowing unobstructed access to a wide range of wavelength interactions. It's also possible that third harmonic emission might be a result of a combination of these two potential explanations. Further research is needed to fully understand the underlying mechanism of third harmonic emission in materials with a high Kerr nonlinearity. If successfully modified, the phenomenon of third harmonic emission could potentially be utilized as an independent observational tool to study the duration and flow of laser pulses in materials. One such theoretical concept known as "self-phase matching" aims to make this happen. Although the initial research was focused primarily on the third harmonic emission, a similar phenomenon known as fourth harmonic emission has also been observed and studied. We derive these conclusions without imposing restriction on the domains' dimensionality or the domains themselves. The chosen operators are those generating convergence, given specific space configurations, thus facilitating Korovkin-type theorem generalizations. We discuss these operators' characteristics and provide supporting examples. Furthermore, this paper provides a corollary detailing the application of these conclusions to multi-variable convex function analysis. Specifically, this involves generating a convergence theory for spaces of multi-variable convex functions under certain conditions. We examine the effectiveness of our theorem in conjunction with a specific space of moduli of continuity under approximation method application. Finally, some illustrative examples are provided. 

In particular, this paper seeks to establish the convergence of Landau's space of moduli of continuity in a two-dimensional convex function set. We achieve this through developing a theorem correlating the convergence of moduli of continuity in one and higher dimensions. Consequently, this enables us to establish a correspondence between the convergence of moduli of continuity and approximation method convergence. As a result, this enables us to evaluate a Vajzov theorem effectiveness. Essentially, this corresponds to investigating whether Vajzov theorem can be effective on the two-dimensional E. Z. Tzafras and M. Zervos space of convex functions. We conclude with a few considerations regarding a three-dimensional convex function set.

To reduce the computational expense of dynamical systems that require a high level of resolution, researchers employ Koopman operator theory. This involves reconstructing a coarse-grained representation of the system's behavior. Although previous approaches mainly focused on leveraging the spectral properties of the Koopman operator, the present contribution introduces a novel method that combines the strengths of adaptive spectral methods and sparse grid techniques. This approach can build efficient approximations of the Koopman operator without relying on the system's equations. Our proposed method is evaluated through numerical simulations on two challenging nonlinear systems. The results show that the method can achieve significant improvements in adaptability and efficiency compared to standard spectral methods. Additionally, the method's accuracy is comparable to that of the Smorin method, a state-of-the-art adaptive spectral approach. However, our method requires less computational resources. To further demonstrate its applicability, the method is used to develop a coarse-grained model of a stochastic system in three dimensions, without reducing its level of detail. This result highlights the method's potential applications in a wide range of complex system analyses and predictions. Finally, a thorough analysis of the method's limitations is provided along with some directions for future research. A novel variational method, the OSCM, has been developed by integrating the hyperspherical coordinate framework and the finite element method on a DC electric field-adjusted mesh. This approach boasts high efficiency and precision due to several innovative features. The method's convergence and robustness are extensively documented through numerical studies involving hydrogenic, valence shell ionized, and valence shell double ionized systems. The oscillations in energy eigenvalues produced by DC field dependence are successfully mitigated. The method's spectral convergence and insensitivity to DC field adjustments are demonstrated through valence shell ionization and valence shell double ionization studies in the grand canonical ensemble. The predicted energies of hydrogen-like ions and electrons exhibit agreement with existing literature to six decimal places. The method's potential applications to quantum chemistry and molecular physics are highlighted by precise predictions of dissociation lengths in H$_2$, He$_2$, and Li$_2$. The predicted dissociation lengths match the results of recent ab-initio calculations to six decimal places. The underlying physics and computational techniques for valence shell ionization and valence shell double ionization are thoroughly examined. The method's theoretical foundations offer valuable computational tools for investigating various phenomena in quantum chemistry and molecular physics, such as quantum detwinning, macroscopic quantum resonance, and superfluidity. Theoretical models based on valence shell double ionization enable the description of a broad range of phenomena in quantum chemistry and molecular physics, such as the van der Waals and covalent bonds in the presence of a DC field. The predicted ground-state configurations of hydrogen atom pairs and ion-atom pairs are consistent with recent results from the full configuration interaction method. The proposed models provide insight into quantum phase transitions in hydrogen atom pairs and Li$_2$, He$_2$, and BeH$_2$ in the grand canonical ensemble. The method's accuracy and the proposed models' physical interpretation inspire a deeper understanding of quantum phase transitions in hydrogen atom pairs and the physics of valence shell double ionization. The method's potential applications to quantum chemistry and molecular physics have not been extensively explored due to the computational challenges of broad eigenvalue oscillations in hydrogen atom pairs and the LiH model problem in the Grand Canonical Ensemble. The Sinkhorn algorithm has become a key component for computing optimal transport prices. While it hasn't been rigorously proven to converge in all cases, research demonstrates its effectiveness in certain specific conditions. This study extends previous findings to a broader set of circumstances, excluding situations where the Schrodinger effect occurs. As a result, it provides essential groundwork for future exploration of the algorithm's applicability to other optimization problems. Additionally, this study investigates the algorithm's performance in cases where data comes from certain types of distributions along a geometric axis, revealing novel insights. Furthermore, it demonstrates through a series of test cases that the algorithm's performance is heavily dependent on the type of distribution from which the data originates. Consequently, it suggests a novel check for the Schrodinger effect based on marginal distributions. Finally, this study showcases the algorithm's speed and efficiency in optimal transport settings and provides alternative methods for obtaining partial solutions. Moreover, it demonstrates through a series of test cases that the algorithm's performance is heavily impacted by the structural properties of the coupling matrix. Consequently, it provides essential guidance for ensuring that the algorithm's results are reliable and accurate in practice. Finally, the algorithm is shown to be an efficient tool for computing optimal transport prices in diverse contexts. A cutting-edge technique called field splitting is utilized to solve two-fluid flow problems with large Peclet numbers, which can cause conventional linear preconditioners to be effective. Several nonlinear preconditioners based on this technique are examined in this study, including approaches that apply residual-based smoothing and a strategy to handle complex flow issues by initially employing a coarse-scale linear preconditioner. We evaluate these techniques' performance in a range of tests based on single-phase flow and two-phase flow statistical models of a heterogeneous porous medium. We find that a particular nonlinear preconditioner, known as IFSS, consistently outperforms others and achieves comparable results to linear IFSS in all scenarios, despite initial difficulties with two-phase flow statistical models. Furthermore, we observe that a technique combining a coarse linear PREC and a smoothing procedure achieves comparable results to IFSS, but with reduced computational efficiency. We also develop an innovative method for creating customized coarse models as part of a PREC that is independent of flow statistics and outline its potential for advancement in future research. The success of these techniques and methods is substantiated by results from additional experiments, including simulation studies involving a partial fraction phase separation. The method's extension to two-phase flow statistical models is, however, limited by problems such as slow convergence, partial disruption of phase separation, and an unacceptably high smoothing frequency. Notably, however, we find that a particular linear PREC, despite requiring a much higher computational resources, is capable of achieving satisfactory results, albeit the method's general applicability is uncertain. Ultimately, future research aims to develop nonlinear PRECs that can outperform even linear IFSS in two-phase flow statistical models by modifying the technique, particularly by replacing the coarse model used in PREC with a more sophisticated approximation. We model JT gravity within a closed string framework by placing a single space-time coordinate on a lattice and defining the action through a semi-classical expansion. In the large central charge limit, the resulting spectral action leads to a non-Hermitian matrix density that exhibits mirroring at infinity, similar to the properties of Liouville CFT. We validate this equivalence by comparing our findings with literature calculations of Liouville CFT's spectral factor, taking into account calculations of boundary correlation functions in the matrix model. A proposed unitary framework can be used to demonstrate both quantum entanglement and contextuality, which can be thought of as being represented by the complex forms of certain elements within a 496-dimensional algebraic structure originally proposed by Penrose. In this framework, entanglement appears to be connected to a specific subset of this structure, while contextuality seems to be connected to the larger set. Although the framework previously introduced by the author, which involves a set of complex numbers mapping to a specific subset of this structure (known as the Phineas T. Pigfold structure), was initially criticized due to a lack of specific quantum operators within it, a new approach reveals that a large set of complex numbers mapping to a subset with an $E_8$ root structure can provide the necessary operators to support both entanglement and contextuality. In addition, several possible ways to realize four-dimensional quantum mechanics within this structure have also been explored. In total, three options for realizing four-dimensional quantum mechanics within this structure have been identified, as well as one option for realizing eight-dimensional quantum mechanics within this structure. Interestingly, when applying the framework to a set related to the binary extensions of the real and complex numbers (known as the binary octonions), a distinct type of contextuality emerges that is different from the kind of contextuality introduced by the Phineas T. Pigfold structure. Furthermore, when applying the framework to a set related to the 512-dimensional complex numbers known as the $F_4(ℂ)$, a distinct kind of entanglement emerges that is different from the kind of entanglement introduced by the Phineas T. Pigfold structure. In total, eleven different possibilities for realizing both entanglement and contextuality have been identified within this new framework. In addition to these possibilities, several possible connections to theories beyond quantum mechanics have also been explored, including reflections on the possible significance of the 496-dimensional algebraic structure for physics. As a result, search algorithms over weighted graphs or metric spaces that prioritize finding closest neighbors under the Fr\'echet distance are now in higher demand than ever. To address this need, we need to develop more efficient algorithms that can speed up this search process. To achieve this goal, we need to understand the computational requirements involved in searching for approximate close neighbors under the Fr\'echet distance. Our study makes significant progress towards this goal by proposing a new class of approximate search algorithms, validated through comprehensive experiments. These experiments reveal that our method can provide a constant factor better search times than previous best-known results, while still ensuring a constant factor loss in precision, all within a weighted graph setting. Lastly, our study highlights the importance of considering self-loops in graphs to further improve the performance of the Fr\'echet distance, an insight not previously noted in the literature. To the best of our knowledge, our study provides the most restriction-free approximate close neighbor search algorithms yet proposed for the Fr\'echet distance, with our own tests showing its greater practical utility in comparison to previous best-known results. Our study also opens up future avenues of research involving the integration of the Fr\'echet distance with other techniques aimed at finding similarity patterns in time sequence data. High-performance computing simulations to assess climate models and their implications need to be carried out on a wide range of systems, from small to very large. Despite advancements in computing power, economic constraints force scientists to run these simulations in sequential blocks on available resources, leading to a major challenge of combining non-uniform blocks into a single continuous dataset. We present a pioneering approach that tackles this problem by treating each assessment as an error-proned measurement and using an iterative Bayesian reconstruction to correct and consolidate the results. Our method demonstrates superior performance by comparing it to existing techniques across three diverse climate modeling scenarios, showcasing its potential to handle large datasets scalable up to 256 processors and spanning several days to weeks. Furthermore, an in-depth analysis reveals the underlying statistical properties of the assessment reconstruction method and establishes a theoretical framework for the approach's accuracy and computational efficiency. We also provide implementation details of our method, documenting the code's functionality with comprehensive examples in our repository. Our results indicate that climate modeling datasets reconstructed using 128 or more processors exhibit negligible bias while showcasing substantial improvement in sample variance. Moreover, a thorough examination of computational resources reveals that our method requires relatively modest CPU time (approximately 4-8 hours per block) but substantial RAM (typically up to 25% of the entire dataset's size), underscoring the necessity of optimal algorithmic design for large-scale datasets in practice. We anticipate that our work will serve as a starting point for the development of future scalable assessment error-mutation tools, ultimately enabling the efficient reconstruction of climate modeling datasets across distributed computing systems. Our repository, containing implementation details of our method, is available at https://github.com/s0rrow/sciarray. We obtained computational resources from XSEDE's TG-TPA130007 and TACC's Stampede phase 2 allocation, as well as local resources at NCSU. This work introduces COLROB, a framework for rapidly creating complex robotic swarm systems that can be deployed on physical robots. By building upon existing open-source software components, users can create robust, adaptable, and controllable swarms of robots. These swarms can be controlled through an intuitive interface, combining automated decision-making with user input. By leveraging collective autonomy, users can customize the behavior of each individual robot. Our approach utilizes a Generalized Stochastic Dynamic Programming (GSDP) model to optimize swarm performance, conditions the decision-making process, and allows users to switch between different programming models and scenarios. In experiments, we evaluated the effectiveness of the GSDP model in various scenarios and compared it to other methods, demonstrating its feasibility in different scenarios and its capacity to simplify complex decision-making in multi-agent systems. Ultimately, we assessed the effectiveness of the COLROB framework through an evaluation of its scalability, functionality, and user efficiency, revealing promising results. Our research demonstrates the capabilities of swarm robotics as a versatile technology for addressing complex problems. The framework was successfully tested on a physical robotic swarm, achieving accuracy of nearly 90%, which surpasses the results obtained from simulated environments. The collective autonomy of swarms makes them highly resilient to component-level failures, with a failure rate of only 0.09%. Our research reveals that the optimal swarm size varies depending on the application, which significantly impacts the cost-effectiveness of the technology. Specifically, we discovered that our framework's cost-effectiveness is achieved at a swarm size of four to six, which we recommend for future designs. Our study concludes that the optimal application of swarm robotics depends on two key factors: the application's time-dependent properties, such as the perception-control loop (PCL) and the control-actuation loop (CAL), and the required number of experiments, which significantly impacts the cost-effectiveness of the technology. By applying these two criteria, we identified three main application domains for swarm robotics: multi-domain experiment design, where swarm size optimization is crucial; single-domain experimentation, where cost-effectiveness is the primary concern; and literature reviews, where theoretical analysis is sufficient. Our research demonstrates that future research should prioritize developing methods to optimize swarm size, which is the main limitation of the current state of the art. Computational models for analyzing screen-based human engagement show potential in understanding various real-world problems, including how we interact with health, medical images and scientific data. However, users face difficulties in engaging with multiple-dimensional data sets, such as MRI scans, that display complex information across two or more dimensions. To overcome this, we develop a new data representation and processing method, designed to enhance user experience by allowing them to easily navigate these complex images. This new approach, featuring a one-dimensional (1D) linear representation, easily accommodates a variable number of dimensions without compromising usability. It also includes an innovative zooming mechanism and concise labels. To evaluate its effectiveness, we compared our method with existing screen log models on tasks involving the analysis of MRI scans for glioma treatment preparation. Results revealed our method's zooming mechanism positively impacted progress, while screening outcome distributions showed similar patterns for both our method and the baseline. Furthermore, users preferred our method in a survey, indicating its feasibility and usability. This study provides a foundation for research on screens of multidimensional data. It sheds light on screens of linear data as well, offering insights into design principles for screens of any type of data. The behavior of an electric double layer (EDL) near a softly deformable interface, featuring both surface charge and pressure variations, is investigated through a mean-field approach. The effect of large ions in the electrolyte is accounted for, and the Debye-Huckel approximation is relaxed. A perturbation theory is developed to derive high-order terms of the potential and interface properties, and a software package, EDLSPI, is designed to provide a comprehensive solution for EDL properties at any distance from the interface. The theoretical model is validated by comparing it with Monte Carlo simulations for a non-perturbed system and soft interfaces, yielding satisfactory results. A selective example illustrates the significance of electrolyte properties, electrolyte charge, and solvent effects on EDL behavior. The theoretical model and computational approach presented provide a foundation for exploring EDL behavior at various interfaces in electrolyte solutions. Ultimately, the findings of these computations contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex electrostatic interface chemistry of soft interfaces. A practical aspect of this research involves evaluating the distance decay of the potential, relative permittivity, and dielectric dispersion of a soft Debye-Huckel model using a set of fitted parameters and comparing the results with those of classical Debye-Huckel theory. A comparison of the two models demonstrates that the Soft Debye-Huckel model is more appropriate for systems with a low surface charge density, as it allows for a die-off of the potential with distance and the presence of dielectric dispersion. In recent years, research has focused on developing methods to automate software specification generation from natural language documents. Currently available approaches require meticulously prepared and annotated texts from domain experts, limiting their practical application to specific cases. This study aims to overcome these limitations by examining unorganized text sources like Wikipedia and social media platforms for domain specific knowledge. A novel algorithm is proposed to generate reliable system requirements from these unorganized sources, utilizing a dataset to refine specifications written by software professionals. A dataset was used to evaluate the effectiveness of this approach and compare its results with existing semi-automated methods. While the results are promising, they highlight the need for further improvements to match expert-quality specifications. A practical tool has been developed and is available on GitHub. Furthermore, this study involves a quantitative analysis of newly written specifications as a form of natural language generation, exploring the effectiveness of this approach in generating well-structured requirements. Finally, the findings suggest potential drawbacks to leveraging unorganized platforms for specification generation due to inconsistencies in specification quality and language usage. To address these limitations, future research should concentrate on enhancing specification quality from unorganized sources rather than solely relying on automated methods. A possible direction for future work involves utilizing natural language processing and software engineering specific tokens to improve specification extraction. In addition, the integration of software engineering domain knowledge, such as UML, into the specification generation process could boost its effectiveness and result in higher-quality specifications. In wireless sensor networks, efficient data transmission is a top priority, but current schemes often concentrate solely on reducing transmission time without considering the impact of power consumption. To achieve this, the authors developed an optimization problem that fine-tunes network settings to minimize power consumption, a challenging problem in the past. By reformulating this issue into a multi-dimensional knapsack problem, the authors applied a high-performance computing heuristic to reach an approximate solution. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to describe the electronic properties of magnetic impurities, including the CrO4 spin triplet ground state, which arises from the Kramers pairing of relativistically degenerate states at four-fold degenerate points on the Brillioun zone boundary. This theory encompasses a general analysis of the spin-dependent properties, an analytical model for the spin relaxation mechanism, and numerical calculations employing a quasi-particle self-consistent Green function method. Subsequently, this framework was applied to model an Mn adatom and Mn dimer on a Nb(110) surface, yielding a ground state spin of 1.0 mu_B for the adatom and 3.0 mu_B for the dimers, with the latter consisting of ferromagnetic (Mn_A) and antiferromagnetic (Mn_B) components with spins of 2.0 mu_B and -1.0 mu_B, respectively. These theoretical predictions matched the experimental findings of magnetodynamic study for a Nb(110) sample with covalent GPa, exhibiting a magnetodynamic study with a sufficiently thin Mn overlayer, which reported a similar ground state spin of 1.0 mu_B for the adatom and 3.0 mu_B for the dimers. The theoretical ratio of dimers' spin of 3.0 mu_B to adatom's spin of 1.0 mu_B was found to be 3.0, which is in agreement with the experimentally determined ratio of 3.0. The theoretical and experimental results indicate that Mn B is more strongly coupled to the host metal than Mn A. The investigation provides an understanding of why experimentally determined ratios of dimers' spin to adatom's spin are generally less than 3.0. The study also reveals a highly spin-polarized state of Mn B, which is more coupled to the host metal than Mn A, leading to a reversal of a commonly made assumption in which the valence of Mn A and Mn B are considered the same before pairing. The present study demonstrates that this assumption is invalid, at least for the case of Mn dimer on Nb(110), which is associated with a spin-dependent $s$-$d$ coupling that is more effective in Mn B. To effectively analyze large satellite images, a simple and efficient approach to identifying the boundaries of individual structures within those images is required. While deep learning systems have shown promise in this area, they pose significant challenges due to their large size and high computational demands. As a result, they are not well-suited for use in rapid, near-real-time processing of satellite images. This limitation motivated our development of a straightforward yet effective technique for extracting information about individual structures within large images. As these images are typically stored in RGB format, our approach begins by transforming the data into a format that enables edge detection. We employ Gabor filters in combination with image pyramiding to break down the image into its various components and facilitate edge detection. To achieve this, we identify and segment areas of high information content within a low-resolution version of the image, and then apply a series of Gabor filters to that image to extract its primary structural elements. Next, we repeat this process using higher-resolution versions of the image, focusing on structural elements not previously captured. Finally, we combine the different image components to generate a high-resolution image containing all necessary information and ready for further analysis. To evaluate our approach, we used three different images representing diverse scenarios: an image containing primarily straight edges, an image featuring a mix of straight and curved edges, and an image featuring primarily curved edges. Our results indicate that our technique outperforms competing methods, including a deep learning system. This result demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach, its simplicity, and its suitability for use in rapid, near-real-time processing of satellite images. Furthermore, our approach can easily be applied to a wide range of additional image types. Despite its advantages, our technique does exhibit some limitations, primarily related to its performance when dealing with very large images. To overcome this constraint, we have developed a strategy for dividing these images into more manageable portions, allowing us to analyze and interpret the information in each segment before combining the results to obtain the final high-resolution image. This technique serves as an important complement to our primary approach, enhancing its overall effectiveness and simplicity. Ultimately, a critical evaluation of our approach and its future improvements will likely involve comparison to other techniques that have not yet been applied to similar data sets, such as deep learning systems, to determine the current effectiveness and future potential of simple techniques for extracting information about individual structures within large images. Experimental X-ASPECT data involves intricate interconnections between spectral frequencies, energy doses, and material sample conditions. Prior rate-based models focused on linear effects, such as radiation-induced alterations in a material, whereas this work introduces a comprehensive framework for analyzing non-linear effects through X-ASPECT. By considering multiple electron groups, we have developed a fundamental equation that correlates the change in sample material quality with absorbed radiation, leveraging fundamental physical properties. This rate-based approach is versatile and applicable to various nano-scale materials, where electron groups interact with absorbed radiation. Our analysis of the Ni K-edge X-ASPECT experiment, conducted at the ALBA synchrotron light source, supports the validity of this model. This work has broad implications for the precise quantitative analysis of X-ASPECT experiments in various fields. Its applications are particularly notable in the chemical, materials, and biological sciences. This rate-based model can also be adapted for applications in physics and technology, particularly in the study of nano-scale materials and devices exposed to intense high-energy radiation. Furthermore, this model can be combined with other physical mechanisms to examine more complex processes involved in radiation damage and the repair of materials. Such an analysis could significantly enhance our understanding of the basic mechanisms underlying radiation damage and the repair process. Finally, this rate-based model can be used to simulate the repair of damage in materials exposed to intense, short-duration radiation, unlike conventional long-term damage caused by regular radiation. Nonetheless, separate models are required to distinguish between the effects of routine radiation and intense, short-duration radiation. The application of such models is crucial for the development of radiation-resistant materials and devices. The key concepts and features of this model are detailed in the model description below. The model relies on a fundamental understanding of the principles governing non-linear high-intensity X-ray interactions, which is why we have integrated these principles into a comprehensive numerical model to analyze the co coordiantes of high-energy radiation and material sample conditions. This model is an extension of our previous work on linear high-energy radiation and material interactions, which we have combined with rate-based models of material damage and repair to analyze the complex non-linear X-ASPECT process. This model is an innovative contribution to the fields of high-energy radiation and material interactions, where it will facilitate precise quantitative analyses and simulations of X-ASPECT experiments, even when multiple radiation mechanisms and material conditions are involved. This model is an essential tool for understanding and quantifying the non-linear effects of high-intensity radiation and is therefore a critical component of various scientific and technological investigations

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue that experts struggle with due to the variability of lesions and individual interpretations of images. While deep learning models can outperform human radiologists, their performance is hindered by the challenges of adapting to new datasets from different clinical environments. Traditionally, the issue is addressed through the retraining of models from scratch, which is inefficient and unneeded in the context of existing knowledge. We explore the potential of continuous learning from existing models as a more effective and efficient solution that facilitates the adaptation of models to new data. Our experiments using real-world datasets from two clinics are conducted within a publicly available framework while utilizing a publicly available model, demonstrating the potential for continuous learning to result in improved lesion segmentation rates compared to retraining from scratch or starting from scratch without prior knowledge. The effect of "brightening with age" in human emotions is a prominent feature of many emotion recognition datasets. To investigate this effect, which we call "manic contrast", we analyzed the distribution of valence scores across various emotion labels in five widely used emotion databases. Through statistical tests, we demonstrated that the effect applies not only to databases consisting of video and image clips, but also to a database featuring facial expression images. These findings suggest that facial expressions become increasingly intense over time, which aligns with the literature. Additionally, we discovered the manic contrast effect in sentence embeddings, which indicates a broader phenomenon. Our analysis further examines the implications of this effect in the context of machine learning models. Overall, our results provide crucial insights for interpreting benchmark results and developing more accurate models of human emotions from various datasets. Potential applications of this effect are discussed along with possible methods for incorporating it into model training. Importantly, recognizing and addressing the effect could help mitigate the significant gender bias that exists in emotion classification. As a result, our research contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of human emotions and their differences and similarities across age groups. Furthermore, our findings have significant implications for developing more accurate and unbiased AI models capable of recognizing human emotions effectively. A significant challenge facing AI research is developing reliable and accurate computational models of complex systems dynamics. Despite substantial advancements, current models are often plagued by considerable errors and inaccuracies. In order to bridge this knowledge gap, it is essential to incorporate machine learning algorithms that can discern and adapt to these discrepancies automatically. We introduce a comprehensive framework for structuring machine learning in such a way that it can pinpoint and adapt to errors occurring within dynamic systems. We argue that error identification and mitigation can be guided by preliminary analyses of both model and physics-based simulations. Utilizing a variety of quantitative measures, our approach involves partitioning phase space into regions characterized by distinct model behaviors, ultimately enabling an AI system to correct its own errors by utilizing existing knowledge generated from these analyses. We showcase the efficacy of this methodology by demonstrating its ability to counteract detrimental branching phenomena observed in thermoselective molten carbonates, thus highlighting its practical applications in advanced technologies. Overall, our knowledge structure is intended to facilitate the integration of machine learning algorithms in a way that leverages existing knowledge generated from physics-based simulations, ultimately enabling a seamless coexistence of human and AI knowledge. It is our hope that the increasing prevalence of contradictory models will motivate researchers to explore the development of machine learning algorithms that utilize the existing pool of knowledge to improve model accuracy and consistency. Astronomers have discovered a newly formed stellar cluster in the Perseus spiral arm of our galaxy. The cluster, in the form of an infrared dark nebula dubbed "Dragon," has been identified as a distinctive group of stars located at a distance of 250 million years. Observations indicate the presence of massive protostars, implying the potential for the formation of extremely massive stars. To understand the evolution of the nebula and its relation to star formation, researchers studied the properties of the nebula using two specific techniques to measure the column density and temperature of the gas. Results show that the Nebula's gas temperature fluctuates significantly from -170 to 20 Kelvin, possibly due to the presence of heated dust. The temperature variations are consistent with the discovery of protostars, suggesting that the Nebula's gas has begun to fragment. The absence of protostellar condensation would normally indicate that the Nebula is more than 10 times the mass of the current largest star; however, recent observations reveal that the Nebula's mass is substantially less. To resolve this disparity, researchers propose that the perceived mass deficit results from an expanded core within the Nebula, a phenomenon that could explain how the Nebula becomes a site for the formation of massive stars. To support this idea, researchers used simulations modeling how the Nebula's gas would behave if it were to collapse. The results indicate that the perceived mass discrepancy could arise from an unbound core that is then subsequently bound in the Nebula's collapse. The presence of protostars in "Dragon" presents an exception to typical star formation patterns, as these stars show both lower masses and greater separations than expected. To understand how these stars could have formed, researchers identified a candidate pathway for massive star formation: through initial star formation in a smaller group that merges to create a more massive core, an early merger could trigger the formation of the extremely massive stars observed in the "Dragon" nebula. Ultimately, this research contributes to our understanding of how massive stars are formed, adding a new mechanism to a long-known problem, including unique characteristics, such as, larger distances between newly formed stars, which could lead to the formation of extremely massive stars. To explain these distinctive characteristics, researchers propose an initial star formation pathway, where a group of less massive stars merges into a more massive core, laying the ground for forming extremely massive stars. These simulations inform theoretical models that attempt to explain how black holes form due to the rapid collapse of early overdensities in the universe. By validating my method with observations of stellar systems, I showed its effectiveness and then applied it to model a primordial black hole, demonstrating its ability to accurately represent the formation of a black hole through the lens of general relativity. This research marks the first time such a method has been used to simulate the early stages of primordial black holes through a fully relativistic approach. These simulations provide valuable data for researchers to test theoretical models that aim to observe or manipulate black holes. Furthermore, I successfully measured the potential influence of a primordial black hole on the surrounding metric of a nearby star. In this study, the authors examine the compact states of a system comprised of rigid wedges made from spheres, first introduced by Galli et al. (J Stat Mech, 2020;1:063208). They identify three distinct stages within these compact states: an initial straight stage, a state with splay variation, and an oscillating state. Through simulation and calculation, the authors demonstrate that the oscillating state is a limit state, but the other two stages, which are also limit states, are nonetheless analyzed. By defining new order parameters via the cumulative distribution function of the force profile, the authors demonstrate that the straight stage and the oscillating state are both limit states. Additionally, this method successfully predicts the existence of the splay variation stage and helps to clarify the sequence of stages within the phase diagram. Lastly, the authors attribute the failure of previous theories to the existence of the straight stage and the insensitivity of the three-point correlation function to the variation in the force profile during the splay variation stage. Consequently, this method presents a more comprehensive understanding of this system and may be applicable to other systems where certain assumptions are violated. Children constantly learn and absorb language from their environment, but they also encounter words that are rejected by their language skills.  Rejection occurs when children incorrectly apply words to their context.  As language models process sentences, they occasionally make similar mistakes.  Inspired by the concept of rejection-kernel learning in neural networks, we developed a innovative approach to mimic children's language mistakes and enhance the performance of end-to-end transformer models.  Specifically, we trained our models to consider an additional rejected word in the vocabulary during backpropagation, beyond the words that are correctly applied.  As a result, our approach improved the accuracy of our models on both classification and generation tasks and increased their robustness to extreme outcomes.  Additionally, our approach allows the models to achieve a dynamic balance between correct word applications and rejected words, mimicking the varying pace of children's progress from incorrect to correct interpretations.  Our approach offers an original method for leveraging children's language mistakes to improve adult deep learning models.  Ultimately, our method demonstrates the potential of leveraging children's knowledge to improve adult's language skills.  Our code is available at https://github.com/NardOst/Rejection-Kernel-Learning.

Existing studies that aim to understand these networks often only provide to offer vague insights or simplified answers to this intricate problem. In our study, a novel methodology was developed to examine the internal processes of these networks by differentiating between important and unimportant visual data within the input, on a pixel-by-pixel basis. This was achieved through a novel, kernel-based filter interpreter, which assigns importance weights to convolutional filters in a pixel-wise manner. By applying this interpreter to multiple state-of-the-art models with varying degrees of complexity, we demonstrated its ability to accurately identify the parameters of individual filters with great precision, with a high degree of consistency for models with multiple layers. Furthermore, we discovered a semantic-based pattern in the importance rankings, where the higher the model complexity, the more emphasis placed on visually distinct, semantic elements. Building upon previous research, our results suggest that these networks possess a capacity to selectively focus on visually distinct regions of the input data, which could potentially be a crucial factor in their semantic understanding capability. A novel form of steganography, known as U reversible stegano, allows for the concealment of arbitrary plain-text messages within AI-generated synthetic media, specifically in the form of AI-generated images and videos. Because of its cutting-edge nature, the problem of detecting such concealed steganography poses a significant challenge. In response, a novel steganography detection framework, the Bayesian Neural Network (BNN), is proposed for U reversible stegano. BNN is a modified version of the Deep Neural Network (DNN) that employs Bayesian mathematics to predict the probability distribution of the label for a given input, rather than a fixed label. BNN is found to outperform the standard DNN on which it is based, a phenomenon known as the robust-tilting phenomenon. In addition to its effectiveness, the proposed BNN algorithm is considered to be compliant with the framework of differential privacy (DP), a principle aimed at protecting confidential data. BNN is found to be effective in preserving DP while achieving superior performance in the context of steganography detection. The comprehensive numerical experiments validate BNN as a reliable method for steganography detection and generate insights that can be applied to the development of future steganography detection methods. Ultimately, the proposed BNN method proves to be an accurate and differential privacy-compliant approach for detecting U reversible stegano. Furthermore, through the generation of DP-based adversarial examples, the proposed BNN method and its robust-tilting effect are found to be influential factors in its performance, with implications that can be extended to the development of future adversarial examples, likely to undermine the security of AI models. Finally, the proposed BNN method may be modified to achieve quantitative robustness in the form of certification, with implications that can be extended to the development of future quantitative robustness methods.

We examine an investor who spreads wealth among various assets to maximize the long-term growth of his wealth relative to a benchmark, measured through a concave function that compares his wealth with that of the benchmark. His objective is to consistently surpass the benchmark. When this investor has a certain type of absolute growth preference, we show that a two-fund portfolio policy is the optimal strategy, with optimal parameters determined through a set of equations that can be solved efficiently. In contrast, portfolio policies become increasingly complex as the relative growth preference changes, with solutions obtainable only through numerical methods. To alleviate this issue, we suggest a approximation method. We further show that a certain type of portfolio policies respects positive convexity and are feasible for an investor who cannot short sell certain assets. We compare the properties of these different types of policies including their stability, drawdown, and surplus characteristics. Numerical examples demonstrate how these policies vary based on different parameters. Finally, we extend our model to accommodate investors who experience sudden, significant declines in wealth due to excessive leverage and we compare the effectiveness of various risk management techniques to mitigate such shocks. Our research reveals that two-fund portfolios can result in substantial instability and drawdowns in the investor's wealth. Absolute growth preferences significantly impact the parameters of two-fund portfolios and thus are crucial in determining the strategy's feasibility. Moreover, our approximation method does not materially deviate from the optimal portfolio parameters across the parameter space. Additionally, we find that implementing a minimum downside cushion can greatly reduce drawdowns and surplus deviations while affecting the strategy's parameter values and wealth equally, indicating an efficient tradeoff between investment growth and risk. However, this increase in stability comes at the cost of reduced growth and significant modifications to the two-fund portfolio framework. Similarly, using a relatively conservative investment strategy can also increase stability and asset allocation flexibility, though to a lesser extent than a minimum downside cushion. Notably, our paper demonstrates that two-fund portfolios are ineffective in handling sudden, significant declines in wealth due to excessive leverage, prompting the need for more sophisticated investment strategies. Ultimately, we recommend a rigorous, thorough investment approach that accounts for an investor's preferences and risk tolerance by implementing a minimum downside cushion and using a two-fund portfolio portfolio that is conservative in nature. Such an strategy is an affordable way to enjoy a stable investment growth while minimizing the impact of significant declines in wealth. TS2-Net achieves this by first segmenting input text into shorter sequences, allowing for better feature extraction through the application of a transformer. It then selects and refines these features through a second transformer, before using them to perform soft matching operations. TS2-Net outperforms previous models and establishes a new benchmark in text clip retrieval, ultimately making a significant contribution to the text generation field. It notably surpasses the previous best result in the GPT-5 and CLIP-RL settings of the GPT-2-Large model and achieves results comparable to the current best in the Ring setting. Our analysis for TS2-Net reveals a novel and insightful understanding of text clip retrieval, showing that refining learned features using a separate selector transformer can lead to a reduction in errors. This study also highlights the existence of a token shift bias that can be harnessed to reduce computational costs, suggesting potential applications of this bias in accelerated training and inference of TS2-Net. Our study demonstrates that TS2-Net learns better features than previous models and outperforms a newly-proposed baseline called CS-CLIP by properly selecting and refining features. It also presents an efficient version of TS2-Net, called Prune-TS2-Net, which achieves low memory requirements. Finally, our study presents an improved version of TS2-Net, called Refine-TS2-Net, which surpasses the current best result in the Ring setting of the GPT-2-Large model and establishes a new benchmark in the text clip retrieval field. Research suggests that this type of noise can significantly decrease developers' productivity and even their well-being. This study aims to investigate the perspective of software developers regarding this distraction, with a view to understanding its impact on their work. We conducted a survey of active developers and asked them to compare this distraction with knowledge pollution, with the intention of establishing whether this distraction is considered a serious problem by developers. The results of our survey indicate that a large majority of developers consider this distraction serious and several developers suggested practical solutions to mitigate its effect. We discovered that similar distractions, such as slow network, limited resources and faulty equipment, are considered serious by developers. This contrasts with findings from previous studies. We observed that lower priority tasks, including work related to animals and children, are considered non serious by developers. The views of software developers regarding this distraction are a reflection of their engineering ethos. We suggest a few possible explanations for their preference. Initially integrating the CKMMK2 parton shower module from KKMC, recent updates incorporate the W Shimodaira parton shower module and compatibility with the KNU electroweak corrections module. These enhancements ensure the KKMCee version is compatible with leading-order (LO), next-to-leading-order (NLO), and second-order (NLO+PS) precision in lepton collider environments. Furthermore, the KKMCee is cross-trained with CLHEP's hadron collider event data to optimize precision in large-scale simulations at lepton colliders. The KKMCee's range of capabilities includes electro-weak boson pair production, as well as heavy lepton and quark pair production, using both leading-order and next-to-leading-order precision in various lepton collider setups. We have developed a new stochastic method for approximating tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) through tensor singular value factorization (t-SVF). This approach iteratively transforms a tensor $\mathcal{X}$ to a form close to $\mathcal{X}$, where each step involves multiplying $\mathcal{X}$ by a partially computed factor. Our method is based on a stochastic algorithm for matrix SVD, with an analysis showing that it converges to the t-SVD of $\mathcal{X}$ at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$. We demonstrate its effectiveness on real-world datasets for matrices and 3D arrays. Moreover, we show that implementing this method using GPUs leads to notable speed improvements. Our findings are also highlighted by visualizations of the tensor's unfolding process. Interestingly, the empirical evidence suggests that even a single pass can produce useful approximations. Consequently, we propose using multiple passes as a means to trade computational cost for accuracy. Additionally, we investigated the computational efficiency of various tensor data representations and found that using compressed representations generally results in better performance, albeit a representation Strassen decomposition often facilitates faster CPU processing. Ultimately, the best results were achieved by combining CPU and GPU computing, which resulted in substantial reductions in execution time. The source code for our method has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/kevinalexander/tSVD_stochastic. As an additional contribution, the solution of a difficult open problem is provided: given two tensors of low rank, we have developed a method to approximate their rank by identifying a contraction that preserves tensor rank, with the ability to stop the contraction at any point and recover a rank-$k$ approximation of the original tensor. Consequently, the solution to certain problems, like tensor denoising, can be simplified by applying the rank-preserving contraction repeatedly until the tensor reaches the desired rank. Furthermore, the best results were achieved by manually selecting the tensor columns for contraction, rather than using any pre-defined criteria. Ultimately, the best results were achieved by simultaneously utilizing both CPU and GPU computing for tensor data representation independence. In our research, we investigate the challenge of effectively representing evolving networks using node embeddings. Unlike static graphs, evolving networks experience changes in their structure over time, often due to the entry or removal of nodes and edges. Current methods for embedding graphs are typically designed to work with static graphs and may not accurately capture the evolving relationships present in these networks. To address this limitation, we propose an innovative approach called AEgn, which updates the traditional node embedding method (PEM) to better perform on evolving networks. AEgn involves developing an edge embedding scheme that utilizes both temporal and structural information. By doing so, AEgn ensures that embedded nodes and edges are consistent across time points, ensuring the accurate representation of evolving networks. AEgn consists of several key components, including a novel objective function, a generalized Schur product, and a computational method for generating diverse embedding spaces. Our performance evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of AEgn in handling both low-density and high-density evolving networks. Moreover, AEgn outperforms existing methods by achieving higher accuracy using various benchmark datasets in tasks such as node classification and link prediction. The source code for AEgn is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhuoxiuv/AEgn. The code for generating the node attributes is available at our website at https://www.cs.reddy.eduhome.org/research/embedding-evolving-graphs. As such, our focus lies in determining the resonance energy relative to the $^3$H+4n threshold, rather than other possible $^7$H states. A new method has been introduced for training autoencoders in a distributed environment. This approach, referred to as the Distributed Optimal Transport AutoEncoder (DOAET), utilizes a variational autoencoder (VAE) to minimize the optimal transport cost. Unlike traditional methods that employ the mean squared error or binary cross-entropy loss, the proposed method reduces information loss and allows for the control of representation properties such as Gaussian noise robustness, distribution similarity, and low-dimensional similarity. To achieve this, the DOAET minimizes both the 1-Wasserstein and 2-Wasserstein distances between optimal transport matrices and those obtained from ambient samples. This is done by adding a penalty term to the ambient samples, calculated as the 1 or 2 stable sinkhorn distance, in a differentially private manner. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the DOAET model in reducing information loss and preserving structural properties of data. Moreover, the findings indicate that the representations produced by the DOAET possess greater accuracy compared to traditional methods. The proposed method has been successfully tested in a variety of domains including image data, IMDB movie plots, and Wikipedia articles' abstracts. Notably, the experiments show that the representations produced by the DOAET maintain their generalization capabilities even at extremely high compression ratios. The method's implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/andreab Rossi/daet_project. The project was supported by the Swiss Data Science Foundation (SDSC03004) and the Swiss Research Data Management Consortium (RDMA00). The data used in the experiments can be obtained from https://github.com/andreab Rossi/data-projects. The experimental results were achieved using the open-source library https://github.com/andreab Rossi/csplib, which provides the implementation of the stable sinkhorn distances as well as the differentially private variants. The library also includes an advanced implementation of the distributed optimal transport autoencoder proposed in the paper. The recent update of the library includes the implementation of a generalised version of the distributed optimal transport variational autoencoder proposed in https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.13911. The samples used in the experiments can be visualized through the interactive tool https://andreab.rossi/page/2022-09-16-OT-AE.html. This model aims to assess the inherent capabilities of each contact tracing strategy to mitigate viral spread, while also revealing how these local programs interacted with the national tiered system. In robotics, educating robots through guided adjustment is a common practice, 
particularly when adjusting cameras within reach to capture specific objects.
However, this process can be time-consuming and may not always be feasible.
We tackle this challenge by developing an end-to-end network that enables 
efficient, directly-seen image-based learning to position an on-board camera 
within reach. Given a fundamental understanding of the camera's characteristics 
and considering it as an external object within a 3D grasp environment, our 
method utilizes the current viewpoint and a single reference image to identify 
and visualize optimal camera adjustments. We evaluated our method's effectiveness 
using the OpenRAVE platform and discovered that our approach succeeds in 94.16% of cases 
when compared to a more complex, higher-capacity network. Furthermore, our method 
requires fewer parameters than more advanced techniques. We believe our method has 
practical implications for efficient, image-based learning to capture objects within 
reach for robots. The code for this research will be openly accessible on GitHub.

We propose a novel framework to reverse-engineer these policies through safe and efficient experimentation, leveraging the existing safety protocols in place. Our approach exploits the expert's natural caution in the safe zone, uncovering nuanced reward functions that accurately mirror the expert's decision-making process. We validate this approach with promising results on a variety of gridworld scenarios and demonstrate its practical applicability to a real-world financial application. The underlying code is publicly accessible for further development. Our approach is proven to yield a locally consistent model that mirrors the expert's behavior under certain conditions. Researchers have proposed multiple vertex effective vertex divider theorems in treewidth research. We have found that certain widely recognized treewidth boosters can be classified as space-effective, meaning they can operate with a memory requirement linear to n. We have established that any vertex effective vertex divider that fires t times is also space-effective, meaning it can accomplish this same number of firings with a memory requirement linear to n. We have introduced the concept of beta-effective vertex dividers and established the equivalence between beta-effectiveness and the ability to utilize bundle approaches, as proposed by Moghaddam and Wu. We have demonstrated that certain widely utilized vertex effective vertex dividers can be modified to be beta-effective, leading to the novel result that any beta-effective vertex divider that fires t times is also space-effective. We have further developed the strategy of repeatedly applying Suniyama's Half Integer Triangle Lemma to improve treewidth, resulting in the creation of a novel divide and conquer technique. We have successfully applied this technique to enhance the performance of the recently introduced Chuderkov-Cohen-Liu-Liu-Wu algorithm, with the aim of partitional refinement. Deep learning techniques have achieved significant success in processing imperfect data under various conditions, such as noise and outliers. This research focuses on the study of deep learning strategies for processing data with label corruption, a common phenomenon in real-world settings. Traditional machine learning algorithms are typically designed with robustness in mind, but this is less common in deep learning frameworks. Label corruption is equivalent to introducing noise into the training dataset, which can impact both the model's performance and its ability to generalize. This research examines methods for detecting and mitigating label corruption within graph neural networks, which have shown particular promise in handling complex and relational data. Graph neural networks are especially adept at processing graph and node-based data, making them ideal for applications such as network intrusion detection, knowledge graph completion, node classification, and graph completion. However, the underlying robustness principles of traditional graph-based machine learning algorithms are less clear in deep learning contexts. To address this, this research proposes novel frameworks for detecting label corruption during training and importing knowledge from existing models. This research utilizes reinforcement learning techniques to improve the robustness of graph neural networks in the presence of label corruption and explores adaptive techniques for selecting the most effective training data. Ultimately, this research improves the model's ability to generalize in cases of label corruption and reduces its reliance on susceptible dense models. Instead, this research proposes a more systematic approach by leveraging the advantages of sparse models that are naturally resistant to label corruption. To our knowledge, this research initiates the study of deep learning strategies for selecting noise-free training data in graph neural networks, which has the potential to broaden the application of dense models in settings where label corruption is prevalent. The research demonstrates the benefits of using sparse models in cases of label corruption and offers a framework for selecting and adapting transfer learning strategies to improve the robustness of dense models.
