The alignment of star catalogs is a crucial function that certain units within an astronomical organization can provide as a service to others. The process involves utilizing a set of landmarks found in all the catalogs and aiming to minimize the overall mean position discrepancy of these landmarks. A novel approach to this challenge is being proposed, drawing inspiration from the field of photometry and utilizing a method known as ZPZEst, which was initially developed primarily for astrometry. The ZPZEst estimator calculates the most effective way to adjust the positions of the catalogs to minimize displacement, combining information from multiple stars to achieve more accurate results. By incorporating more photometric data, a higher total signal strength can be achieved, resulting in significantly better alignment performance. The ZPZEst method's small scale factor is approximately 1.5, indicating that a ~25% increase in displacement error is necessary to justify a larger factor, providing a quantitative basis for this decision. The presented research demonstrates that utilizing supplementary photometry does not lead to a significant increase in dispersion for the alignments of various synthetic catalogues. Furthermore, using synthetic catalogs representing Gaia and Pan-STARRS1 datasets, the ZPZEst estimator with additional photometry demonstrated a ~30% reduction in displacement, whereas when applying a dispersion constraint, a ~50% reduction was achieved. The approach was also successfully tested using actual data from Gaia and Pan-STARRS1 datasets with adjusted astrometry, resulting in a ~30% reduction in displacement. The demonstrated framework is not limited to these two datasets and can be applied to other actual datasets with adjusted astrometry. The ZPZEst estimator with additional photometry was released as an open-source R package named 'AlignCat'. AlignCat can be used to align various star catalogs. Shifting towards a more general case, a theoretical framework is developed for calculating the most effective way to adjust the positions of the catalogs to minimize displacement, drawing inspiration from classic results in least-squares estimation. By assuming a multivariate normal photometry distribution, the most effective estimator has a covariance matrix proportional to the inverse of the astrometry covariance matrix, indicating a dependence on the dispersion in the star identification process. The derived expression for the most effective estimator was confirmed to be accurate. The theory was applied to a set of actual Gaia and Pan-STARRS1 datasets with adjusted astrometry. The calculated expressions for the most effective estimators have been released as an open-source R package named 'AlignCat'. AlignCat can be used to align various star catalogs

In this paper, we investigate thinness and minimality within infinite hypergraphs, specifically focusing on hypergraphs where every subset of a certain size is represented. We introduce and study two new hypergraph parameters, $ex_{1}^{k}$ and $ex_{<k}^{r}$, which facilitate the discussion on the minimality of infinite hypergraphs. We derive upper bounds for these values and demonstrate the effectiveness of these bounds through the construction of specific hypergraphs. Additionally, we show that hypergraphs meeting a particular condition have a degree of minimality that can be expressed in terms of these values. We further extend our research to hypergraphs where the number of hyperedges assigned to a given subset of a certain size is restricted. We introduce corresponding new parameters, $ex_{1}^{k,m}$ and $ex_{<k}^{r,m}$, and apply these to study the minimality of such hypergraphs. Ultimately, we examine the minimality of infinite hypergraphs where the colors of hyperedges assigned to a given subset of a certain size are restricted. We introduce corresponding new parameters, $ex_{1}^{k,m}$ and $ex_{<k}^{r,m}$, and establish upper and lower bounds for these values. A key finding of this study is that, despite the possibility of significant differences in the values of $ex_{1}^{k}$ and $ex_{<k}^{r}$, the values of $ex_{1}^{k,m}$ and $ex_{<k}^{r,m}$ tend to converge as $m$ increases. We discuss the implications of this finding and explore its applicability to the study of the minimality of colored hypergraphs defined by primitive sets. Specifically, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our bounds within two cases where the colors of hyperedges are either completely or partially defined. As a result, for colored hypergraphs where the colors of hyperedges in $F_{k}$ are completely defined, we find that the number of hyperedges does not exceed $ex_{1}^{k}+2^{k}-2$ and may be less than this value. Furthermore, for colored hypergraphs where the colors of edges in $F_{k}$ are partially defined and $F_{k}$ is non-empty, we find that the number of hyperedges does not exceed $ex_{<k}^{r}+\frac{2^{k}-1}{r}+2^{k}-2$ and may be less than this value. Recent advancements in deep learning based speech transcription models have shown improved performance, but these models are only effective when provided with extensive amounts of labeled data. We propose a novel method for creating a viable system for automatic speech transcription without sufficient transcription training. Our approach involves using a cycle-consistent deep learning framework to facilitate robust, unsupervised mappings between speech and text. Furthermore, we incorporate a novel penalty term into the training of the transcription model, thereby maintaining the inherent characteristics of a transcription loss function even in the absence of perfect transcription data. We evaluate our approach by comparing it with other widely used techniques, including an attention-based deep learning model, and a shallow network approach for automatic speech transcription. These comparisons demonstrate that our proposed method is a reliable solution for end-to-end automatic speech transcription in low resource environments. Crucially, we showcase the effectiveness of our approach by achieving an improvement of over 5% in WER when the amount of transcription training data is limited to just 2 hours. When applied to speech data with no correct references available, our approach achieves comparable results to Transcriptor - a state-of-the-art speech-to-text deep learning model, saving significant time and resources that would otherwise be spent on hours of transcription. Such hours are crucial in determining the viability of a deep learning model for automatic speech transcription. To investigate the influence of soft molecules' internal flexibility on their diffusion and migration, we performed simulations within a diffusing frame reference frame, allowing us to average over various configurations before and after the diffusion step. These simulations, conducted on fatty acid chains and esoteric combinations of bonds, revealed how flexible molecules respond to temperature gradients. A relative migration coefficient was developed to evaluate temperature-induced migration, and a thermal diffusion coefficient was defined as the ratio of migratory to diffusive transport. Our findings indicate that a species' migration can occur independently of its limited diffusion and that highly flexible molecules may exhibit reversed migration under certain temperature conditions, akin to observations in diatomic gases. Additionally, we discovered that variations in the thermal diffusion coefficient are closely related to the species' heat capacity and temperature sensitivity, explaining why temperature is a critical factor in the thermal diffusion and migration of flexible molecules. Finally, we explored the concept of pseudo-ideal mixtures, in which the species' thermal diffusion coefficients balance out, resulting from auto-correlated molecular movements that cancel out during migration events. These findings provide a theoretical foundation for evaluating the thermal diffusion and migration properties of complex, flexible molecules. A discussion on the measurement of thermal diffusion coefficients is also presented, along with proposals for experimental evaluation via NMR methods and nanosecond pulse polarization techniques. Music notation can be utilized for both educational and creative purposes, with research interests focusing on the automated evaluation of compositions to provide constructive feedback and streamline the creative process. Established methods, including the Cope metric and Generative Versus Human Models (GVHM), have been designed to gauge musical compositions' merit by comparing them to those created by human composers. These methods, however, primarily rely on local contextual self-attention mechanisms and overlook crucial aspects of compositions. This study introduces a novel method that leverants a different attention model, known as Localised Hierarchical Attention (LHA), to evaluate both local and global sequence features in compositions. The LHA model prioritizes novel and interesting ideas in contrast to those found in auto-generated music, even when the composer's intent is ambiguous. The performance of LHA-based models is compared to traditional models and those generated by language models in a thorough evaluation. The study further examines LHA's adaptability by training it on a lesser-quality dataset and applying it to the task of suggesting interesting musical ideas. The proposed approach outperforms existing methods by providing valuable, customizable, and adaptable metrics for music composition evaluation. We introduce an novel method, capable of generating multiple positive box candidates in a discriminative and discriminative-free manner. Our approach is based on the observation that only a subset of annotated boxes contributes significantly to the classification loss. Our unsupervised strategy selects the most influential box permutations from the training data, allowing us to synthesize novel positive samples through box reordering. Our experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, outperforming state-of-the-art unsupervised and semi-supervised approaches while also achieving comparable results to supervised proposals. Utilizing a random vector encoding model, we can isolate and isolate distinct elements of an image and create distinct textures and patterns by extracting and manipulating these features. To achieve unique effects, we apply random vector synthesis to combine these elements with a range of frequencies and timbres. This method allows real-time sonic integration of images, providing new visual-sonic correspondences, and is used to create original soundscapes in an experimental composition. Moreover, the potential for collaborative music-making through this process aligns with the principles of abstract expressionism. To further explore the potential for meaningful artistic integration, we examined in depth the ways in which two artists interpreted and interacted with the method, finding opportunities for significant artistic engagement and feedback loops. Ultimately, the paper outlines a framework for enabling two artists to work simultaneously on using images in music, with prospects for investigating the ways in which this process could be utilized in a competitive setting.

The traditional top-down parsing approach is being revitalized through integration with the latest neural language models, resulting in superior syntax preservation. Our proposed model, TTF-DOMIP, incorporates Tree Autoencoders with variable length syntactic links, which allows for linear tree structures and automatic detection of leaf nodes. Moreover, TTF-DOMIP utilizes a modified attention mechanism that focuses on multiple parent nodes and uses additional features from each potential parent to improve tree decoding. By being trained as a tree structured model, TTF-DOMIP outperforms other models in the interpretation and parsing of trees, especially in the task of constituent parsing according to the standard benchmarks. Furthermore, we have developed a new standard benchmark for constituent parsing called Grammatical Error Classification-Constituent Parsing (GECC-CP) which combines elements of parsing and grammar error correction, demonstrating the capabilities of TTF-DOMIE in this task. Our model's source code can be found on the following repository: https://github.com/EdouardMoussa/TTF-DOMIP.

A new web-based platform, the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAP), was created to help scientists determine the binding energy of molecules by comparing experimental and theoretical values. The BEAP hosts a database of free energy of hydrogen bonding and other types of noncovalent interactions, along with tools for calculating these energies using both experimental and theoretical methods. The BEAP allows researchers to assess the accuracy of their calculations and identify areas for improvement. To demonstrate the platform's effectiveness, we used it to analyze calculations of hydrogen bonding energy, confirming that theoretical values for the water-dimer binding energy of -6.0 kcal/mol were consistently high when compared to experimental values of -9.4 kcal/mol. We also showed how the BEAP could be used to evaluate the accuracy of a particular computational method, finding that its predictions for the binding energy of CO-CO interactions were significantly worse than those for the water dimer. Ultimately, we hope the BEAP will facilitate communication and provide valuable tools for researchers studying astrochemical binding energy, ultimately helping to advance the field. We're analyzing a multiplicative stochastic model with lower bounds, found in dynamic models describing how a signal spreads through a medium, such as infectious diseases or simply how a signal itself was generated. This type of model prevents the growth from dropping infinitely as time progresses, yet it offers no concrete guidance on the final lower limit, whose influence is typically significant. Therefore, determining this final limit manually from various models can be a daunting task. Faced with this challenge, we first establish two mathematical methods for predicting the final limit, one statistical and one structural. We demonstrate the accuracy of these methods by applying them to a Covid-19 tensor model and a signal propagation model, providing specific numerical examples. Additionally, we discovered an unexpected property - the expectation of the final limit is directly proportional to the initial value of the corresponding initial equation. This property is validated through both the Covid-19 tensor model and the signal propagation model. Consequently, this model allows for the inclusion of lower bounds in the ordinary multiplicative stochastic model, enabling a smooth transition from pure stochastic to deterministic behavior. Moreover, it accommodates a wider range of initial values by preventing the growth from dropping infinitely as time progresses. Lastly, its realistic outcomes are facilitated by the minimal additional parameters required. Ultimately, this model may find more practical applications in the future. Analyzing the scenarios of outward and inward soliton configurations, the behavior of the reflection coefficient is determined for large wave number magnitudes, and an unexpected dependence on wave number direction is observed. This research reveals that the reflection coefficient can never change sign. Additionally, an analytical model is developed to study the behavior of the reflection coefficient under a weak perturbation regime, and it's compared to numerical results using the direct integration method. Furthermore, it's numerically demonstrated that the solutions to the Davey-Stewartson II equations exhibit a new type of resonance phenomenon, and it's proposed that this strong resonance is a universal attribute of nonlinear Schrödinger equations with multiple soliton initial conditions. Lastly, a comparison of our direct integration model with the solutions to these equations is shown to successfully account for the strong resonance phenomenon. The importance of considering the multicomponent NLS equations in their natural form, particularly in relation to the strength of the resonance, is also emphasized. In the process of this investigation, a note regarding the accuracy of the dsII-FFT model for the TSII equation is provided. Consequently, a numerical method is proposed to distinguish between cases where the solutions exhibit positive, zero, or negative values for the reflection coefficient. In the realm of machine learning, meta-learning focuses on leveraging knowledge gained from previous experiences to streamline the discovery of new models. This research aims to develop meta-learning within the context of supervised learning for function approximation, considering only linear representations as the underlying model. By making this linear assumption, the associated computational problems become significantly more manageable. This study introduces a novel, prototypical approach to bias introduction at the feature level, enabling diverse data transformations to be represented as linear in relation to the target features. Due to the robustness of linear models, the predicted functions for varied levels of bias are co-linear. Consequently, a solution to this problem is to update the bias introduction mechanism solely based on the prediction's normal vector. Initially, we propose a meta-learning algorithm where a high-level learning system, dubbed 'Meta-Teacher,' aids a low-level learning system, 'Base-Learner,' by introducing an additional objective to minimize the angle between the base learner's prediction and the introduced bias. Notably, the 'Meta-Teacher' is an online learning entity that adapts to various data distributions. This research provides a new perspective on the role of bias in function approximation and showcases that both the 'Meta-Teacher' and base learner entities are learnable in an online, online-first setting. Next, we present a robust and efficient algorithm for solving 'Meta-Teacher's' objective by introducing a model-to-model distributionally robust optimization strategy that can effectively handle a variety of data distributions. This approach is a combination of two conventional techniques: convergence through data averaging and regularization of the regularization parameter. By adopting the MMO framework, we can derive a closed-form solution for updating the meta-bias introduced by the 'Meta-Teacher,' resulting in a highly efficient computational process. Finally, we compare the performance of the proposed algorithm with existing function approximators, such as RFF and SRL, on four realistic applications: multi-level graph fingerprint prediction, 3D point cloud representation, electronic structure calculation, and audio classification, showcasing that it significantly outperforms the baseline methods. Moreover, the research demonstrates the existence of a prototypical approach to bias introduction at the feature level, denoted as 'SLMO,' which is applicable to a wide array of supervised learning tasks and function approximators, resulting in a marked improvement of the prediction accuracy for these models. The proposed algorithm effectively minimizes the prediction's normal vector's angle with the introduced bias, resulting in improved robustness and variability of the predictions. Utilizing small language models has gained significant attention due to its cost-effective potential for NLP tasks, especially when dealing with limited data sources. Achieving model size reductions through knowledge distillation while minimizing performance losses has become a primary focus. This research compares two primary methods for reducing model size: quantization and post-training adaptation. Initially, we employed quantization to create smallMT models by applying different quantization configurations to the existing base models, evaluating their performance using the WMT metrics. Notably, we discovered that smallMT models created through word-quantization achieved a mean BLEU score of 22.2, only 0.7 below the corresponding largeMT models on the English-Swedish WMT19 dataset. This impressive result suggests that large MT models can effectively utilize a relatively small number of unique words, thereby reducing model size without compromising translation quality. To complement this approach, we also explored the concept of lightweight MT models using pre-trained models with different tokenization settings, specifically by reducing wordpiece tokenizations and increasing word tokenizations to minimize performance losses. Similar to the word-quantization results, we discovered that our approach yielded a mean BLEU score of 22.3 on the WMT19 dataset. Ultimately, we observed that modifying the tokenization of large MT models can efficiently create smallMT models without requiring a separate training process, thereby making low-resource MT more feasible. Building on this concept, we are currently evaluating post-training adaptation as a means to mitigate losses incurred during tokenization modifications. This involves creating adaptation smallMT models using MT model compression, MT model pruning, and memory optimization techniques that minimize performance degradation. To accelerate the development of smallMT models for low-resource MT, we are exploring an automated pipeline that automatically creates these models from large MT models, leveraging adversarial robustness to optimize translation performance in low-resource scenarios. The detection and classification of pulmonary issues are facilitated by computer-aided analysis, which involves a reliable diagnostic technique to detect early and late stages of lung diseases. However, the reliability of such tools is contingent on ample data, which can be costly to procure, particularly in low-resource settings. This study investigates the viability of using image enhancement techniques to decrease the necessity for labeled data in the context of pneumo-skeleton segmentation. Initially, the proposed method applies Gaussian distribution-based noise and sharpening operations to simulate real-world imaging conditions, which are based on previous research. Following this, pulmonary structure detection is executed using an amalgamation of region growth and part-specific identification. The subsequent steps involve using the combined structures to perform pneumomiaspecific detection. As demonstrated in the results section, the proposed method yields accurate pneumo-skeleton detection with an accuracy of 85.76%, while reducing required labeled data by 67%. The study also examines the influence of varying amounts of noisy data and the efficacy of distinct noise types on the final results. The experimental framework was grounded in evaluating the impact of noise on the reliability of medical image analysis, which is an area of growing concern in the field. The provided code serves to facilitate future research. Captions within images possess a higher semantic value when compared to their visual content, especially in understanding what an image is depicting. Although it is feasible for captions to contain errors, ProfoundPrompt, a state-of-the-art image description model, achieves remarkable results by leveraging large datasets and image quality enhancements. Upon closer inspection, we notice that ProfoundPrompt's outstanding performance and robust image robustness capabilities make it impractical for interpretation due to its massive size of 3.5 billion parameters. In response, we introduce a novel approach that combines a conventional image encoder with a smaller language generator, keeping the model's size under 220 million parameters. Our evaluation demonstrates that this integrated model, referred to as CausalVisuer, surpasses ProfoundPrompt in image description quality and achieves comparable robustness levels, all while reducing its size by nearly 93%. Furthermore, CausalVisuer lies within the top 10% for image robustness among all models it surpasses in quality and description, showcasing its exceptional capabilities. In extension, we explore the possibilities of incorporating our approach to other large pre-trained models characterized by their large size and complexity. In this case study, we adapt our methodology to support the application of large text generators to machine translation, a task. Our findings indicate that this adaptation results in substantial size reductions across a range of well-known translation models. Ultimately, our work promotes the concept that top-tier NLP models do not need to be overly massive. Instead, their size can be assessed based on their functional capabilities, allowing other models to be considered as viable solutions. Our code for CausalVisuer is publicly available at: https://github.com/InsertNameHere/CausalVisuer. We outline the capabilities provided by this integration, including automated model loading, prediction, tuning, and scaling. These capabilities are demonstrated through a series of experiments involving the training of Spark-scale neural networks in AzureML environments. Low voltage grid management is becoming increasingly complex due to growing consumption variability, which poses significant challenges to traditional distribution network designs. Effective low voltage grid management requires accurate short-term load forecasting, but this task is complicated by limited information and high forecasting errors. We examined the unique characteristics of low voltage grid load forecasts, which exhibit substantial day-to-day and time-of-day fluctuations. A key feature of low voltage grid load is its tendency to peak in the morning and afternoon euros, making effective forecasting crucial to navigating these periods. We developed a two-stage model combining individual forecast performances and population data to create robust EU forecasts. Our approach aligns with the principles of industrial machine learning and relies on real-world EU data from a major low voltage grid. We demonstrated the need for morning and afternoon forecasts within a specific time frame and stressed the importance of account-to-account correlation in EU forecasts. Our method produced EU forecasts with less than 2% error and an overprediction rate of less than 1.5%. This research highlights the requirements for successful low voltage grid forecasting and outlines the potential implications of these demands. Additionally, we provide our code and use cases so that others may replicate and expand upon our research in low voltage grid forecasting. Our methodology can easily be adapted for application in other fields. We discuss possible extensions to our model, such as data exchange among accountants and the assessment of forecast performance by clients. Our research demonstrates that a well-designed forecasting challenge can effectively assess a classifier's ability to generalize. Furthermore, it illustrates the concept's potential can be evaluated and its intermediate steps understood. Moreover, our study shows that a large enough dataset can effectively capture the inherent characteristics of a specific problem. Our model's success stems from its ability to minimize bias and emphasize aspects of a problem with limited training samples. Our research encourages other industries to develop their own forecasting challenges and risk assessments. Our model's failure to require domain-specific data and terminology shows its adaptability and potential for application in a wide variety of fields. However, our study's complexity also serves as a good benchmark for semantic parsing and can help other industries and researchers achieve state-of-the-art results in their specific domains. Our code and data for the low voltage grid forecasting challenge can be found at https://github.com/aparturek/forecast_combination. Our work at LinkedIn on CTR prediction can be found at https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/predicting-click-through-rate-ctr-models/. The integration of domain expertise in machine learning has become a crucial factor
for achieving successful models. This integration presents unique challenges, 
primarily because domain and machine learning professionals operate in distinct
mannerisms. While both sides share the same goal, they are confronted with
different problems, utilizing diverse terminology and following distinct 
methodologies. Prior research attempts to address this gap by providing a framework
for transferring domain expertise to machine learning settings; however, this 
effort is hindered by limited participation from domain experts in machine 
learning partnerships, coupled with difficulties encountered by machine 
learning professionals when decomposing domain data. This study offers a step-by-
step guide on incorporating domain knowledge into machine learning. First, it 
explores common difficulties encountered during domain data decomposition. Next, it 
proposes a straightforward methodology for this task and provides a sample 
illustration. Finally, the study reflects on the importance of organizing ML-DI 
workshops to foster collaboration and knowledge exchange between the two fields. 
By outlining a clear roadmap, this paper aims to promote successful ML-DI 
collaborations and bridge the existing gap between domain and machine learning 
experts. Additionally, it suggests including domain-based features in public 
datasets to facilitate ML-DI partnerships. Lastly, by offering a comprehensive 
guide on incorporating domain knowledge into machine learning, this paper aims to 
reduce the difficulties typically encountered by machine learning professionals. 
Using knowledge from computational neuroscience and genomics, this paper shows 
how domain features can be utilized in these fields. A key finding of this study 
is that domain features positively impact lighting conditions in both fields. 
This paper also explores potential automated integration points for future research. 
Ultimately, by outlining a blueprint for ML-DI partnerships, this paper aims to 
facilitate successful and effective ML-DI collaborations and bridge the 
existing gap between domain and machine learning experts. A related project is

COVID-19, caused by SARS-CoV-2, has become one of the most significant global health issues since 2020. Analyzing chest computed tomography (CT) scans plays a crucial role in understanding the progression and variations of the disease. Researchers have been working to develop accurate methods for analyzing COVID-19, but most existing techniques require large amounts of manually labeled data to train sophisticated deep learning models capable of analyzing lung lesions. Unfortunately, collecting such labels can be time-consuming and costly. To address this challenge, we propose a new learning method that utilizes weakly labeled data, including whole-lung masks to help in detecting and precisely defining lung lesions in COVID-19 cases. This new approach can leverage large amounts of unlabelled data and whole-lung masks, significantly speeding up the process. We use the FEUNet, a tried and tested framework for detecting and defining lesions, and introduce two novel losses that utilize whole-lung masks to guide learning. We also propose to utilize whole-lung masks to generate partial labels to enable semi-supervised learning. Our model, named Masked-FEUNet, offers improved performance compared to other models, including the standard FEUNet and other state-of-the-art networks, particularly in accurately defining lesions and comparing lung densities. Our study is supported by a large, the first publicly available dataset of COVID-19 and control subjects, each with whole-lung masks, whole-lung lesions, and precise definitions of lesions to serve as training data. This new dataset enables researchers to develop partially-guided learning algorithms to analyze medical data in the absence of complete labels. You can obtain the dataset through this link. Our source code is available at https://github.com/pointware/PW-MaskedFEUNet. The models we developed are available on https://dove.med.louisiana.edu. To verify our findings, a virtual experiment was conducted using our proposed framework. The results show that our method for analyzing lung lesions is accurate and reliable, with an DL_{s} score of 0.3562, a Tim/Spc of 0.6422, a Tim/Dl score of 0.5875 and a mean Dice score of 0.60. Our findings also highlight the importance of partial whole-lung masks in facilitating learning to analyze lung lesions. The proposed algorithm achieved a significant increase in accuracy, with a mean Dice score of 0.60 compared to the baseline FEUNet and other state-of-the-art networks, demonstrating its efficacy for analyzing lung lesions

Accurate vertebrae identification is crucial in various medical applications related to spine surgery, disease diagnosis, and radiographic measurement. However, standard techniques face challenges with incomplete or distorted scans, incorrect initial positions, or inadequate markings. To address these limitations, a novel approach to automatic vertebrae identification is presented, minimizing the need for user input. This method initializes vertebrae with a rectified spine contour and a corresponding label, and through a proprietary cost function, it optimizes the vertebrae alignment and rotation. Once the vertebrae are correctly positioned, a classification module determines the type and number of vertebrae. This approach is enhanced by anatomically constrained enhancement, increasing its robustness in scenarios with missing discs or distorted structures. By testing the method with 42 cervical X-rays and X-ray scans, a high degree of accuracy was demonstrated. Additionally, the research team evaluated its performance using a dataset comprising 304 CT scans, achieving 95.8% accuracy in identification, and a mean deviation of 1.3 degrees in terms of endplate position. Furthermore, the method received a score of 0.91 in terms of its modified metropolitan ankle/hip alignment metric. This proposed method is shown to outperform existing techniques with a greater degree of accuracy in vertebrae identification. Based on its performance, the approach is considered suitable for complex up and down scrolling case in X-rays, and is also capable of handling various types of vertebral anomalies. The research team is confident that with further enhancements, the method will be effective in CT scans with complex vertebral structures. Electrons radiating keV-scale photons in a strongly coupled cavity experience an unusual form of quantum stabilization. This stabilization results in an incredibly long lifetime for electrons, which is characterized by an unusual lag between the electron's emission and radiation. This phenomenon arises from the vacuum oscillation in the cavity, causing a transient quantum state characterized by high coherence and deep non-classical characteristics, featuring excess negativity in its Gaussian representation. To study this highly coupled cavity, we investigate resonant scattering, which allows us to reveal the hidden features of the quantum state through the analysis of emitted photons. Our analysis indicates that the number of emitted photons follows a Q^2 pattern, while the energy distribution displays sudden variations around the resonant peak. Moreover, we have discovered that the quantum stabilization period can be determined by the duration of vacuum oscillation, which is influenced by the cavity's transmission coefficient. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the role of vacuum oscillation in the stabilization of open quantum systems. Furthermore, the consequences of vacuum oscillation may contribute to the development of extremely strong light-matter coupling schemes, potentially leading to the creation of entangled states with increased energy coronas. This development of light-matter coupling research could also pave the way for advancements in quantum information processing. To bring this concept closer to practical realization, we suggest a plan for optimistically achieving the ELMMC state by numerically designing a cavity with a quantum bit located near its extremity. This plan involves constructing the cavity from materials with low loss rates and utilizing a topological structure to inhibit the propagation of photons, effectively creating an extremely strong light-matter coupling regime. Our theoretical model indicates that the ELMMC state could be realized under specific conditions for months to years, where the significant effects on the system would be observable for minutes to ongoing periods of time. This work offers a pioneering example of the potential for entanglement and is a significant development in the field of light-matter coupling research. Moreover, in the physical context of the scattering process, we have discovered an extremely strong light-matter coupling regime in which the role of vacuum oscillations is similar to the Landau-Khalatnikov effect in the Faraday configuration. This regime could be achieved through an induced anomalous dispersion, resulting in the lags being detected at the photon energies of Rabi splitting. This research explores the potential of using highly-elastic actuators in legged systems' mobility, utilizing a quadruped robot built with these actuators to improve upon traditional rigid actuators. Traditional Euclidean-based control strategies are shown to be insufficient due to the dynamic motion of the actuators' tips causing inconsistent trajectory tracking. To overcome this limitation, we establish a novel phase delay model that accurately predicts this dynamic motion, allowing us to develop a control strategy that capitalizes on the actuators' elasticity for enhanced mobility. By optimizing the tip speed and phase delay, our elastic actuator-based quadruped can match or surpass the speed achieved by traditional rigid actuators. Furthermore, our elastic actuator-based quadruped can maintain stability at a higher speed, exhibiting a 10% improvement in gait stability. To validate the effectiveness of our method, we conducted a series of gait experiments on the built quadruped robot, demonstrating our findings. The code supporting these findings, including the elastic phase delay model and the developed control strategy, has been made available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/CATLAB-project/Elastic-Actuators-4LeggedRobots. In the realm of fashion, where images, shapes, and styles intertwine, retrieving images with similar styles poses an additional challenge beyond standard image retrieval tasks. Traditional methods focus on manipulating image properties such as color, style, and shape, but a lesser-known aspect is altering fashion traits like sleeve type, collar style, and garment type. This work aims to pioneer a novel paradigm for extracting fashion trait embeddings from data and demonstrating the effectiveness of these embeddings in retrieving fashion images. Unlike existing methods that rely solely on labeled data, our proposal leverages both supervised and unsupervised examples to extract embeddings. This is made possible by a deep-mining method that identifies unlabeled images with visible fashion traits without human annotation, followed by the extraction of these traits and the embedding of unseen images. To validate our proposal, we created a dataset called FashionTraityBank comprising a large collection of fashion images adorned with visible fashion traits. Our proposal has successfully extracted fashion trait embeddings from this dataset, yielding an impressive 51.0% boost in retrieval accuracy compared to the current state of the art. Furthermore, our proposal enables the manipulation of fashion trait embeddings to achieve superior results, with manipulated embeddings yielding a 67.4% improvement in retrieval accuracy over baseline methods. Ultimately, our proposal embodies a pioneering semi-supervised fashion image retrieval approach that utilizes fashion trait embeddings to great effect. The research code and FashionTraityBank dataset are available for download on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/wugrad/FashionTraityBank. Moreover, our research model allows for the discovery of the spatial correlation between extracted fashion trait embeddings, paving the way for future research to utilize these embeddings as prior knowledge to synthesize novel fashion images. The research model and generated embeddings are available for download on our demo website at https://FashionTraityBank.github.io. We are studying the effectiveness of using IEEE 802.11k/v standards in enhancing WiFi networks, particularly in optimizing performance by allowing the dynamic reorganization of access points and extenders within the network. To achieve this, we leverage channel load data to determine the optimal configuration. Our method collects data on channel usage across the network and visualizes it through a minimum spanning tree graph, indicating high-usage channels and thus inefficiently utilized resources. By strategically relaying the extenders to improve their line of sight with the access points, we can reduce interference and increase data transmission speeds. Our results demonstrate a significant improvement in network throughput, with up to a 25% increase in 60 MHz networks and a 35% increase in 20 MHz networks, without altering the physical setup of the network. Additionally, we found that our method outperforms a comparison industry solution, even when utilized without the IEEE 802.11k/v metrics. Furthermore, we take into account the limitations of practical implementation and offer suggestions for how to effectively deploy IEEE 802.11k/v in real-world applications. In addition to these suggestions, we provide a decision-making algorithm for choosing between installing an access point or extender, based on the analysis of channel usage and network coverage. Our method is validated through experiments conducted in both controlled environments with multiple devices and real-world settings with various obstructions such as walls and furniture. Our results are made publicly available through our repository on github, including the data, the configuration of the access points and extenders, the visualization tools and the code for channel load analysis. Our code is also deployed on our website where users can access the visualization tools and configure their own WiFi network. Using the tool, we were able to determine that the optimal configuration is often not the one that provides the absolute best line of sight with the access points, due to the interference caused by the channel load. Therefore, the optimal configuration is best represented by a trade-off between the quality of the line of sight and the coverage area of the access points. Our method is especially useful in real-world scenarios, where the optimal configuration is not the one that provides the absolute best line of sight.
